en: The *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*, Scroll One:
The *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* encompasses the great principles of the eight classes of Mahāyāna scriptures and accords with the essential tenets of all sūtras.
That which it elucidates concerns exclusively the eternal fruit, the Buddha-nature, and the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the cause:

when the nature of the fulfillment of the cause is manifested, there is a responsive engagement with the world; therefore, the eight classes of the *Prajñāpāramitā* were taught, using ten kinds of meanings to explain and counteract ten [obstructions].

The first part, consisting of one hundred thousand verses, is the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (*Dapin*); the second part, consisting of twenty-five thousand verses, is the *Prabhāsa-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (*Fangguang*); the third part, consisting of eighteen thousand verses, is the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (*Guangzan*); the fourth part, consisting of eight thousand verses, is the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (*Daoying*); the fifth part, consisting of forty thousand verses, is the *Svalpākṣara-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (*Xiaopin*); the sixth part, consisting of two thousand five hundred verses, is the *Devaparipṛcchā-sūtra* (*Tianwangwen*); the seventh part, consisting of six hundred verses, is the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (*Wenshu*); and the eighth part, consisting of three hundred verses, is this very *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
These are the names of the eight sections.
In the preceding seven sections, the elimination of conceptual signs was not yet complete, so they were simply titled "Prajñā";
in this eighth section, the elimination of conceptual signs is most thorough, and thus it is established separately under the name "Vajra."
The first part was spoken by the Tathāgata five years after his attainment of enlightenment in the city of Rājagṛha.
The next five parts were also spoken in Rājagṛha.
The seventh and eighth parts were spoken in the city of Śrāvastī.
In this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, it is solely Subhūti who is inspired to pose the questions and the Tathāgata who provides the answers.
Regarding the ten obstacles:
the first is the obstacle of the mark of non-existence (*avastu-nimitta*).
As it is taught in the Prajñā[pāramitā], all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, even up to nirvāṇa, are empty.
Sentient beings do not understand this and give rise to the view of annihilationism, claiming that all phenomena do not exist.
Regarding the antidote to this hindrance, the Buddha told Subhūti:
"There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) up to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."

And so forth. Regarding the antidotes within this sutra, they are found in the third section, where the sutra states: "The bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on things," and so on; this dispels the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
Second, there is the obstruction of the characteristic of existence.
When sentient beings hear the Tathāgata say that there are bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās, they become attached and give rise to the view of eternalism, asserting that all dharmas exist.
Regarding the antidote to this hindrance, the Buddha told Subhūti:
"A bodhisattva does not perceive a self as a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the various pāramitās," and so forth.

In this sutra, the "antidote" refers to the section on practice; the sutra states, "If a bodhisattva gives rise to the notion of a sentient being or the notion of a person, they are not a bodhisattva," which dispels the view of eternalism.

Third, regarding the obstruction of that which is non-existent appearing as existent: the Tathāgata says that all phenomena such as form are existent; if they were truly existent, he should not further say that all phenomena are empty.
Regarding the antidote to this hindrance, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The essential nature and characteristics of all phenomena, such as form and so forth, are empty; they are like a mirage—non-existent yet appearing to exist. Thus it was said.
In this sutra, the "antidote" refers to the removal of the view of real existence held by ordinary persons who are greedily attached to things and so forth.
How does this third [section] differ from the first?
The first section above generally clarifies that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) do not exist because all dharmas are empty;
this third section specifically clarifies the emptiness of conditioned dharmas.
However, a doubter may say:
If all phenomena are empty, why can they be perceived and yet possess utility?
This is because they are distinct [from one another].
Fourth is the obscuration of the characteristic of slander.

The King heard the Tathāgata say that the essence and characteristics of all phenomena, such as form, are empty like a mirage—neither existent nor non-existent, yet appearing as if they were. Failing to understand this, sentient beings gave rise to slanderous thoughts, claiming that even the Buddha-nature, nirvāṇa, and unconditioned dharmas are likewise empty of nature and devoid of substance, just like conditioned phenomena. If this were so, there would be no one who could practice or attain the fruit of realization.
This demonstrates the remedy; the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"It is not emptiness-emptiness," and so forth.

Regarding the antidote within this sūtra, it refers to the section on the emptiness of all phenomena as the sixth, which states that there is also no characteristic of non-existence, thereby dispelling the view of emptiness.
How does this fourth hindrance differ from the first and second?
The first [section] clarifies that all phenomena, both conditioned and unconditioned, are empty; the third specifically clarifies that conditioned phenomena are empty;

this fourth [section] clarifies only that the essence of the wondrous existence of unconditioned phenomena is empty because it lacks the ten thousand marks, which is different from conditioned phenomena being empty because they lack intrinsic nature.
This is what constitutes their difference.
Fifth, there is the obstruction of a single characteristic:
when they hear the Tathāgata say that form is empty, sentient beings give rise to the thought that there is form distinct from emptiness.
Regarding the antidote to this hindrance, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"That which is empty is not form," and so forth.
In this sutra, the antidote refers to such passages as "that which is a unified whole is inexpressible," which dispel the very perception [of such a whole].
Sixth is the obstacle of the characteristic of distinct existence.
When the Tathāgata previously stated that emptiness is not form, sentient beings did not understand and claimed that there is a separate emptiness distinct from form.
To counteract this obstacle, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"There is no form apart from emptiness."
"Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form," and so forth. In this sutra,
the remedies refer to such statements as, "Therefore, the Buddha taught that all phenomena are without self, without person, and without sentient beings," which dispel erroneous views.
Seventh is the obstacle of the appearance of real existence.

Having heard the Tathāgata’s previous teaching that the essence of the ten thousand dharmas is empty because they are void, one asks: "For what reason does the Buddha say that form and all other dharmas exist?"
Regarding the antidote to this hindrance, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"All phenomena such as form possess only names and functions," and so forth.

In this sutra, the remedies refer to such statements as, "The Tathāgata says that 'motes of dust' are not motes of dust, and 'worlds' are not worlds," which dispel the views of the retributive teachings.
How does this seventh [section] differ from the first, third, and fourth above?
Herein, the clarification of emptiness is not different from what precedes; it merely provides a method for raising an objection.
If it were empty, for what reason would the Tathāgata say that it exists?
It is on this basis that they differ.
Eighth is the obstruction of mutually distinct characteristics.

I have heard the Tathāgata say that the essence and characteristics of all phenomena, such as form and so forth, are empty and exist merely as names and functions. If the minds and phenomena of sentient beings, such as form and so forth, were empty, they should not undergo arising, abiding, and ceasing;
if there were truly arising, abiding, and ceasing, then they would not be empty.
Regarding the antidote to this hindrance, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"All dharmas are neither produced, nor abiding, nor extinguished; they are neither pure nor defiled.
Such are his teachings.
Regarding the antidotes within this sutra, they are explained in the seventh section of the *Pramāṇabhāga*: "For what reason?
Because the departure from all phenomena is itself called the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas," and so forth; this dispels the view of the existence of signs (*nimittadṛṣṭi*).
Ninth is the obstacle of the characteristics of names and meanings.
When the Tathāgata says that all phenomena such as form are visible and tangible, sentient beings give rise to the thought:
"As is the name, so too is the meaning; it is likewise visible and tangible."
Regarding the antidote to this obstacle, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
“All phenomena are merely names and provisional designations,” and so forth.
In this sūtra, the antidote refers to such statements as, “In reality, there is no dharma called ‘bodhisattva’”; this dispels the view that clings to the meaning of the retribution based on names.
Tenth is the obstacle of names and characteristics according to their meanings.
As the Tathāgata has previously stated that dharmas such as form are quiescent and empty, existing merely as provisional designations of names;
yet, if this were so, sentient beings would give rise to the following thought:
As it is with meaning, so it is with names; because there is meaning, there are names.
If there were no meaning, how could there be names?
To counteract this obstacle, the Buddha told Subhūti:
"A bodhisattva does not perceive any names.
Because they do not perceive any names, they do not cling to any referents," and so forth.

In this sūtra, the remedy is found in the eleventh section, which states: "All conditioned phenomena are like stars, a medical lamp, a reflection, and a magical illusion. This serves to eliminate the view that clings to names based upon their referents.
Because of these ten obstacles, the eight sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā* were taught so that omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) may be ultimately fulfilled.
Why are these ten called "obstacles"?
Because each one, either individually or by its very nature, is capable of obstructing true understanding; therefore, they are collectively termed "obstacles."
Regarding the term "Vajra," it is named after a metaphor, taking its meaning from its solidity and firmness, like the *vajra* of the mundane world. It has two meanings:
first, its substance is solid and firm, capable of shattering all things; [the second is that it cannot be destroyed by anything].
Second, the myriad phenomena cannot destroy the vajra;
this clarifies that the unconditioned *dharmakāya* at the stage of fruition, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, and the wisdom of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) likewise possess two meanings:
First, it can crush the demonic enemies and destroy all afflictions;
second, no demons or afflictions can dismember or destroy it.
Therefore, it is named "Vajra."
Furthermore, because ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles cannot understand or enter into this principle and teaching, it is also called "Vajra.
"Prajñā" is the authentic pronunciation from the Western Land (India); here in Wei, it is transliterated as "Huìmíng" (Wisdom-Illumination).
This vajra-like signlessness is the ultimate principle; its essence is true reality (*tathatā*).

Because wisdom can illuminate and penetrate the source of this principle, comprehend the characteristics of all phenomena, and manifest the eternally abiding fruit of Buddhahood, it is called *prajñā*.
"Pāramitā" (Bōluómì) means "reaching the other shore," as translated in the Wei dynasty.

This clarifies that the principle expounded by this sutra is the essence of the eternally abiding Dharmakāya, the other shore; because it enables sentient beings to cross the river of birth and death and reach the other shore of Nirvāṇa, it is called "Pāramitā."
Regarding the term "Sūtra," earlier scholars traditionally explained it as "constant.
According to the authentic texts from the Western Regions (India), it is called *sūtra*.
If one were to propagate its name, in foreign lands it is called *sūtra*, while here in this land it is propagated as "root" (*ben*).
This clarifies that both principle (*li*) and teaching (*jiao*) possess a fundamental meaning.

Regarding principle as the foundation: it clarifies that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) principle of the realized Dharma (*dharmasākṣātkṛta*) serves as the basis for the verbal teachings of the twelve divisions of the scriptures; therefore, principle is called the foundation.

Regarding "taking the teaching as the basis": this clarifies that by investigating these verbal teachings, one is able to attain the realized Dharma; therefore, it is said that the verbal teaching serves as the basis for the realized Dharma.
Thus, the teaching is taken as the basis.
Therefore, what is now called "sūtra" (jīng) is not merely a popularized name.
Rather, for those here, the meaning of the character "jīng" clarifies the locus of the *sūtranta*, and thus it is called "jīng."
Regarding the "Treatise" (Lun): during the period after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there was a Mahāsattva of noble conduct named Vasubandhu, which in Wei is translated as Tianqin.

This person is truly a Bodhisattva of great expedient means, manifesting in form to transform beings universally and having fully perceived the intent of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings spoken throughout the Tathāgata’s entire life.

Because the textual phrases of this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* are extremely concise while its meaning is profoundly vast, worldly people are unable to understand these deep and wondrous meanings; therefore, for the sake of sentient beings, he has composed this treatise as an explanatory commentary on the meaning.

Regarding why these two verses are established at the beginning of the treatise: the author, Vasubandhu, intending to compose this treatise to explain the profound and subtle meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, must first clarify the essence of the Dharma and place it at the outset of the treatise, as well as honor the Buddha and the Saṃgha at the head of the scripture; otherwise, how could he compose a treatise to explain the profound meaning of this sutra?

However, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, whenever the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and great masters of treatises wished to compose extensive commentaries on the Buddha’s authentic scriptures, there were none who did not first take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem, invoking its spiritual majesty before composing their treatises.
The general purport of these two verses lies herein.
Within these two verses, they are divided into two sections:
the first consists of one and a half verses (six lines), clarifying the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem.
The two lines of the latter half of the verse explain the meaning of paying homage.
Within the first six lines, the preceding line clarifies that the principle and teaching of this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* are profound and subtle; this is the very essence of the Dharma Jewel.

The second phrase clarifies that since the principle and teaching of the aforementioned Dharma-gate are profound, worldly fools are unable to understand them; this refers precisely to those who do not comprehend.

The third phrase clarifies that both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to penetrate [this principle]; this reveals the two jewels of the Buddha and the Sangha, who are those capable of providing the explanation.

The fourth phrase indicates that because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to penetrate this principle, they instruct us that we ought to practice the teachings; this is the obstacle of disrespecting the teacher.
The fifth and sixth lines re-explain the meaning of paying homage.
The two lines of the second half-verse specifically explain that the Bodhisattva possesses virtues worthy of veneration.
"Dharma" functions by means of its normative standard (*viniyoga*).
Furthermore, "Dharma" is defined as the non-loss of its own characteristic (*svarūpa*).
What is this characteristic of the Dharma's own essence such that it is said not to be lost?

This Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā is a profound and wondrous Dharma capable of preventing the unrighteousness of birth and death, ensuring that sentient beings do not fall into the three evil realms. It enables sentient beings to attain the fruits of the two vehicles of humans and devas, and ultimately allows them to fulfill the practices of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) to achieve the supreme bliss of Buddhahood; therefore, it is called the "Dharma."

"Gate" (môn) means that both this principle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* and its teaching are able to serve as a passage for the practitioner to travel afar and reach the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, it is called a "gate."
"Phrases" (pada) refer to this teaching that can express the diamond-like Prajñāpāramitā.
"Meaning" (artha) refers to the principle realized through what is expressed.

It is clarified that the principle and teaching of this Prajñā are profound and subtle; they cannot be understood by the mind, thought, or consciousness of ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles. Rather, they are the ultimate and concealed discourse of the Tathāgata for the eight classes of beings.

This is known from the following passage in the Sūtra: "The Tathāgata says that sentient beings are themselves not sentient beings," and so forth; this is precisely what is meant by the term *juyi* (phrase-meaning).
Because both principle (*li*) and teaching (*jiao*) are difficult to comprehend, it is called "phrase-meaning."
Regarding "and the sequence," this clarifies the sequential order of the twelve sections of this dharma-gate.
From one section to the next, the arising of dharmic functions may follow a temporal sequence or may involve leaps; therefore, it is difficult to comprehend.
The phrase "How does he abide? in the subsequent scripture gives rise to the section on abiding.
The phrases "How does he practice?
How does he subdue his mind? give rise to the section on practicing according to reality.
This refers to the meaning of the sequence being difficult to discern; hence, it says "and the sequence.

Regarding the phrase "The world does not understand how to be apart from [ordinary] wisdom": although the preceding line clarifies *prajñā*, its principle and teaching are difficult, and its essential nature remains unknown. Who, then, is it that does not understand?
Therefore, the second phrase clarifies that the foolish people of the world cannot understand it.
"The world" refers to the world of sentient beings.

"Cannot understand" means that these ordinary persons have not yet attained the supramundane superior understanding (*adhimukti*) arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation; because they have not severed the obstacles of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) or brought them to perpetual exhaustion, they are unable to penetrate the source of principle or awaken to this profound Dharma.
One should ask:
"Why do the foolish people of the world not understand?
To which one should immediately reply:
This is because they are devoid of luminous wisdom (*vidyā-jñāna*).

Those devoid of luminous wisdom—namely, the aforementioned foolish people who have not yet attained the true, untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti*) that eliminates the darkness of delusion from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward—are said to be "devoid of luminous wisdom. Because they lack this supramundane luminous wisdom, they are unable to understand this profound Dharma of Prajñāpāramitā.

Regarding the phrase "Great Wisdom thoroughly understands and instructs us": although the preceding line clarifies those who do not understand, it has not yet implicitly indicated those who can understand. Therefore, the third line clarifies that both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas uphold sublime understanding and are able to penetrate this principle; this simultaneously brings forth the two jewels of the Buddha and the Sangha.

Regarding "one who has attained great wisdom through thorough penetration": the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have eternally exhausted the two obstacles and perfected all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). They have illuminated this Dharma-gate to its ultimate limit, exhausting both its principle and its teaching; since there is no one superior to them, they are said to have "attained great wisdom through thorough penetration."

If we speak in terms of the bodhisattva, they likewise gradually eliminate the obstacles of affliction and possess a partial portion of the knowledge of all modes; their fragmentary awakening is identical to that of a Buddha, and by understanding the sequence of the phrases and meanings of this dharma-gate, they may also be said to have attained the penetration of great wisdom.

Regarding the second point: if this principle and teaching of Prajñā were so profound and difficult to understand, by what means would the Master of the Treatise have attained understanding to compose this commentary for its explanation?
Therefore, he replies that it is because of his great wisdom and thorough penetration that he can teach us.

Regarding the phrase "instructing us," this clarifies that the Master himself states that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess great skillful means (*upāya*). They provide instruction for myself, other masters of treatises, and all sentient beings by expressing, through names and signs, the principle of namelessness and signlessness which they have themselves realized. Thus, it is possible to understand the profound meaning of this *Prajñāpāramitā* and compose a treatise to explain it; since this merit derives from the Great Sage and is not something I could understand through my own power, he says, "instructing us."

Regarding the phrase "I take refuge in the body of immeasurable merit," although the persons and dharmas worthy of veneration were distinguished above, the intent behind offering such veneration was not yet discussed; therefore, the fourth section clarifies the meaning of this veneration.

Alternatively, this profound Dharma-gate of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas; it is able to give birth to and manifest the eternally abiding essence of nirvāṇa and its universally immeasurable merits. For this reason, one takes refuge in it.

Furthermore, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas each possess ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and other immeasurable aggregates of great merit; they are able to instruct me through the aforementioned principles and thus have bestowed upon me a most profound kindness. For this reason as well, I speak of taking refuge.
This single phrase should be applied throughout beneath the third line, stating in each case "I take refuge.
Regarding the passage "One should revere such as these," the following two lines provide a further explanation of the meaning of the fourth line concerning the expression of reverence.

Although it was previously stated that one "takes refuge," this had not yet fully expressed a heart of reverence and honor; because one now wishes to pay further respect through the three karmas (of body, speech, and mind), the preceding persons and dharmas who were objects of veneration are brought forward collectively, as in the passage beginning, "One should revere me in this way."

Regarding the phrase "bowing one's head to his feet and receiving him upon the crown," although the preceding section spoke of paying respect, it did not yet explain the reason for such respect; this sentence precisely clarifies the matter of reverent devotion.

The head is the most honored part of a single form, while the feet are the lightest part of the body; now, by using that which one holds in highest esteem to pay homage to the feet of the Buddha and the Sangha, one manifests the ultimate degree of reverence toward the field of merit. Therefore, it is said that one prostrates with the head and face at the feet and bears [the teaching] upon the crown of the head.
One should also say that mental action is to be honored and verbal action is to be praised; however, these are omitted here because they are intended for the verses.
This single phrase also applies universally beneath each of the three preceding Jewels, and in all cases, it signifies "I prostrate."

Regarding the phrase, "Because they are able to shoulder the Buddha’s difficult-to-vanquish task," these two and a half verses specifically explain that Bodhisattvas possess qualities worthy of veneration.
Here, the Master of the Treatise provisionally raises a doubt, thinking:

"The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*), possessing clear understanding and complete discernment of all phenomena; they transcend the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*) and there is none who can surpass them. They may rightly be called 'Great Wisdom' and it is logically fitting to pay them homage."

Since a Bodhisattva occupies a stage of training and dwells in a state of insufficiency—wherein their understanding is not yet perfected and their afflictions are not fully severed—how can they be called one of "Great Wisdom" and be revered as equal to a Buddha?
Therefore, the verse and its commentary state that [the Bodhisattva] is able to shoulder the difficult-to-conquer tasks of the Buddha.
What are these difficult-to-conquer tasks of the Buddha-family that the Bodhisattva is said to bear?

Herein it is clarified that the difficult-to-conquer tasks of the Buddha-family consist in this very Prajñā, whose principle and teaching are profound and far-reaching; they are not within the scope of calculation or speculation for ordinary persons or those of the Two Vehicles, and thus [the latter] are incapable of receiving, upholding, circulating, or benefiting others through them.

Nevertheless, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva alone upholds this sublime understanding and bears this heavy responsibility; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, within the Semblance Dharma, he maintains the great transformation and continues the legacy of the former sages.

This is precisely the bearing of the Buddha’s difficult-to-conquer task; therefore, their merit is equal to that of all Buddhas, and they are named "Great Wisdom Thoroughly Penetrating," receiving veneration identical to that accorded to the Buddhas.
This clarifies that there are two kinds of bodhisattvas:

first, those from the first bhūmi upward who have already accumulated practice throughout three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, directly perceive the fundamental principle, and have severed the afflictions; because they speak from their own realization, they are able to shoulder the burden, uphold, and propagate [the teaching] for the benefit of beings.

Second, there are Bodhisattvas on the stage of faith prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*), who have also accumulated practices for a long time; though one great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* is nearly but not yet fully completed, although they have not yet directly perceived the fundamental principle (*tattva*), because they can perceive it through a semblance of understanding that approximates the truth, they deeply subdue their afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, they too are able to shoulder the burden, uphold, propagate, and benefit sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of gathering and benefiting sentient beings": it is now asked whether a bodhisattva, while propagating the sublime Dharma of the *Prajñāpāramitā* during the Semblance and True Dharma periods, would act out of a desire for personal fame and profit?
Is it for the sake of benefiting all things?

Therefore, the second line of the verse says, "for the sake of gathering in and benefiting sentient beings," clarifying that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas propagate this sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they do so to extensively encompass all living beings and to equally nourish all conscious creatures.
Therefore, by using the Dharma to record and guide all things so that they follow one's own transformation, one enables them to attain the inexhaustible merit of supramundane, unsurpassed Bodhi.
This clarifies that it is not for one’s own benefit; hence it is said to be for the sake of gathering in and benefiting sentient beings.
The preceding two verses constitute the author’s homage to the Triple Gem and his declaration of the purpose for composing this treatise.
From "In this way" (*evam*) onwards, until the end of the scripture, the essential nature of the sūtra is correctly analyzed.
The meanings of the introduction (*nidāna*), the main body (*dharmadeśanā*), and the dissemination (*pariṇāmanā*) are distinguished as usual.

Within this, they are further divided according to their respective meanings into twelve sections; these range from the introductory section at the beginning to the section on dissemination at the end. This is precisely what is meant by those matters.
The explanation of the titles in the twelve sections may be understood through their detailed exposition in the sequence that follows.

Now, as for why the introduction (*nidāna*) is clarified first among these twelve sections: it is because when the Tathāgata is about to preach the Dharma, he employs his majestic spiritual power (*prabhāva*) to secretly summon those with karmic affinity; since this serves as the cause for the teaching’s emergence, it is called the "Introduction."

However, regarding the sequence for initiating the exposition of the meaning as clarified in various sutras, they all first emit light and shake the earth to assemble those with the karmic affinity, extensively establishing the causal conditions before finally delivering the teaching.
The reason this sutra differs from other scriptures is that the Tathāgata’s manner of preaching the Dharma and introducing its meaning comprises many types:
first, he emits light, shakes the earth, and summons those with the karmic affinity, extensively manifesting auspicious signs before he then preaches the Dharma.

Second, the Tathāgata emits light and causes the earth to tremble, extensively manifesting auspicious signs; knowing the capacities and responses of sentient beings, he spontaneously teaches the Dharma without waiting for questions.
Third, among the assembly there are timid sentient beings who harbor doubts in their hearts but do not venture to question the Buddha;
therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims of his own accord: "I am the Omniscient One; why do you not question me?"
"If you question me, I shall preach the Dharma for you.
Fourth, through the secret empowerment of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power, he is granted the wisdom and strength to preach the Dharma.
Fifth, when various bodhisattvas have finished preaching the Dharma in other places, they go to where the Tathāgata is to receive his seal of approval for what they have said.
Sixth, when there are people who give rise to doubts and pose questions, the Tathāgata explains them for them.
Seventh, the Tathāgata directly uses his own physical appearance as the introduction to the teaching of the Dharma.
Now, this introduction to the present sutra is precisely the fourth [aspect], the subtle empowerment of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power; therefore, it is spoken of as the introduction.
In the *Prajñāpāramitā* in one hundred thousand verses, the Tathāgata bestowed his three karmas upon Subhūti;
in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, and so forth—within these six sections—he bestowed only the two karmas of speech and mind upon Subhūti;
this *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* bestows only the karma of mind, lacking both body and speech.
If this meaning of the sutra is taught by way of addition, why does the textual passage not distinguish that matter?

It is because the Tathāgata has preached the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā* such that their power and influence continue in succession without interruption; therefore, it is not explained separately again.
The first five phrases of the sutra constitute the general introduction common to all scriptures: first, "Thus";
second, "I have heard."
Third, the time; fourth, the Bhagavat;
fifth, the dwelling place.
The reason why these five phrases are placed at the beginning of all sutras is that they possess three kinds of meaning:
first, to verify that the principles of the sutras are not false, thereby inspiring faith in those born in the final age.
Second, to distinguish itself from non-Buddhist schools, it takes "Āyu" as an auspicious term.
Third, to cease contentious debate, it demonstrates that its own tradition possesses a definitive foundation.
Because it gives rise to faith through equal realization, it is explained first.

Regarding the term "Thus" (*evam*): it is intended to enable people to recognize the sutra and comprehend its purport, clarifying that the principle and teaching of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* are exactly as I have spoken them, and are no different from what the Buddha previously taught; therefore, "Thus" is explained at the outset.
Although it is said that the principles and teachings of the Prajñā now being expounded are no different from those taught by the Buddha in the past, it remains unknown who the listeners are;
if there are no listeners, it may not necessarily be trustworthy.
For this reason, the second time it says "I have heard," this clarifies that there is a person who heard it; it is not merely a transmission of what was overheard, and thus it is trustworthy.
Although Subhūti says "I have heard," his teaching must necessarily have occurred at a specific time.
If one were to say that there is no specific time, it would likewise not necessarily be credible; therefore, for the third time, the "one time" (ekasmin samaye) is clarified.
Although the time of the discourse's delivery has been established, there must necessarily be someone present to hear it.

It is not yet known who the speaker is; if it were spoken by a celestial Mara, a non-Buddhist, or any other person, it might not necessarily be trustworthy. Therefore, on the fourth occasion, it clarifies that the speaker is the Buddha Bhagavat, and because it is what he has spoken, it is trustworthy.
Although it is said that this principle and teaching of Prajñā were spoken by the Buddha, it is not yet known in what place the Tathāgata spoke them.

If it were said that there is no specific location, it might not necessarily be credible; therefore, for the fifth time, the place where the sutra was spoken is clarified as being at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in the city of Śrāvastī.
Regarding the five phrases, why is the first named "Thus" (*evam*)?
If one explains its meaning according to worldly conventions, there are many ways to interpret it; briefly stated, there are generally four types:
the first is the "thusness" of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
Second, instructing others;
third, using analogies;
and fourth, providing definitive determination.
Regarding "generating the mind in this way," one reflects:
"I shall thus generate the bodhicitta and cultivate all virtuous practices," and so forth; this is called generating the mind in this way.
"To instruct others in this way" means to tell the person before them:
"You should thus resolve upon bodhicitta and cultivate all virtuous practices," and so forth.

"To employ such analogies" means that their majestic power is as blazing as the light of the sun, their wisdom is as deep and vast as the great ocean, their countenance is as upright and handsome as the full moon, and their courageous strength is like that of the lion king; this is what is meant by employing such analogies.
Regarding "decidedly thus" (*evam etad iti*), it means "I have seen, heard, and so forth in this way," which is termed "decidedly thus.

Now, when we say "thus," we take only the fourth sense of "decidedly thus": it clarifies that Subhūti himself declares, "I have personally heard from the Tathāgata this principle and teaching of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. What I have spoken is exactly as the Buddha spoke it—neither more nor less, neither embellished nor erroneous; it is decidedly thus, free from the defects of hearsay. Therefore, it is called "thus."
Regarding the phrase "I have heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*): since such a meaning necessarily implies that there was someone who heard it, the text next says "I have heard.
In this context, who is it that refers to themselves as "I" and says "I have heard"?
Many commentators say:
Subhūti stated, "I heard this sutra together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus," and therefore it says, "Thus have I heard.
However, while this reasoning is sound, the literal expression is also consistent with that interpretation.
Ānanda said, "What I have heard is of a different meaning, and thus it is not so.

There are three types of Ānandas who transmit and uphold the Dharma-piṭaka of the Three Vehicles—namely, those of the Mahāyāna, Hīnayāna, and Madhyamāyāna; their respective meanings may be understood accordingly.
How is this known? Subhūti says, "I have heard it," rather than anyone else. This is verified by two general principles:
[1] the principle of direct testimony, and [2] the principle of logical consistency.
First, according to the section on "Comparative Evaluation" at the end of the sutra text, Subhūti asks, "What should this sutra be named?
How should we uphold it? Based on the evidence provided by this passage, it is known that the one who says "I have heard" is Subhūti.
Although at that time Subhūti posed such a question, why must it necessarily be Subhūti who later says, "Thus have I heard"?
Furthermore, by what textual evidence can it be verified that it was Subhūti who said, "Thus have I heard"?
In the past, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there were three occasions for the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka.
First, at the Indrasailaguha Cave in Rājagṛha, five hundred bhikṣus compiled the Dharma-piṭaka; Śāriputra and other arhat bhikṣus each declared:
"This such-and-such sūtra was heard by me thus: the Buddha spoke it in such-and-such a place."

Later, when an evil king destroyed the Buddha-dharma, thereafter seven hundred bhikṣus again compiled the Dharma-piṭaka; they all stated, "I heard such-and-such a sūtra from such-and-such a bhikṣu," rather than saying, "I heard it from the Buddha."
This second council was convened by those of the Hīnayāna to compile the Dharma-piṭaka.

Furthermore, while the Tathāgata remained outside the Cakravāḍa Mountains and did not travel to other worlds, immeasurable Buddhas gathered together in that intermediate space between the two realms. Having finished reciting the *Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, they wished to compile the Mahāyāna Dharma-piṭaka and again summoned their followers; there were eighty billion nayutas of Arhats and an immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable number of Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all assembled there.
At that time, both Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas would have said, "Thus have I heard: the Tathāgata spoke such-and-such a sūtra in such-and-such a place.
Subhūti, however, says, "Thus have I heard: the Buddha spoke the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in the city of Śrāvastī. Therefore, we know that the one who says "I heard" here is Subhūti.
Regarding the term "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*): since it is stated "I have heard," there must necessarily have been a time for the teaching;

therefore, it is followed by the phrase "at one time. Now, time is of many kinds: there is the time of a single thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*), the time of a day and night, the time of a hundred years, the time of a kalpa, and the time of spring, autumn, winter, and summer.
What is now called "at one time" does not refer to such [conventional] times; it is precisely the time when the Tathāgata spoke this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Although it says "at one time," it does not specify a particular year, month, or day, and therefore it is not known exactly when.

As stated in the "Chapter on the Pure Eye of the World" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Tathāgata preached it on the very day he attained enlightenment at the site of the path of cessation (*śama-vimokṣa-maṇḍala*);
the "Ten Grounds Chapter" was preached during the second seven-day period in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*);
and the *Prajñāpāramitā* in one hundred thousand verses was preached five years after the Tathāgata’s enlightenment.
The sūtra contains explicit textual evidence.
Regarding the other seven sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, they merely state "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) and none indicate the year in which they were preached.
The *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* was preached ten years after the Buddha attained enlightenment.

As stated in the "Chapter on the Jewel Banner" (*Ratnaketu-parivarta*) of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, this was spoken at the Bamboo Grove of Kalanda in Rājagṛha one year after the Buddha attained enlightenment.
The "Chapter on the Sovereign King of Dhāraṇīs" (*Dhāraṇīśvararāja-parivarta*) was spoken sixteen years after his enlightenment, in the intermediate space between the desire realm and the form realm.
That which is explicitly stated in the sūtras can be known; that which is not explicitly stated in the sūtras cannot be known.
Nevertheless, although it is unknown how many years have passed since this sūtra was spoken, it is sufficient to know that it was spoken during the middle or later period.
How is this known? A sutra states:

"At the time of eating, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food; having obtained food and returned to the monastery, he finished his meal, and only then did the bhikṣus assemble to recite this sutra. Therefore, we know it was spoken after midday.

It is traditionally said that from the time the Tathāgata attained enlightenment until his parinirvāṇa, he constantly preached the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* without interruption.

Among the eight versions of this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, this is the last to be spoken. Subhūti directly states, "I heard at one time," rather than specifying how many years it was; therefore, he simply says "at one time."
Although it was said above that I heard this teaching on the principle of Prajñā at one time, I did not yet know from whom I heard it.
If I had heard it from anyone else, it would not be trustworthy.
Now, by saying "I have heard from the Buddha," it is clearly known that this was spoken by the Tathāgata, and thus it is trustworthy. Next, he says "Bhagavān.

However, this name is the correct phonetic transcription of the Western [Indian] language; as there was no standardized Chinese name for it during the Wei period, it has been retained in its foreign form.

The commentary on the meaning states that it can destroy afflictions; alternatively, it says it is fully endowed with merit and wisdom; it also says it possesses great renown such that devas and humans pay homage to it; and it further says it can subdue the celestial Māras and restrain all non-Buddhists.
Such meanings are numerous and cannot be discussed in full; for now, only these four have been mentioned.
According to the original texts from the Western Regions, the title *Bhagavat* appears at the beginning of every sutra.
In the sūtras of this region, it is frequently stated that "the Buddha was staying at such-and-such a place"; there are also instances where two names are preserved together.
This fourth section clarifies the person who is able to preach [the Dharma].
Although it was previously stated that [the teaching] was heard from the Buddha’s presence, it was not yet known at which location the Tathāgata had spoken it.
If there were no specific place, it would be impossible to believe; therefore, it next states, "In the city of Śrāvastī."
However, the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is wondrously transcendent of form and appearance, and it eternally dwells within the noble practices and the Brahma-conduct.
Therefore, the sutra below states: "The Buddhas take non-abiding as their dwelling place. How could such a body have any fixed location or spatial boundaries?

As for the statement that [the Buddha] was in Śrāvastī, this clarifies that the various Buddhas manifest their response precisely because they wish to go forth to meet the resonance of sentient beings.
Since sentient beings have specific locations, the Sages likewise conform to them.

Furthermore, it is because he wishes to cause future sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata preached the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* at this location, so that they may give rise to a mind of reverence and respect—whether by prostrating, or praising, or erecting stupas, or making offerings of incense and flowers with veneration—thereby generating merit within the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).

Regarding this city of Śrāvastī: in the past, at the beginning of the kalpa, there were two brothers who were rishis. The younger brother was named Śāva (translated in Wei as "The Young"), and the elder brother was Āvati (translated in Wei as "The Unassailable").
These two men resided in that place seeking the Way, and it was for this reason that it was named after them.

The younger brother’s name was abbreviated by omitting "Vā," while the elder brother’s name was abbreviated by omitting "A"; as both names were thus preserved together, it is called the City of Śrāvastī, also known as the City of Śāvatthī.
For example, because of the seer Kuśinātha, it was named the city of Kuśinagara;
because of the seer Kapila, it was named the city of Kapilavastu.
These are all cases where names are derived from people.
The city of Ayodhyā was named for a specific reason; in the Wei language, it is called "The City That Cannot Be Overcome.

Regarding "the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park," although it was previously stated to be within the city of Śrāvastī, that location is still vast; therefore, this second mention specifies its particular site.
"Ji" (祇) is a foreign pronunciation; the crown prince of that country was named Jeta-kumāra.
"Jeta" (祇陀), according to the Wei translation, means "crown prince," while "kumāra" (鳩摩羅), according to the Wei translation, means "youth."
"Tree" (*jīva*) is the name for this region.

This grove originally belonged to the Prince; later, the elder Sudatta purchased it by covering the ground with gold. He gathered the poor, the orphaned, and the elderly there to provide for their sustenance, and furthermore, he constructed a vihāra within it. Because of these circumstances, people subsequently named it the Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma (Givaka’s Grove).
Both primary names are mentioned together, placing the foreign (Hū) and Chinese designations side by side; thus it is called "the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Regarding the phrase "with a great assembly of bhikṣus," although it was previously stated "I have heard," one must know with whom the narrator heard this together; therefore, those listed as the assembly who heard it together are all a host of Arhats.
The phrase "one thousand two hundred and fifty people" cites the current large number.
If one were to formulate six categories, these co-hearers would correspond to the sixth category.
If one were to formulate five categories, then this would be subsumed within "Thus have I heard.

Since the subsequent *parīndanā* (concluding) section fully enumerates the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly along with the eight classes of beings who heard the sutra with joy, why is it that in this [opening] section it mentions only the twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, without fully listing the various assemblies?

Although the meaning of this sūtra is vast, its text is extremely concise; therefore, within this introductory section (nidāna), the persons who heard it together are not explained in detail. Only the number of great bhikṣus is given, while the full enumeration of the followers who constantly attend them is provided later.

In other sutras, the names are listed first, followed by praises of their virtues and an enumeration of their qualities; that this sutra lacks such listings of names and praises of virtues is likewise due to its concise style.
The term "great bhikṣu" (mahābhikṣu) has many meanings; however, in this context, it refers specifically to one who has completely severed the afflictions and attained arhatship as a "great bhikṣu.
Since this does not include the nine types of bhikṣus such as those ordained by the formal ritual of the fourfold motion (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), they are designated as "great."

"Bhikṣu" is the correct phonetic transcription from foreign lands; as for its semantic interpretation in this region, it is sometimes called "mendicant" (qǐshì), sometimes "one who destroys evil" (pò'è), and sometimes "one who terrifies Māra" (bùmó). Since no single standard name has been widely disseminated, I have retained the original Western term.
"At that time, when the World-Honored One was at his mealtime" refers to the period before midday; this signifies that the śramaṇa has few desires and that there must be a fixed time for eating.

"Donning his robes and taking up his bowl" signifies the mark of contentment in one who has left the household life: possessing nothing more than the three robes and the bowl, he follows them wherever he goes, just as a bird does not abandon its two wings; whether departing or staying, he acts according to his will, his mind free from attachment.
Regarding "entering the great city of Śrāvastī," tradition states that the Jetavana Garden was located to the east of this city, and thus one enters from the outside.

As for the "great city," this city is vast and expansive, measuring twelve *yojanas* in length and breadth; it contains eighteen hundred million households of residents, and is therefore called a "great city."
The reason the Tathāgata enters the city is for the purpose of begging for food.

However, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, being of a vajra-nature, does not depend on food to exist. As for what is called the Tathāgata’s begging for food, it is because the Tathāgata manifests the practice of begging for food for many kinds of benefit; therefore, the Tathāgata enters the city to beg for food.
The benefits of alms-gathering are manifold; although the sutras mention only twenty, we shall now discuss ten of them. First:

when the Tathāgata enters the city for alms, sentient beings behold his thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, his wondrous features as majestic as Mount Sumeru, and they resolve upon bodhicitta, seeking the body of a Tathāgata.

Second, sentient beings suffering from various afflictions such as deafness, blindness, and muteness, upon seeing the Tathāgata, have their suffering momentarily stilled and give rise to the bodhicitta.

Third, wealthy and noble elders who, relying on their own lineage, give rise to arrogance, see the Tathāgata’s majestic virtue and extraordinary, world-transcending deportment; their pride subsides and they give rise to the bodhicitta.
Fourth, there are three ways in which women are protected:

while at home they are protected by their parents; after marriage, they are protected by their husbands; and in old age, they are protected by their sons. Furthermore, those who are indolent and unable to see the Buddha, upon seeing the Tathāgata entering the city, feel joy in their hearts and resolve to attain Bodhicitta.

The five [kings], Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, along with the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and so forth, escorted the Tathāgata, each offering praise and making offerings of celestial incense, flowers, and music. Those people among the crowd who saw this immediately conceived this thought:
"If even the devas have abandoned their celestial pleasures to make offerings to the Tathāgata, why do we not do the same?"
Thereupon, they emulated the various devas and spirits by making extensive offerings and resolving their minds upon Bodhicitta.
As the six Tathāgatas entered the city for alms, the four Heavenly Kings each presented them with an alms bowl; having accepted them, the Tathāgata joined the four bowls into one.
The Buddha manifested such inconceivable wonders that those who saw them rejoiced and resolved to attain Bodhicitta.
Seventh, he accepted alms-food from two people, one poor and one wealthy.
Although the wealthy man had abundant food and wished to give much to the Tathāgata, he saw that the Tathāgata’s bowl was empty; thus, he was able to give generously.
Those who were greedy ate little and feared they would not dare to give; seeing that the Tathāgata’s bowl was already full, they were thus able to offer only a small amount.
To cause each person to have their wishes fulfilled, this rare occurrence took place, whereby they resolved to attain bodhicitta.
Eighth, he places a hundred-flavored meal within the Tathāgata’s almsbowl such that all the flavors remain distinct and unmixed, as if held in separate vessels;
he offers this to all the Saṃgha and to all sentient beings, yet it neither increases nor decreases as they eat, and those who see it rejoice and resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
Ninth, it is for the sake of future disciples who might be criticized by laypeople, saying:
"Even your teacher, the Tathāgata, does not beg for food; why then do you beg for food?
For this reason, the Tathāgata manifests the practice of begging for alms.

Tenth, the Tathāgata’s body is of vajra-nature and is not empty within; furthermore, he constantly abides in samādhi and, in reality, does not eat. Only the various devas know that the Tathāgata does not eat, yet for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he enters cities to beg for food.
Practicing alms-gathering brings these many benefits; therefore, one enters the city to beg for food.

Regarding the phrase "begging for food in sequence within that city": according to the custom of the Western lands (India), the four castes reside within the city, while butchers and executioners live outside the city. When entering the city, [the mendicant] rings a bell to signal his presence, and they each go about their separate ways without intermingling.

Now, regarding "in sequence": within the four castes of the city, one does not abandon the poor to follow the wealthy, nor does one discard the lowly to follow the noble; therefore, it is called "begging for food in sequence."
If that were so, would it not mean that the Buddha’s mind is not impartial toward sentient beings?
This clarifies that the Tathāgata’s mind is not unequal; it is simply because he conforms to the laws of the land.

Nevertheless, the Tathāgata also enters the homes of the lowly to beg for food. However, if the Tathāgata should go to the home of a lowly person, he does not allow others to see him. If members of the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa castes were to see him there, they would immediately mock and revile him, saying:
"The śramaṇa is an impure person, begging for food from lowly individuals," they thought,
and thus failed to give rise to respect.
If those of noble status do not give rise to respect, then the Buddha-dharma cannot be established.

In the Western lands, śramaṇas generally do not go to beg for alms from butchers or caṇḍālas, nor do they go to the houses of those who keep wicked elephants, wicked horses, or wicked dogs to beg for alms.
"Only the Tathāgata alone may practice sequential alms-gathering; other bhikṣus may never do so.
Regarding "returning to his original place," it means that having finished begging for food, he returns to the Jeta Grove.

Regarding the phrase "having finished eating": the Tathāgata does not eat the food as it appears; he divides the contents of his bowl into three parts. One part he places upon grass and leaves to give to sentient beings dwelling on land; one part he places in the water to give to sentient beings dwelling in the water; and one part he eats himself.
However, the Tathāgata does not actually eat; it is only the devas who know that the Tathāgata does not eat while appearing to eat.
"Collecting the robes and bowl" means folding the saṃghāṭī and, having washed the bowl, placing them in their usual location.
Regarding the phrase “having washed his feet”: although the Tathāgata’s feet are like lotuses, such that dust and water do not adhere to them;

and although it is the constant law of all Buddhas to practice walking, when the Tathāgata walks upon the earth, he remains four finger-widths above the ground so that his feet do not tread upon it, and lotuses spring up from below to receive the Tathāgata’s feet—how, then, could there be any dust or grime?
As for the mention of "washing the feet," this demonstrates that those who have left the household life possess a majestic and pure demeanor worthy of veneration.

Regarding the phrase "as if a seat were normally spread," this is not something created by the eight classes of beings among humans and devas, nor is it something spread by disciples, nor does it exist merely because the Tathāgata has thought of it. It clarifies that because the causes planted by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are profound and vast, there naturally arises a hall of seven treasures and a wondrous seat of various jewels as a karmic retribution; since these do not require artificial arrangement, it is said that "a seat is normally spread."
When the Buddha wishes to sit, it appears; once he has departed, it is gone.

Regarding the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), among the four modes of deportment, the mode of sitting is supreme. If one were walking or standing, one would become weary; whereas this posture is free from affliction over time and accords with meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Those who see him rejoice, and all give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
"Standing with his body upright" clarifies the Tathāgata’s bodily karma (*kāyakarman*).
It indicates that the Tathāgata is free from the turbidity of deportment; he possesses the marks of samādhi, remaining solemnly motionless like a cast golden image or a wooden puppet.
"Right mindfulness is immovable" clarifies the mental karma (*manas-karman*) of the Tathāgata.
Because he has attained supreme samādhi through single-minded concentration on a single object, and possesses no further shifting or agitation, it is called "immovable."
Since right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*), how can this be known?

Although right mindfulness is indeed a mental factor, it is obscure and difficult to perceive; however, by observing the stillness of the physical form, one can sufficiently know that concentration (*samādhi*) exists within the mind.
Just as a bhikṣu who has attained meditative concentration may remain unmoving for one day or even seven days;
because his body is unmoving, it is clearly known that there is concentration within his inner mind.
From this point forward is its introductory section.
From "At that time, the bhikṣus... down to "...well-entrusted to the bodhisattvas," this is the second section of the sūtra, titled the Section on Good Protection and Mindfulness.

This is why he is called "well-guarded and remembered": Subhūti, having already received the power of the Tathāgata’s secret empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), was about to receive instruction from the Tathāgata.

By virtue of this power of secret empowerment, he stood in the presence of the Tathāgata and preached the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattvas, intending to initiate the subsequent sūtra by inquiring about the three matters pertaining to the stages (*bhūmi*).
At the outset, he uttered this exclamation: "How rare, World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata skillfully protects and entrusts all Bodhisattvas. This clarifies that the Tathāgata is well-able to teach and transform both types of Bodhisattvas—those whose faculties are mature and those whose are not—thereby causing their worldly understanding to reach fulfillment and enabling them to swiftly enter the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) of the Ground of Nature and the First Ground.
Next, the second section is explained.
As for "the bhikṣus," these are none other than the Tathāgata’s regular retinue of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

As for the reason for saying "they came to where the Buddha was," it is because it is the constant rule for these bhikṣus to each remain on the four sides, at a distance of perhaps one or two hundred paces from the Buddha’s dwelling, practicing the Path according to the Dharma as suited to them, and not being permitted to approach the Buddha.
If one stays near the Buddha, there are many obstacles to the practice of *caṇḍāla* (or *cāndrāyaṇa*); for this reason, he dwells at a distance.
The Tathāgata goes on almsround carrying his own robe and bowl and does not bring his disciples with him; likewise, the bhikṣus each go on almsround individually and do not follow the Tathāgata.

It is the constant law of the Tathāgata that, after his meal, he teaches the Dharma as appropriate to the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings; therefore, through the Tathāgata’s majestic power and secret empowerment, he caused the bhikṣus to come to where the Buddha was.
"If the Tathāgata did not empower them with his mental power, these bhikṣus would have no means by which to come.

When Subhūti Sūtra-jīvita stood respectfully and addressed the Buddha, saying, "It is rare, World-Honored One," it was because whenever any śrāvaka or bodhisattva wishes to pose a question before the Tathāgata, they do not dare to do so unless they receive the Buddha's empowerment.
However, Subhūti, if he were truly a śrāvaka, he would have to rely on the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) before being able to pose a question;
even if he were a bodhisattva employing skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and acting as a śrāvaka, he too would have to rely on the Tathāgata’s empowerment before being able to ask.

The Tathāgata has only just now begun to assemble the assembly and has not yet said anything; for what reason, Subhūti, do you suddenly praise the Tathāgata in the midst of this great assembly, saying, "It is rare, World-Honored One!"?

Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgata well protects and well entrusts all bodhisattvas": because Subhūti had previously received the power of the Tathāgata’s secret empowerment, his wisdom and eloquence were no different from the Buddha's. He was about to expound the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for the sake of other bodhisattvas and intended to initiate the subsequent sūtra by questioning the Tathāgata on three matters concerning the stages (*bhūmi*). For this reason, he uttered words of praise, saying, "It is rare, World-Honored One!"
Regarding this term "rare" (āścarya), it does not mean that it is rare because it occurs only occasionally.
This sound "rare" may be said to mean "increasing," or "capable," or it may also be called "excellent."

This clarifies that the Tathāgata is truly able to protect and entrust two kinds of bodhisattvas; by bestowing medicine according to their faculties without missing the opportune moment, he ensures they do not lose the time for receiving the Way, and is therefore called "rare."
"Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha" is a brief praise of the three titles.
Regarding "skillfully protecting and mindfulness of all bodhisattvas, and skillfully entrusting all bodhisattvas," it is generally taught that there are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who are supramundane bodhisattvas from the first bhūmi upward; [and second, those who are mundane bodhisattvas].
Second, there are worldlings prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
Worldlings prior to the stages are further divided into two types: first, those who are ordinary persons (*bāhyapṛthagjana*);
[and second, those who are noble ones].
The second is the inner ordinary person (*antarapṛthagjana*).
Regarding the bodhisattvas who are inner ordinary persons, there are again two types: first, those whose faculties are matured; [and second, those whose faculties are not yet matured].
The second refers to those whose faculties (*indriya*) are not yet mature.

What is now called "skillfully protecting and mindful" praises the Tathāgata’s skillful protection of Bodhisattvas of the stages prior to the Grounds (*bhūmi*), whose lineage, species, understanding, practice, and faculties have matured.
"Skillfully entrusting" praises the entrustment to Bodhisattvas within the stage of the nature of practice (*śikṣāgotra*) whose faculties are not yet mature.

Regarding why these two types of bodhisattvas are said to be "protected by mindfulness" (*anuparigṛhīta*) and "entrusted" (*parindita*): if the Tathāgata did not protect them through mindfulness and entrust them, there would be the possibility that the objects of observation arising from their resolve and practice might be erroneous or lead to regression, such that they could not definitively enter the stage of nature (*gotrabhūmi*). Furthermore, they might even remain in the world for many eons without being able to quickly enter the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). Therefore, it is necessary for the Tathāgata to provide protection through mindfulness and entrustment.

Regarding those whose faculties are matured: within the stages of the lineage-nature (*gotra*) and the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*), they contemplate the three types of two truths and the two types of selflessness. During the period when one great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* is either nearly full or not yet full, and while desiring to realize the semblance of seeing the principle, the light of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) has already manifested before them. At this stage, being fully endowed with the two kinds of adornments—merit and wisdom—they are certain to realize the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*.

Because they never again fall back from the first stage, they are said to have "mature faculties"; however, they are not yet called "Bodhisattvas of Great Power who have realized the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" from the first stage upward.
Those whose faculties are not yet matured are within the stage of the nature of the cultivated seeds (*śrutavāsanāgotra*).
Furthermore, these individuals of the nature of the cultivated seeds are also of two types:
first, those who are decisively fixed for a time; [the second being those who are not so fixed].
The second is the indeterminate.

As for the indeterminate: although they practice the virtues and wisdom of the mundane paths of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as well as the various pāramitās, they have not yet definitively entered the stage of nature (gotrabhūmi) or even the first bhūmi; because they are subject to advancement and regression, such a person who regresses is said to have "roots that are not yet mature."

Regarding the seven types of persons who generate the bodhicitta, those of the first three types generally do not regress. Those of the latter four types may either regress or not; if they encounter Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), they will not turn back, but if they do not encounter such spiritual friends, they will regress from the bodhicitta and enter the stages of ordinary worldlings or the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
This refers to those of the lineage of the stage of practice (*śikṣā-bīja-gotra*) who may either fall back or not;

some even say that bodhisattvas of the lineage of nature (*prakṛti-gotra*) still fall into hell. However, the *Sūtra on the Adornment of Joy* states, "Bodhisattvas of the stage of nature are definitively non-retrogressive. Therefore, in the *Ratnāvalī*, someone asked Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva:
"The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* states that 'bodhisattvas of the stage of nature fall into the Avīci hell'; how is this to be understood?"
Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna replied:
"Although the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* states that 'a bodhisattva of the nature-ground falls into hell,' I do not dare to speak in such a manner."
Why is this? The *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa Sūtra* clarifies that bodhisattvas of the stage of nature (*gotrabhūmi*) ultimately do not fall into hell.

Furthermore, the *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* states: "If a bodhisattva of the stage of nature were at one time to kill all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, despite committing such a transgression, they would still not fall into hell."
If all sentient beings from the four continents up to the trichiliocosm were likewise not to fall into hell, why is this?
It is because this person has practiced for kalpas, made extensive offerings to many Buddhas, and their roots of merit, wisdom, and goodness have reached full maturity.
"Even if one commits grave offenses, because the power of their merit and virtue is great, the offenses are immediately extinguished and they do not fall into hell.
It is like a drop of water cast upon a red-hot iron pan; it is instantly consumed."
Based on this evidence, it is known that Bodhisattvas of the Stage of Nature (gotrabhūmi) do not fall into hell.
If this is so, how can the apparent contradiction between these two sūtras be reconciled?
The explanation is as follows:

When the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* speaks of "entering," it is intended to urge bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) who have not yet attained them, instilling in them a sense of urgency so that they may swiftly realize the first stage; it does not mean that they actually enter the Avīci Hell.

As in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, there are seven exhortations; in one such exhortation to a bodhisattva of the eighth stage, it is said: "Do not take pleasure in dwelling in the samādhi of cessation. Yet, since a bodhisattva of the eighth stage has already transcended the realm of effort and forever severed the activities of consciousness, with every thought-moment being non-arising and advancing spontaneously in every movement, how could there be a need for the encouragement of dwelling in cessation to prompt further progress?

It is because one wishes to cause them to enter quickly into the ninth stage, the tenth stage, and even the stage of Buddhahood; therefore, this is an exhortation, not a claim that they truly delight in abiding in quiescent extinction.
How is this known?
Therefore, the Sūtra says, "Do not abandon this gate of patience," making it clear that this is not an actual dwelling in bliss.
This case is likewise: in reality, one does not fall into hell.
As for the mention of "falling," it is intended to mean that one should quickly realize the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), not that there is an actual falling away.
Thus, we know that from the stage of the innate lineage (*prakṛtisthagotra*) upward, there is absolutely no retrogression.

The reason for saying "skillfully protecting and mindful of" refers exclusively to bodhisattvas whose faculties are mature; "skillfully entrusting" refers only to those whose faculties are not yet mature.

This clarifies that although the Buddhas possess the power of sovereign mastery, they can only deliver sentient beings with whom they have a karmic affinity, and cannot deliver those with whom they lack such affinity.
What constitutes having a karmic connection (*sapratiṣṭha*)?

As stated in the *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*: "The Buddhas come from the stage of the causal ground; those who are embraced by the Buddhas through such methods as the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) have a karmic connection with the Buddha, because the Tathāgata has attained liberation himself."
Regarding those sentient beings whose faculties are matured, this clarifies his protective mindfulness (*anurakṣaṇā*).

For those who are not yet embraced by the Tathāgata’s dharmas such as the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they lack a connection with the Buddha; therefore, he entrusts them to bodhisattvas and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) with whom they have a connection. Through mindfulness of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, they do not regress from practices already attained, and regarding practices not yet attained, they do not lose their progress toward the superior and supreme dharmas of realization.

However, it is not that the Tathāgata fails to protect and mind those whose faculties are immature, nor does he fail to entrust them to those whose faculties are mature; rather, it is simply because the intention of the sūtra compiler could not tolerate prolixity, and thus only one side was presented above.

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'well-guarding and mindful of,' this is spoken in reference to bodhisattvas whose faculties are mature," and so forth; here, the author of the treatise first distinguishes between two types of bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, the statement "How does one well-guard and well-entrust? is a provisional question posed in order to provide an explanation through verse.
Question:

With what kind of mental activity, by what method, and with what power of mindfulness does the Tathāgata bestow the "power of protective mindfulness," and why are these two types of bodhisattvas called those who receive "protective mindfulness" and "entrustment"?
Therefore, he replied with a verse: "One should know the meaning of skillful protection.
Thus, this master of the treatise composed eighty verses in total to explain this sutra.
Regarding the first two verses, the Master of the Treatise, being about to compose this work, first clarifies his homage to the Triple Gem and articulates his intention for composing the treatise.
From here below, there are seventy-seven verses that correctly explain the text of the Sūtra.
The final verse, following the completion of the treatise, expresses praise and dedication.
What meaning does this single verse of skillful protection clarify?
It correctly explains the "rare and marvelous" passages within the preceding sutra.

However, this rarity consists in praising the Tathāgata for his skillful ability to mindfully entrust two kinds of bodhisattvas; thus it is called "skillful. Since this very skillful protection constitutes the rarity, this skillfulness explains the rarity.
Regarding the term "protection" (*hù*), it serves as a general explanation for both "skillfully protecting and mindful of" (*shàn hùniàn*) and "entrusting" (*fùshǔ*).
This verse should have read "skillfully protecting and mindful of, and entrusting," but because of the constraints of the meter, only "protection" is mentioned.
Regarding "the meaning should be known": the principle is precisely as such, intended to cause the questioner to understand.

Now that this first phrase has finished explaining "skillfully protecting and mindful entrustment," the reason the second phrase further states "augmenting their bodies and practicing together" is to resolve the doubts and difficulties concerning the preceding sutra passage.
An objection is raised:
This sutra should not be stated in this way; rather, it should say, "skillfully protecting and mindful of all sentient beings" and "skillfully entrusting all sentient beings.

The reason for this is that it clarifies that the Tathāgata’s compassion is impartial and extends to all things without partiality; thus, he should universally mind the six realms of existence, leaving out neither the ordinary nor the holy.
If one says that he protects and mindfully remembers all sentient beings, then the meaning extends to both ordinary persons and sages;
if one simply says he protects and mindfully remembers bodhisattvas, this would only include those who are engaged in practice and thus fail to encompass everyone.
Why does it not say "skillfully protecting and mindful of all sentient beings," but rather only "protecting and being mindful of all bodhisattvas"?
Therefore, the answer is: "He adds his own body to act in concert with them."
To speak of "protecting and mindful of all bodhisattvas" is equivalent to protecting and mindful of all sentient beings.

Regarding "empowering their bodies," it means that the Tathāgata, through the power of his wisdom, empowers the bodies of these two types of bodhisattvas, causing them to enter the stage of nature (*gotrabhūmi*) and even to realize the wisdom of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).
If this is so, the previous doubt returns:
it would still mean that the Tathāgata protects and mindfully attends only to bodhisattvas, and not to sentient beings.
Therefore, the next two characters say, "practicing together" (tóngxíng).
"Companions" refers to how the Bodhisattva, by means of the four methods of attraction and the six perfections, gathers all sentient beings as his companions and his retinue.
If this is so, while the Bodhisattva cultivates the ten thousand practices, sentient beings have not yet done so; how, then, can it be said that they "practice together"? Answer:

The intention is to clarify that when the Mahāsattva perceives True Suchness (tathatā) and Buddha-nature, he attains an analogous understanding within the principle of equality and likewise attains an analogous mind of compassion as one body. Consequently, he does not perceive sentient beings as different from his own body, nor himself as different from sentient beings; thus, the cultivation of his own body is the cultivation of all sentient beings.

This clarifies that the Bodhisattva is identical with sentient beings, rather than sentient beings being identical to the Bodhisattva; therefore, it is said that he "empowers their bodies to act in concert.

This explains how the Buddhas empower Bodhisattvas to transform sentient beings, with these transformations transmitted and mutually encompassing one another; this is precisely the *Kauśalya-dharmaparyāya* (the Dharma-gate of Skillful Means).
From the perspective of principle, this single phrase generally explains both types of bodhisattvas;
from a specific perspective, it explains only those who are "well-guarded and mindful.
Regarding the phrase "not retreating from what has been attained or not yet attained," it explains the "good entrustment" (*suviniścita*) mentioned in the sūtra.
"Those who have attained" refers to those who have already practiced;
"those who have not attained" refers to those who have not yet practiced.

Regarding "non-retrogression," it is because one wishes to cause those of the lineage of the stage of practice (śikṣamāṇa-gotra) to remain firm and not lose what they have already attained, and to ensure they advance further without retreating regarding what they have not yet attained, that they are entrusted to a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
