Since the fruit already possesses these three characteristics, by inferring the cause from the fruit, it is clearly known that the cause must likewise possess characteristics; therefore, one knows that there is no cause devoid of characteristics.
How can it be said that by practicing giving without grasping at signs, one can attain the fruit of the unconditioned Dharma-body and immeasurable merit?
To sever this doubt, the Buddha replied: "Subhūti!..."
"Do not entertain such a thought.

As for your statement that the Tathāgata at the stage of fruition possesses the three conditioned characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, these exist because the expedient body appears in accordance with karmic responses; they do not belong to the unconditioned Dharma-body.
However, the unconditioned Dharma-body is eternally serene throughout past and present, with all virtues perfectly complete; its essence transcends the three marks, and is therefore not conditioned.
Why do you say that because the body of skillful means possesses the three marks, you claim that this is the same as the unconditioned Dharma-body being called "the three marks"?
In this regard, questions and answers ought to be posed; yet no such questions and answers are provided because, from beginning to end, this sutra frequently lacks them.

However, as Subhūti is a Dharma-body Bodhisattva manifesting as a Śrāvaka and has attained the power of the Tathāgata’s profound wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*), he well understands the Tathāgata’s intention; therefore, the Buddha directly asks: "Subhūti!"
"What do you think?

Can one see the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of marks? This clarifies that one cannot see the Tathāgata—the fruit-stage, unconditioned Dharmakāya—by means of the perfection of the three conditioned characteristics, such as arising, abiding, and ceasing.

Therefore, Subhūti, understanding the Tathāgata’s intention, replied: “One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of the accomplishment of marks. This clarifies that the Dharma-Buddha Tathāgata is the unconditioned *dharmakāya*, whose essence lacks the three marks; thus, he cannot be seen by means of the three conditioned marks.

Furthermore, there are ordinary beings of the Two Vehicles who cling to the two kinds of nirvāṇa of the sixteen-foot Tathāgata, regarding them as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and likewise as eternally abiding unconditioned phenomena. They maintain that when Śākyamuni Tathāgata, from the time he first resolved for enlightenment, completed the practices of the ten stages over three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and attained perfect awakening beneath the Bodhi tree, he first subdued the Māras of the heavens and severed the Māra of afflictions; yet his body and wisdom still remained, which is called "nirvāṇa with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
Because he was no longer subject to the influence of afflictions, it is termed "unconditioned."

Regarding *nirvāṇa without remainder*: when body and wisdom are exhausted, one is no longer subject to the three marks of arising, abiding, and ceasing; therefore, it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because these two meanings are present, the sixteen-foot [form] is named the unconditioned *dharmakāya*.

Regarding the term "eternally abiding," it clarifies that once the sixteen-foot Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa, he does not return again to the twenty-five realms of existence; therefore, the sixteen-foot form is called "constant."
From this point onward until the end of the sutra, there is an extensive explanation of the meaning of the three Buddhas being identical or distinct.

In this present section, only the Dharma-Buddha is clarified; as for the discussion from here on regarding the Reward-Buddha and the Response-Buddha, it is conducted within the context of their specific characteristics.
The scriptural text explains this clearly and extensively of its own accord.
Herein, those following the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) may harbor doubts:

"If the Response-Buddha (nirmāṇakāya-buddha) possesses the three marks and is not the unconditioned Dharma-body Buddha (dharmakāya-buddha), then is this body sixteen feet tall to be considered the Buddha?"
Is he not a Buddha? Furthermore, one wonders:

since the body of the Reward-Buddha (vipākabuddha), adorned with immeasurable marks and signs of wondrous form, is not the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), is it conditioned (saṃskṛta) or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)?
Is this with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)?

Is it permanent or impermanent? Furthermore, as for the Reward Buddha’s environment—the Pure Land—is it a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) or an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)?
Is it subsumed within the three realms, or is it not subsumed within the three realms?
Such a doubt may arise.
This shall be explained individually and in detail below in the sutra itself, so that it may be understood.
Regarding the phrase "For what reason": because it was previously stated that the Tathāgata cannot be seen through the accomplishment of marks, a doubt arises:

if the Dharmakāya Tathāgata does not possess the three marks, for what reason did the Tathāgata himself declare, "I cultivated the path for three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas; in my final birth, I was born into the Śākya clan of King Śuddhodana; I practiced austerities for six years; I attained Buddhahood at the site of enlightenment; and for over eighty years I remained in the world preaching the Dharma"? Furthermore, he said of himself, "My body is impermanent; after three months, I shall enter parinirvāṇa," and subsequently passed away between the twin śāla trees?
Therefore it is asked: "Why is this so?
The Sūtra answers: "The characteristics spoken of by the Tathāgata are themselves non-characteristics.
Why are the characteristics spoken of non-characteristics?

The manifestation from birth in the royal palace to extinction at the twin śāla trees is the mark of the expedient means of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya); it is not that this very mark is the unconditioned mark of the dharma-body (dharmakāya).
These Buddhas exist because they manifest in accordance with the perceptions of sentient beings; they possess no actual physical form.
When one examines their essence, it is simply the single *dharmatā*, quiescent and profoundly still, devoid even of the characteristics of the four great elements, such as color or fragrance.
When the Buddha told Subhūti,
"All that has marks is false speech," this was a general discourse on the delusive discrimination of the world's mind, thought, consciousness, and mentation.
Whatever belongs to the Sambhogakāya Buddha that is constituted by the three marks is entirely illusory and unreal.

It may also be said that, from the perspective of the specific characteristics and meanings of the myriad meritorious marks of the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha—the fruit of retribution—these are not the eternal, fixed Dharmakāya of empty space throughout past and present; therefore, it is said that "all marks whatsoever are false speech."

Regarding the statement, "If one sees that all marks are non-marks, this is not false speech": if one sees that the three characteristics of conditioned phenomena are not the characteristics of the unconditioned Dharmakāya, then this is not a falsehood.
If this is so, someone might doubt:
"The Tathāgata may indeed lack the three marks of the conditioned, but could it be that the myriad virtuous marks of the Buddhas' fruition are also non-existent?
The answer is: "One who sees that these various marks are not marks, sees the Tathāgata."
One who understands that these three characteristics of the conditioned are not the characteristics of the unconditioned Dharmakāya is able to see the Tathāgata as the true Dharmakāya.

This clarifies that the Dharmakāya Tathāgata possesses the characteristics of True Suchness (tathatā) and liberation, and is not identical to the three characteristics of the conditioned—arising, abiding, and ceasing—and so forth.
This section of the sutra is explained by a single verse.

Regarding the phrase "discriminating the nature of the conditioned," it clarifies that various lesser bodhisattvas and followers of the two vehicles give rise to mind, intellect, and consciousness through false discrimination, asserting that what is constituted by the three characteristics of the conditioned is itself the primary dharmakāya Tathāgata, and that there is no separate, unconditioned dharmakāya.

Regarding the claim that the Way is the unconditioned Dharma-body (dharmakāya): although one might point to empty space as the Dharma-body, it cannot be seen; thus, it is clearly understood that there is no such thing as an unconditioned Dharma-body.
This single phrase intends to resolve a doubt; first, it cites the calculation of those who are deluded, hence it says, "discriminating the substance of the conditioned.
The second phrase says, "to prevent their attainment of accomplishment."

"Prevention" refers to warding off the opponent's calculation that the entity established by the three characteristics is the primary Dharmakāya Tathāgata; therefore, it is said that one prevents the attainment of such an establishment.
This single sentence explains the passage in the sutra from "What do you think? down to "The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the accomplishment of marks."
Regarding the phrase "Because the three marks have distinct natures": this single sentence explains the passage in the sutra from "For what reason?

The mark spoken of by the Tathāgata is itself no-mark" up to "is false speech. It clarifies that the three marks of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body Buddha) and the ten thousand marks of merit of the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward-body Buddha) are distinct from the essence of the *dharmakāya* Tathāgata; for, from the perspective of the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the *dharmakāya* Tathāgata, it is free from the three marks and the ten thousand marks of the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgata is apart from those," this sentence explains the scriptural passage beginning with "If one sees that all marks are no-marks. It clarifies that the unconditioned Dharmakāya is tranquil and eternally abiding, constant throughout past and present; its essence and characteristics are quiescent and extinguished, and its self-nature is free from the three types of marks and so forth—not because it is severed, but because it is detached from them.
Regarding the question, "What is the meaning of this?"—it asks what the intended meaning of the verse’s exposition of the sūtra is.
From here on, the response explains the meaning of that question.
The answer, "The nature of the conditioned is distinguished," and so forth, points out the conceptual attachments of the deluded regarding the first line of the verse.

To prevent the misconception that one attains the body of a Tathāgata through the perfection of marks, the second line of the verse negates the aforementioned conceptual attachment; this is precisely the explanation of the scriptural passage, "One does not see the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of marks," and thus the scripture is cited.

Regarding the phrase "For what reason": for what reason is it stated that one cannot perceive the Dharma-body Tathāgata by means of the three marks? It is explained that the Tathāgata is named the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) Dharma-body; this clarifies that because the essence of this Dharma-body lacks the three marks, it is unconditioned, and therefore cannot be perceived through marks.
Regarding the phrase "as in the sūtra" and so forth, these are all citations of sūtras and verses used as proof.
The statement "the accomplishment of those marks is itself the non-accomplishment of marks" is an explanation of the sūtra verse.
"Accomplishment of those marks" clarifies that the marks of the Nirmāṇakāya (the responsive Buddha) are threefold.
"That which is not the accomplishment of marks" means that these three marks of the Nirmāṇakāya are not the accomplishment of the marks of the unconditioned Dharmakāya.
This verse from the sutra clarifies that the Dharma-body possesses no conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*); therefore, it serves as a proof.
As for the phrase "For what reason," it intends to introduce the subsequent verse to explain the following passage of the sutra which asks:
"For what reason do the three marks of the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) constitute its accomplishment, while the Dharma-body does not accomplish these marks? Thus, it says, "For what reason."
Regarding the phrase "Because the three marks are different from the essence of the Tathāgata," this again cites the preceding verse as an explanation.

Although the verse was already employed above to provide proof, it is cited once more here as an explanation because this single line universally elucidates the scriptural passages at both locations; therefore, the verse is brought back in the middle to explain the subsequent scripture.

Regarding the statement, "This phrase reveals that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are false," this refers to the Master of the Treatise’s application of this verse to the *Sarvadharmasvabhāvanirdeśa-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Characteristics of All Phenomena).

As for why the verse says, "Apart from those is the Tathāgata," and why this verse is cited separately: while the preceding section generally adduced evidence for the meaning, it had not yet specifically explained the wording of the sūtra; therefore, this verse is further cited here to provide that specific explanation.
The passage beginning with "If one perceives all marks as non-marks" and so forth is the conclusion.

Regarding the statement, "This phrase clarifies that the essence of the Tathāgata is not conditioned," this refers to the Master of the Treatise's application of the scriptural and commentarial passage beginning with "If one perceives all marks as non-marks."
From "The Bodhisattva thus knows the Tathāgata" onwards, the explanation of the doubts via the sūtra is concluded; this summarizes the intent of the response that resolved those doubts.
*Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*, Scroll Two [and] Scroll Three.
From this point onward, the Venerable Subhūti gives rise to doubt and poses a question:
"Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: 'Are there any sentient beings in future ages who will give rise to the perception of reality regarding this sūtra?

And so forth. From here below, there are two sections of the sūtra; this constitutes the sixth major section, titled "The Division on the Emptiness of Self and the Emptiness of Dharmas," which is also known as the "Section on Abiding in Liberated Eloquence."

The reason they are called "emptiness of self" (*ātma-śūnyatā*) and "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is that, in response to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) that conceive of a self, the four propositions that clarify the absence of self are used to explain emptiness of self.

This clarifies that the bodhisattva who is capable of faith understands that, within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings, there has been from the very beginning no fixed, substantial *puruṣa*, *sattva*, *jīva*, or *āyuḥ*—these four being taken as the "self"—nor does there exist a fixed, substantial five aggregates as the causal conditions for "what belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*).
Because one does not perceive a fixed nature of "mine" that can be eliminated, it is called the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*).
As for the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), it is explained through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding phenomena.

Regarding the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*): one directly perceives that while the aggregates (*skandha*) have a determinate nature, the self has no determinate nature; yet, the causal conditions (*pratyaya*) that give rise to these aggregates—the very substance of the dharmas—have not yet been seen as empty.

Now it is clarified that these arising aggregates are not merely devoid of a determinate, substantial *ātman*; their substance is characterized by arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, being false and illusory. From the outset they are quiescent, and even their provisional names do not exist; therefore, this is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Furthermore, one knows that the Buddha-nature and True Suchness (tathatā) are eternally constant throughout past and present, their essence being without direction or form; this is also called the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasūnyatā).

It is also called the "segment of unrestrained eloquence" (*yìnfàng biàncái*). The reason it is named "unrestrained eloquence" is that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have attained the sovereign eloquence of the *amogha-dhāraṇī*, whereby they are able to answer according to any question with a transcendent explanation. Since their responses are entirely at will yet the meanings do not contradict one another from beginning to end, it is called "unrestrained eloquence."
Because this section contains the meaning of "unrestrained eloquence" (*anābhoga-pratibhāna*), it is called the "Section on Unrestrained Eloquence.
It may also be termed the "Part for Those Capable of Faith," as this section clarifies that three types of persons are able to believe in this sutra.
In what sequence does this sutra arise?
In the fourth section above, it clarifies practicing giving without dwelling on signs, thereby explaining the profound meaning of the cause.
In the fifth section, it distinguishes that the Tathāgata does not possess conditioned marks, thereby explaining the profound meaning of the fruit.
Some may harbor doubts, thinking:
"The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is not solely for the benefit of the great assembly present here; it also extends its benefits to sentient beings of the future Semblance Dharma period.

While those in the present assembly have personally beheld the Tathāgata and are themselves great bodhisattvas who have practiced for a long time—possessing pure and thick roots of goodness and profound, subtle wisdom—they may well be able to give rise to faith in this profound sutra. However, sentient beings of future ages will have meager roots of goodness and scant wisdom, and thus they will be unable to give rise to faith in this sutra concerning the profound law of cause and effect."
If this were so, then the Tathāgata’s teaching would be empty and useless; how, then, could it be said that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma non-emptily?
If his teaching were empty and useless, the Tathāgata would not be an omniscient one.

Regarding these two kinds of profound sūtras on cause and effect, will there be anyone in the future, at the end of the age, who is able to believe them, or will there be no one who is able to believe them?
Because such doubts existed,
Subhūti voiced the concerns of the great assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, in the midst of this evil age, will there be any sentient beings capable of believing in this sutra and regarding it as the true mark?"
The Buddha replied below:

"There are those who are able to believe that in the future evil age there will be three types of people—those who uphold the precepts, cultivate merit, and possess wisdom—who can believe this sutra and give rise to the realization of the true nature (bhūtatathatā); therefore, it is explained next."
One should ask:
there are three types of people capable of faith; why, then, is only the sixth section named after the two emptinesses of self and phenomena (*pudgala-śūnyatā* and *dharma-śūnyatā*)?

This is to clarify that the two types of persons who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit reside prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*), where they look up to and practice the two emptinesses, giving rise to faith through hearing.
Those who possess wisdom are those from the first bhūmi upward, who directly perceive the emptiness of both self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā*) and give rise to faith within that realization.

Nevertheless, although the former two individuals have not yet attained direct realization, because they likewise contemplate the twofold emptiness and perceive the principle in a general manner, they are both listed among those capable of faith.

Now, although there are three types of people who are able to believe, these names are designated according to the superior realms perceived by each of those three; thus, they are called the divisions of the emptiness of self and the emptiness of dharmas.

However, as we are now about to state that there are people who can believe, we first offer this preclusion: do not make such a claim. This clarifies that in the evil world of the future, there will be people who can believe in this sutra; one should not ask whether or not there are any who can give rise to faith.
Having heard the Tathāgata’s prohibitory words, "Do not speak thus," Subhūti immediately conceived a doubt:
"I do not now understand the Buddha's intention; does he mean that no one at all can believe this, and that he has simply silenced me?"
Is there anyone capable of believing and restraining me so that I may listen attentively?
Therefore, the Buddha answered, "There is," whereby he clarified that there is indeed someone capable of belief.

Although it was said that there is someone capable of belief, as it was not yet known what kind of person could believe, he immediately stated that in a future age there will be bodhisattvas capable of belief.
Furthermore, what virtues does this bodhisattva possess, and what realms does he contemplate, such that he is able to believe in this sutra?

Therefore, it next states that he "possesses the observance of precepts, the cultivation of merit, and wisdom. This collectively clarifies that there are three types of persons who possess the virtue capable of believing.

The reason this is called "upholding the precepts" is to clarify that such a person has long made offerings to the Buddhas and has previously heard this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* as well as other Mahāyāna sūtras. Within these, they have developed faith, upheld, read, recited, and practiced according to the teachings; they know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and having resolved their minds on Bodhi, they practice with careful adherence to the instructions. Only such a person is said to uphold the precepts in a true and ultimate sense; it is not merely those who uphold the *vinaya* rules who are considered to be upholding the precepts.
Regarding "merit" (puṇya): it clarifies that when this bodhisattva extensively offers precious wealth to the various Buddhas and practices the perfections (pāramitās), it is called merit.
These two individuals, while still on the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), hear [the teaching] and believe it with reverence.

As for "wisdom," it clarifies that these persons have completed their practice throughout the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and have ascended to the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*). They directly perceive the emptiness of both self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā*) and believe through personal realization; thus, they are said to possess wisdom.
This clarifies that these three types of people are able to give rise to faith in the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) regarding this sutra.

As for the term "true aspect," it clarifies that those three kinds of people are able to believe that the aforementioned practice of non-apprehension of marks is the cause of the signless (*animitta*), which truly brings about the unconditioned dharma of the *dharmakāya*; and they also believe that the unconditioned *dharmakāya* is the fruit of the signless, which is real and not false. Because they are able to produce an understanding of the true aspect, it is said that they take this to be the reality.

Although the above passage generally sets forth the qualities of the three types of persons capable of faith, it clarifies that the first two types of persons generate faith through hearing while still on the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrvamgama*), whereas the person of wisdom attains realization-based faith once they have reached the grounds.

Now, regarding these two former individuals: if they were still at the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*), was it because this person had already made offerings to various Buddhas and had previously cultivated the bodhicitta that they were able to believe, or was it that they were able to believe this sutra despite not yet having practiced?
If there are those who have already made offerings to various Buddhas and have long practiced the path, how many Buddhas must they have served?
Therefore, the Buddha told Subhūti: "You should know that such bodhisattvas have not come from having planted roots of goodness under only one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas."
However, among these three types of persons, I shall first separately clarify that the former two do not necessarily possess the virtue of faith resulting from recent practice.

This sutra straightforwardly and generally clarifies the virtue of faith possessed by these two types of persons; it cannot be definitively restricted to those within the stages of the *śikṣamāṇa* (learning), *gotra* (nature), or *mārga* (path) categories, because its meaning applies throughout both the higher and lower levels.

Regarding the phrase "The offerings cultivated by the Buddhas of the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth [assemblies]," this specifically identifies those who uphold the precepts. It clarifies that such Bodhisattvas are able to believe in this sutra; practicing according to what is taught in this sutra so as to accord with the Noble Ones' minds is called the "first offering," and it does not mean that incense, flowers, and the like constitute an offering.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "not having planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas": those who extensively offer robes, rare jewels, wealth, and material goods to the Buddhas and cultivate the practices of the *pāramitās* are called people of merit and virtue.

Regarding the phrase "having cultivated practice, made offerings, and planted roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas," it simply states that one has cultivated practice, made offerings, and planted roots of goodness in the presence of more than one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas, but it does not specify exactly how many Buddhas.

It should now be understood that this person has, under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads, even up to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas, maintained the precepts and cultivated merit; it is not someone of recent practice who can give rise to such faith.

Regarding the phrase "even for a single thought-moment, one is able to give rise to pure faith," this clarifies that both types of persons have long made offerings to various Buddhas and planted causes over a vast period, such that they are now able to give rise to faith in this profound sutra.
This is a semblance of faith arising from hearing, not the faith of realization;
yet, this single thought of faith is certain not to regress and is free from the turbidity of doubt, so it may still be called "pure faith," let alone when it persists for a long time.

Although the Tathāgata above has answered these two types of people—that those who have previously made offerings to various Buddhas can believe in this sutra—the assembly still harbors doubts, saying:
"For what reason is it that although these individuals have made offerings to many Buddhas, he speaks only of generating a single thought of faith? This is far too little."
If this is so, it remains unknown whether these two individuals are definitively able to believe in this sutra or not.

Therefore, the Buddha replies, "The Tathāgata fully knows and sees all these sentient beings," clarifying that the Tathāgata himself declares, "I am one who possesses all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñā). Whatever I say, I know it with perfect clarity; I never speak falsely. You should therefore believe my words and harbor no doubts.
Now, as for the phrase "knowing all," it means knowing through present wisdom;
"seeing all" means seeing with the Buddha-eye.
This knowing and seeing, moreover, logically applies to three types of persons.
Now, we have only clarified the first two persons, but have not yet clarified the third.
Why is this? That which has already been clarified herein is the "unrestrained eloquence" (*anābhoga-pratibhāna*), which is explained according to one's inclination both before and after.

However, because all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have attained the *dhāraṇī* of mastery, their speech accords with principle; they may speak according to their will, whether in sequence or by leaping over sections, yet both the phrasing and the meaning remain consistent. They do not lose the proper order, nor do they contradict one another, unlike ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles who must recite in strict sequence, for if they were to skip ahead, they would fail.
One may also say that he only knows and sees the first two persons, without mentioning the third.
How is this known? Because the meaning encompasses all three persons.

Having finished explaining the three types of people according to the commentary on the *Śālistamba-sūtra*, one then proceeds to explain "knowing all and seeing all. Thus, it is known that for those who exercise their spontaneous eloquence, the sequence may be arranged according to their own preference.

Regarding the phrase "giving rise to such an immeasurable accumulation of merit" and so forth: although it was previously explained that these two types of persons possess both the practices of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and merit (*puṇya*), and are thus able to believe in the two kinds of profound sūtras, even to the point of giving rise to a single thought of pure faith, it remains unknown whether, by virtue of this merit of being able to believe, they will have something attained or nothing attained in future lives.
Therefore, the answer states: "One generates such an immeasurable mass of merit and grasps such immeasurable merit.
This clarifies that the person capable of faith will obtain even more merit in future lives; it is not the case that they gain nothing at all.

"Generating merit" clarifies the two kinds of faith held by bodhisattvas: proximately, it serves as the cause for the first stage (*bhūmi*); distantly, it ultimately serves as its superior cause for the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that "a mass of merit is generated."

Regarding "attaining immeasurable merit": this clarifies that such merit does not merely function as a causal condition; rather, by relying on this faith, one is able to practice with certainty, manifesting the body of the Dharma-realm and realizing the immeasurable merit of the Buddha-fruit—hence, it is said that one "attains" it.
"Why is this? Subhūti!
These bodhisattvas no longer possess the mark of a self," and so forth; this specifically clarifies that the third type of person, one endowed with wisdom, is able to believe in this sutra.

Regarding the phrase "For what reason": previously, it was specifically explained that the first two types of persons possess the practices of maintaining the precepts, cultivating merit, and being able to have faith; however, it has not yet been specifically explained that the third type of person possesses the virtue of being able to have faith.
Now, the intent of the doubter’s question is as follows:

they do not yet know what further significance, what practice, what understanding, or what realization the aforementioned third type of person possessing wisdom has, such that they are called a person possessing wisdom who can believe in this sutra.
Because there is such a question, it is asked, "For what reason?

Now, wishing to set forth the conduct of the third type of person who is capable of faith, he answers by saying, "These bodhisattvas no longer possess the mark of self," and so forth. This clarifies that this person, having attained the first bhūmi and above, possesses the realization of the emptiness of self and the emptiness of phenomena; they believe through personal verification. Therefore, they are called "wise people capable of believing this sutra.
They differ from the previous two types of people, who hear the Dharma from others and give rise to faith based on their teachings.

Regarding the passage "these bodhisattvas no longer possess the mark of self," etc., the Commentary explains these four as the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*); based on the four types of marks of self that are to be countered, it describes the four types of counteractive marks of non-self (*anātman*).
"Having no further notion of a self" (*ātman*) serves as the antidote to the notion of a self.

Outsiders and ordinary worldlings speculate that there exists a divine self (*puruṣa*), which they claim is either identical to the five aggregates (*skandha*), different from them, or neither identical nor different. They argue: "If there were no self, by what means could one look, blink, come, go, advance, or stop? By what could one perceive suffering or pleasure? It is from this that we know the self exists."

In response to this calculation, it is said that there is no mark of self; this clarifies that within the causal dharma of the five aggregates of sentient beings, there is no fixed, real *ātman* or "mine," and therefore it is called the mark of non-self.

Regarding "the absence of the mark of a sentient being": there are non-Buddhists who recklessly speculate that the reason sentient beings do not cease or terminate but continue to abide in the world is because of the existence of a self (ātman) or a sentient being.

To counteract this misconception, it is said that there is no characteristic of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*). This clarifies that there is only the illusory continuity of the aggregates (*skandha*) arising and ceasing; it does not exist by virtue of a permanent self (*ātman*) that neither perishes nor is extinguished. Therefore, it is said that there is no characteristic of a sentient being.
The "mark of no person" (anātman-lakṣaṇa) is the antidote to the mark of a person (pudgala-lakṣaṇa).

There are non-Buddhists who recklessly speculate that the reason a single retributive life-force does not cease is due to the existence of a self (ātman); they thus claim that the lifespan has limits of length or brevity and that there are differences in its quality.
To counteract this misconception, it is said that there is no characteristic of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*).

This sūtra’s statement that "there is no characteristic of a person" is termed the "characteristic of life-force" (*jīva-nimitta*) in the subsequent treatise. It clarifies that the reason for the length or brevity of this life-force is that the karma of sentient beings has varying degrees of thickness; thus, life is either long or short due to karma, and not because of a self (*ātman*).

The Bodhisattva understands that this provisional life is entirely empty and quiescent, and does not perceive a life of a substantial self; therefore, it is said that there is no mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*).
"No mark of a life-sustainer" (*jīvaka-nimitta*) is the antidote to the mark of a life-sustainer.

There are non-Buddhists who hold erroneous views, asserting that because there exists a self (ātman), one dies here and is born there, passing directly through the six realms of existence to undergo rebirth.
They argue: "If there were no self, who would receive the retribution of the various destinies?"

To counteract this view, it is said that there is no characteristic of a life-principle (*jīva*). [The opponent argues: "If the divine self (*ātman*) were eternal, by what means could one be born within the six realms?

Yet, the reason for birth and death existing now is precisely because there is no divine self; rather, it is merely a 'practitioner' designated by a provisional name who, driven by karma such as good and evil, passes through the various destinies to receive retribution."
If there were a self, there would be no meaning to rebirth.

The Bodhisattva understands that the five aggregates of sentient beings are illusory, unreal, and devoid of a divine self or a life-principle; because he does not perceive these characteristics, it is said that he is "without the mark of a life-principle."

Nevertheless, according to worldly conventions of debate, there are one hundred names for "self" and "sentient beings," which cannot be enumerated in detail; rather, we shall distinguish these four dharmas in contrast to the four kinds of false characteristics of self, thereby clarifying non-self and emptiness.
Regarding the passage, "Subhūti!

These bodhisattvas have no mark of dharmas," and so forth, the Commentary explains these four as "the emptiness of dharmas" (*dharma-śūnyatā*); it teaches four kinds of remedial dharmas based on four kinds of marks of the dharmas that are to be countered.
"Absence of the marks of dharmas" (dharmanimittābhāva) is the antidote to the marks of dharmas. What are the marks of dharmas?
Ordinary persons, within the twelve bases (āyatana), perceive a distinction between the grasper and the graspable; therefore, they reckon these to be substantially existent.

To counteract this mind, it is said that there is no characteristic of dharmas; this clarifies that the twelve bases—the six consciousnesses as the grasper and the six sense objects as the grasped—are all empty and quiescent, being fundamentally unarisen from the beginning.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "There is not a single dharma that transcends the nature of dharmas (dharmatā); even nirvāṇa, I declare, is like an illusion and like a magical transformation."
The phrase "nor is it the characteristic of non-existence" serves as an antidote to the characteristic of non-dharmas.

Those who harbor doubts, upon hearing that all dharmas within the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are empty, may then claim that even unconditioned dharmas such as *tathatā* and Buddha-nature are empty by nature, asserting that they are identical to emptiness in the same way that space, a tortoise’s hair, or a rabbit’s horns are non-existent unconditioned things.

To counter this doubt, he replies that it is "also not non-existent. He clarifies that when it is said all phenomena are empty, it is because conditioned phenomena lack intrinsic nature and characteristics, and are thus empty; however, True Suchness and Buddha-nature are replete with the myriad virtues, their essence being wondrous existence, serene and eternally abiding. They are not empty phenomena; rather, they are called "empty" simply because their essence is devoid of the myriad marks.

It is not the same as the non-existence of the emptiness of the nature of previously mentioned conditioned dharmas, nor is it the same as the non-existence of things such as a rabbit’s horns; therefore, it is said that it is also not the characteristic of non-existence.
"Signlessness" (animitta) is the antidote to signs.

Those who harbor doubts, hearing that True Suchness (tathatā) possesses a substantial essence and is not empty, might then claim it is identical to the existence of conditioned phenomena such as form (rūpa).
Furthermore, it is said:
"If it exists, it should be identical to the existence of conditioned phenomena such as form, odor, taste, and touch;
if it does not exist, it should be identical to the non-existence of space, a rabbit's horns, and the like. This is called the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Because of this doubt, the answer states that it is "without marks" (*animitta*), clarifying that the essence of the *tathatā* dharma is a wondrous existence and a wondrous non-existence.
Although it is said to exist in its wondrous truth, this existence is not like that of prior dharmas such as form;
although it is said to be non-existent, this non-existence is not like that of a rabbit's horns. Therefore, it is called "without marks."

This explains, from the perspective of the distinct meanings of both principle and teaching, that the Dharma realized as True Suchness (tathatā) can never be described by means of the names and marks of existence or non-existence.
How does this third [point] differ from the first?

The first section above clarifies that all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are empty; this third section clarifies only that the essence of true suchness (tathatā) is the simultaneous transcendence of both existence and non-existence. This is the distinction between them.
"Nor is it signless" (*animitta*) refers to the counteractive measure against the signless. What is meant by "signless"?

When one who is doubtful hears that the Dharma of true realization transcends both signs of existence and non-existence, they conclude that the Dharma of true suchness (*tathatā*) is exclusively beyond verbal signs, and thus cannot be attained through expressions nor realized by relying on teachings. This is what is called "signless."

To address this doubt, the response states that it is not the case that [the teaching] is without characteristics (*animitta*). This clarifies that although the realized Dharma of *tathatā* (suchness) cannot be described by names or characteristics, it is not that one does not investigate these names, characteristics, and verbal teachings to accord with the principle of the nameless and characteristic-less *tathatā*. It clarifies that because one realizes this unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) Dharma of *tathatā*, one speaks of the unconditioned Dharma; thus, it is also not without characteristics. This demonstrates that from the perspective of the single meaning of both principle and teaching, *tathatā* is not without characteristics, and it can be understood through the provisional teachings of the Śrāvakas.
How does this fourth [section] differ from the second?

In the aforementioned second section, it was clarified that although the essence of the *tathatā* (suchness) is empty and devoid of the ten thousand marks (*lakṣaṇa*), its substance is a wondrous existence. Now, in this fourth section, it is clarified that while the essence of the *tathatā* is utterly beyond words and the like, as well as the ten thousand marks of the conditioned, one realizes the principle through verbal expression and there is discourse based on realization. Thus, because the fundamental and the derivative are mutually inferential and the principle is not entirely detached [from phenomena], one can say that within the realized dharma of *tathatā*, names, sounds, and teachings can be spoken. This is the distinction between them.
However, this twofold emptiness of self and phenomena will be explained in the subsequent verses and commentary.
Furthermore: "For what reason? Subhūti!"

Regarding the statement, "If these bodhisattvas grasp at the marks of dharmas, they are then attached to a self," etc., why does this second [objection] arise? It arises because, upon hearing the fourth phrase of the aforementioned emptiness of dharmas—which states that it is also not the case that there are no marks—they again grasp at the realized dharma as being identical to names and marks. They then doubt, saying:

"If these bodhisattvas are wise persons who have already attained the realization of the twofold emptiness of self and dharmas and have severed the delusions regarding self and dharmas, for what reason do they still give rise to thoughts, claiming that this realized dharma is identical to names and marks; and further, saying 'I possess wisdom capable of contemplating the twofold emptiness of self and dharmas,' 'I am able to practice and sever afflictions,' and 'I am able to teach and transform sentient beings'?"
If that were so, this bodhisattva would either sever the marks of self (*ātman*) and so forth, or fail to exhaust them.
Because there is such a doubt, the text asks, "For what reason?

Furthermore, one who understands "for what reason" may raise an objection; or, when hearing the teaching on emptiness, one might explain the fourth alternative as follows: although *tathatā* (suchness) is devoid of names and marks, it is not the case that verbal expression does not exist by virtue of this *tathatā* as the realized dharma. These sounds and verbal teachings still serve to elucidate realized wisdom, and by means of these verbal teachings, one attains that realized wisdom.

If this were so, then within the realization of True Suchness (tathatā) there would be names and signs; why, then, is it said that True Suchness is without names and signs and is neither existent nor non-existent?

Therefore, the response is as follows: "If these bodhisattvas grasp at dharmas, they are attached to self, person, and so forth. This clarifies that although a bodhisattva of the first stage (bhūmi) has attained the understanding of the emptiness of both self and dharmas, they have only severed the single grade of coarse afflictions to be abandoned in the first stage. They still possess the subtle discriminating mind of functional afflictions—the fundamental ignorance of the Dwelling Grounds (catvāra āśraya-vidyā-sthānīya-avidyā-bhūmi) from the second stage upward and the attachment to wholesome dharmas. Thus, it is said they are "attached to self, person, and so forth"; it does not mean that they still possess the coarse afflictions of the four dwelling grounds or that they grasp at the realization of dharmas as having names and signs.
Previously it was stated that this Bodhisattva is "without marks" (animitta), and subsequently it was stated that there is "no mark of dharmas" (dharma-nimitta).

This already clarifies that the Bodhisattva has attained the realization of the twofold emptiness of self and dharmas; yet, within this same context, it further states, "If one grasps at the mark of dharmas, one is then attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span. Such is the reason for the apparent contradiction between these two passages.
Now, although these two passages appear to be contradictory, their underlying principles are in profound accord. How are they in accord?

The former clarifies that a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*bhūmi*) attains the realization that treats both self and dharmas as empty; when it speaks of the "absence of marks such as self," it merely clarifies the coarse afflictions (*kleśa*) of the four abodes (*catur-vāsa*) to be severed at the first stage. It does not yet address the subtle darkness of fundamental ignorance—the afflictions of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-kleśa*)—which remain within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) from the second stage upward. As stated in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*: "I am able to know the dharmas and enter meditative absorption; I am able to transform sentient beings," and so forth, indicating that even minute afflictions have not yet been exhausted.
We know this to be so because the subsequent commentary explains: "There is only ignorance, but no active gross afflictions. This is how we know.

Regarding the phrase "if one grasps at the characteristics of phenomena," it clarifies that although this bodhisattva has attained the understanding of the emptiness of both self and phenomena, they still give rise to conceptualization. Thinking, "I possess the wisdom capable of understanding the emptiness of both self and phenomena," this subtle conceptualization is the very root of the view of self. Speaking in terms of the gross, it says "clinging to self and person," etc.; this explains the preceding point on the emptiness of self.
If there were any characteristic of dharmas, one would also conceptually declare: "Because I possess wisdom, I am able to understand the emptiness of these two kinds of dharmas.
This explains the aforementioned emptiness of dharmas; it may also be said that this first explains the emptiness of dharmas.

However, the reason why these two are not fixed is that they both clarify attachment within wholesome dharmas; since there is no other distinct object, there is no contradiction between the preceding and the following.

If one were to follow the sequential order, one should first explain the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and subsequently explain the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), since the second section clearly elucidates the emptiness of phenomena; yet here, the explanation of the emptiness of phenomena is set aside, and only then is the emptiness of the self explained.
Furthermore, these two phrases, "if one grasps the characteristics of dharmas," are listed first in the sūtra;
whereas "one should not grasp dharmas, nor should one not grasp them" follows according to the sequence of the sūtra.
Furthermore, the commentary on the following section appears prior to the two verses. Why is this so?

This third scriptural passage serves as an explanation; it is necessary to clarify the distinctions in the arising of faith among the three types of persons, and for the sake of contextual convenience, the explanation is placed first.

The reason why these two preceding phrases are again explained after "knowing all and seeing all" is to establish the practice of faith of the two aforementioned types of persons; only then are the two preceding phrases explained.
Regarding the phrase "For what reason," this is the third instance of "for what reason.
A doubter, having heard the explanation of the third and fourth lines concerning the emptiness of the aforementioned dharmas, might wonder:

"Although the realized dharmas lack names and marks, it is not that they cannot be explained by relying on words; therefore, speech is also not without marks. Thus, one might cling to the notion that if the previously mentioned realized dharmas can be expressed through names and phrases, then these expressive names and phrases must exist within the realized wisdom itself.

If that were so, the realized Dharma would possess characteristics; how then could it be said above that the essence of the realized Dharma, True Suchness (tathatā), is without name or characteristic?
However, the Tathāgata’s words are not fixed: when I say it exists, the Tathāgata says it does not exist; when I just said it does not exist, the Tathāgata further tells me that it exists.
Why is this? It is because [the Buddha] did not provide a definitive statement for me;

thus the question "Why is this? was asked. To dispel this attachment, he replied: "One should neither grasp at dharmas nor fail to grasp at dharmas. This clarifies that the principle of the Middle Way cannot be definitively stated as either existence or non-existence. If one were to definitively state existence or non-existence, one would fear falling into the two extremes. If one falls into the two extremes, one becomes attached to the marks of a self, a person, sentient beings, and so forth; therefore, it cannot be definitively stated.

Regarding the phrase "one should not grasp at dharmas": this clarifies that although [dharmas] are explained by relying on linguistic expressions, their principle is nonetheless beyond names and signs; thus, one should not take vocal teachings as proof of the Dharma by regarding them as having characteristics.

Regarding the phrase "not the non-apprehension of dharmas": upon hearing that one should not apprehend dharmas, one might then realize that dharmas are entirely devoid of names and marks, and thus cannot be explained by relying on provisional teachings.

If there were no names or signs by which one could rely on provisional teachings to explain them, then one would further claim that vocal instructions and verbal teachings are not the Dharma, thereby discarding their capacity to express meaning.
To dispel this doubt, it is said that they are not "not-grasping dharmas.

This clarifies the intent of the ineffable: it does not mean that one cannot rely on names and signs to speak, nor borrow verbal explanations to awaken; thus, verbal teaching is not categorically non-dharmic, which is why it is said they are not "not-grasping dharmas."

The reason one cannot definitively state that it exists or does not exist is to clarify that this dharma possesses both the meaning of non-existence and the meaning of existence. Although the essence of the *tathatā* (suchness) is a wondrous existence, it is without name and without marks; therefore, it cannot be definitively stated to exist, lest people grasp at it as being identical to conventional existence characterized by names and marks.

However, although this *tathatā* (suchness) is devoid of names and marks, it cannot be definitively stated to be non-existent, for fear that people might equate it with the non-existence of things such as a rabbit’s horns.
The phrase "for this reason" provides a dual explanation of these two points.
For this reason, one should not grasp at the teachings of sound, because the Dharma realized as suchness is a principle that is nameless and signless;

yet, for this reason, one should not rely on verbal teachings to realize the Dharma, because verbal teachings and their names and signs are not categorically non-Dharmas, and one must not abandon their meaning.

Regarding the statement, "The Tathāgata has always taught the Dharma-gate of the raft parable": it is like a person riding a boat who both discards and takes up [the boat]; this is explained in detail in the commentary below, so it will not be fully analyzed here.
The phrase "these dharmas should be relinquished" corresponds to the preceding simile of the raft.
Furthermore, other sutras state: "Even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas."

According to the sūtras of the Hīnayāna, the statement that "even dharmas should be relinquished" clarifies that when a Hīnayāna arhat enters nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa), even untainted wholesome dharmas—such as the Eightfold Noble Path, the ten knowledges, and the three samādhis—should still be relinquished; how much more so, then, should unrighteous dharmas such as the ten non-virtues not be relinquished?

Furthermore, regarding the passage in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* which states, "Even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas," it means that even conditioned phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth—which still possess existence—should be relinquished; how much more so should one not relinquish those phenomena such as names for "tortoise hair" or "rabbit horns," which are false and lack reality?
Furthermore, other sutras likewise state, as this sutra does: "This dharma should be relinquished, because it is not the relinquishing of dharmas.

Regarding the phrase "this dharma should be relinquished," it clarifies that although one may encounter the ultimate meaning by following the expressions and thereby attain the principle, one must nevertheless discard the expressions; thus, one should relinquish the teaching, which establishes the aforementioned point that one should not grasp at dharmas.

Regarding the phrase "not abandoning the Dharma": this clarifies that from the initial practice of generating the bodhicitta until the attainment of Buddhahood, there is nothing that does not rely on the teachings to awaken to the principle and depend upon verbal expressions to comprehend the ultimate meaning. One must rely on these verbal instructions and cannot abandon them entirely; therefore, it is said "not abandoning the Dharma," which establishes the preceding point that it is "not the case that one does not take up the Dharma."
Regarding the phrase "The Commentary asks: 'What is the meaning of this? it means that the author of the commentary asks what the purpose of this section of the sūtra is.

The passage beginning with "Based on the preceding... and ending with "...explaining the profundity of the cause and the profundity of the result" serves to introduce the intent of generating doubt; it cites the fourth and fifth sections of the preceding sūtra as the points from which the doubt arises.

From "If that were so" up to "because it is not the relinquishing of the dharma," this constitutes the formal response to the doubt regarding the application of the method; this may be understood as explained in the initial sequential arising [of the stages] in the Sūtra.

Regarding the phrase "What is the meaning of this?": this restates the preceding sutra passage that was not yet challenged in order to raise a doubt; it serves as a general introduction to this section of the sutra to address the intent of the questioner's inquiry, though it has not yet been explained in detail.
The Master of the Treatise now wishes to provide a detailed explanation by means of verses; therefore, he asks what the intent of this sutra’s response to the inquiry is.
This section of the sutra is explained by means of eight lines of verse.

The first verse explains the dialogue between Subhūti’s question and the Tathāgata’s answer within the Sūtra, clarifying that in the evil age of the future, there will be three kinds of people who possess three kinds of virtues, and are therefore able to believe in this sūtra.
The second verse separately explains that the aforementioned two types of persons have long cultivated the causes [for awakening], and thus possess the virtue of being able to believe.

The third verse intends to explain that the third type of person, the one of wisdom, likewise possesses the virtue of being able to believe; therefore, it again summarizes the two emptinesses of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā*) as the remedy and the object to be remedied, serving as the basis for the detailed exposition to follow.
The fourth verse correctly explains the four kinds of emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
The fifth verse correctly explains the four kinds of emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

The sixth verse serves as a response; however, it should have clarified only the third type of person, as there was no need to clarify the doubts and difficulties of the first two types. Therefore, it again summarizes them all to provide the explanation, clarifying that the first three types of persons possess the distinction of being capable of faith and are fully endowed with faith; thus, it is necessary to clarify these three types of persons.
The seventh verse explains "knowing all and seeing all.
The eighth verse explains the parable of the raft.

Regarding the first verse: the first line explains Subhūti’s question, while the subsequent three lines explain the Tathāgata’s response to Subhūti concerning those in future ages who have faith in the Bodhisattvas and so forth, up to regarding this as the truth.

Regarding the phrase "explaining the profound meaning of cause and effect," this explains the preceding sutra by citing both the fourth and fifth scriptural passages on cause and effect from that sutra concerning such teachings heard, thereby formulating the inquiry.
Inquiry: Why is it that future people in the final age will be unable to give rise to faith in the two kinds of profound meanings—the cause and effect and the signlessness—expounded by the Tathāgata?
How is it that the Tathāgata himself has constantly declared:

I am an omniscient one who well understands the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings; I preach the Dharma in accordance with those faculties, and what I preach is invariably beneficial and never in vain.

Therefore, the verse replies: "In that evil age, it shall not be empty, for there will be reality. This correctly explains the Buddha’s response to Subhūti in the sutra concerning future bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: although it is difficult to find those with faith in such an evil age, if there are people capable of faith, it is not a hollow teaching.
Who is the person capable of faith?
The following phrase points this out by stating, "The Bodhisattva is endowed with the three virtues.

This sentence correctly explains those mentioned in the Sūtra who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit and wisdom; it generally sets forth the three kinds of virtues that enable a person to have faith. Thus, we know that the teaching is not in vain.
The second verse separately explains the virtues of the two types of people capable of faith, beginning from: "The Buddha told Subhūti:
'Not toward one Buddha, nor two Buddhas, but even toward as many as... they are able to give rise to a single thought of pure faith.'"

Regarding the phrase "having cultivated precepts in the past and planted various roots of goodness," these two lines identify two types of persons: those who maintain the precepts and those who cultivate merit. It clarifies that such individuals have in the past made offerings to the Buddhas, heard Mahāyāna sūtras and given rise to faith without slandering them, were able to generate the bodhicitta, and practiced according to the teachings; this is what is termed "maintaining the precepts."

Extensively offering internal and external treasures to all Buddhas and all sentient beings, practicing the pāramitās, and planting various roots of goodness—this correctly explains the passage in the sutra: "It is not by practicing and making offerings under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas that one plants roots of goodness."
Question: If these persons have already made offerings to the Buddhas, how many Buddhas must they have served? Therefore, the latter half of the verse answers:

"Having fulfilled the precepts under all Buddhas, their merits are also said to be complete. This correctly explains the scriptural passage, "Having practiced and made offerings under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, they have planted roots of goodness. It clarifies that these two types of people did not merely practice and plant roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas; rather, it was through practicing and making offerings under immeasurable Buddhas, accumulating superior causes over a long period, that they were able to give rise to pure faith in this sutra.

This second half-verse reiterates the two types of persons mentioned above; it is repeated because the sutra contains two layers [of explanation], and thus the Master of the Treatise, following the sutra, cites them once more.

From "As stated in the Sūtra" down to "planting various roots of goodness," this marks the conclusion of the Master of the Treatise’s explanation of the Sūtra in verse; he summarizes both sections of the Sūtra by concluding with these verses.

From this point in the sūtra text down to the phrase "because of being fully endowed with merit," the Master of the Treatise provides a brief exposition of the meaning elucidated in the sūtra’s verses, as he was unable to explain them extensively within the prose of the sūtra itself.
From the third verse onward, there are three verses that explain the "wise person" mentioned in the third section of the sutra.

Following the sequence of the sutra, one should have explained the scriptural passages such as "knowing all and seeing all"; however, since the meaning of this knowledge and vision is pervasive and may be applied freely to what precedes or follows, these are explained later in the treatise despite being listed earlier in the sutra, as this follows the author’s spontaneous eloquence (*pratibhāna*).

The phrase "that living being" (*jīva*) refers to four types [of self-views] within the mark of self (*ātman*). Thus, although it speaks of the "living being" alone, although all four calculations are explained here together, they are all equally calculations of a self; therefore, by citing one name, the other three can be understood.

Regarding the phrase "and phenomena" (*dharma*): this refers to four types among the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), and it is merely citing one name from among those characteristics of phenomena.
One should have said "characteristics of phenomena," but because of the constraints of the five-syllable verse, it is stated simply as "and phenomena."
This single phrase summarizes the eight kinds of dharmas to be remedied.

"Distant from grasping at signs" is the direct explanation of the two sections of the sutra—ranging from "these bodhisattvas have no sign of self" up to "nor even a sign of non-existence"—which clarify that attaining these eight kinds of resolute conviction can remedy the delusions of grasping at the aforementioned eight signs; hence, it is said they are "distant from grasping at signs."

Regarding the phrase "also explaining the knowledge of their characteristics": this clarifies why the two emptinesses of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā*)—the remedies and the objects to be remedied—are cited. It is because one intends to further elaborate on the meaning of the third category, the person endowed with wisdom; therefore, it says "also explaining the knowledge of the characteristics of the non-interruption of that wise person.

Furthermore, it is not only the characteristics of the non-interruption of the wise person that are explained, but also the knowledge of the characteristics of the non-interruption of the preceding two types of persons.
Regarding the phrase "distinguished by eightfold meanings," there are eight types of remedial meanings corresponding to eight types of objects to be remedied.
This single verse serves as the basis for the two subsequent verses on the emptiness of self and the emptiness of phenomena; it does not provide a separate commentary on the scriptural text itself.

Regarding the phrase "What is the meaning of this?", it asks what the intended significance of this single verse is; therefore, the answer is: "Furthermore, because the meaning of *prajñā* is explained without interruption."

This text first explains the third phrase, and subsequently poses the question: "What meaning is being taught? It asks what the meaning of this teaching—that the meaning of *prajñā* is uninterrupted—is, and only thereafter cites the preceding two phrases regarding the remedy (*pratipakṣa*) and the object to be remedied (*vipakṣa*) to provide a brief explanation of the meaning of the remedy and the object to be remedied.

Although the remedies (*pratipakṣa*) and the objects to be remedied (*vipakṣa*) have been briefly explained, their specific numbers have not yet been enumerated; therefore, the fourth line of the verse is cited to conclude by specifying those numbers.
The section beginning with "How, moreover, is this so? details how the remedies and the objects to be remedied correspond to one another in pairs.
Regarding the question, "What is the meaning of this again?", the author of the treatise poses this inquiry in order to introduce the fourth verse below.

Although the preceding verse provided a general explanation of the four types of characteristics of a "life-principle" (jīva) and likewise a general explanation of the four types of meanings, what is the intended meaning now that each is being explained individually?

Therefore, the response is given as "the substance of differentiated continuity"; this single verse explains the four phrases from the preceding sutra beginning with "no longer having the mark of a self.
"Differentiated" clarifies the mark of a self.
"Continuity" refers to the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*).
"Persisting without interruption until the end of life" refers to the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*).
"Again proceeding toward another path" refers to the mark of a life-span (*jīva-nimitta*).
Regarding the phrase "the four kinds of the mark of self," this refers to the four types of the mark of self (*ātman*).
This single verse merely enumerates the four factors that are to be remedied (*pratipakṣya*).

From the words "What is the meaning of this? onwards, first the four names within the [category of] self are listed; next, the meaning of the four types of conceiving a self is explained; and finally, the four types of non-self-understanding (*anātma-adhimokṣa*) from the sūtra, which serve as remedies, are presented in opposition to the four types of conceiving minds.

Regarding the phrase "What about the dharmas?": The preceding verse explained the four lines beginning with the "life-principle" (jīva) and so forth; now, in order to explain the lines concerning "dharmas," the two characters from the second line of the original verse of the treatise are raised again as a question to introduce the following verse. Thus it says, "What about the dharmas? and is answered immediately with a verse.
This fifth verse explains the four lines in the Sūtra beginning with "the absence of the marks of dharmas" (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "all are empty and without marks," this correctly explains the passage in the Sūtra concerning these bodhisattvas' "absence of the marks of dharmas. It clarifies that outsiders (non-Buddhists) reckon the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the six objects (*viṣaya*)—that is, all dharmas consisting of the grasped and the grasper—as substantially existent; this is what is termed the "mark of dharmas."
To counteract this conception, it is said that "all is empty.

As for "emptiness," these twelve bases (*āyatana*) and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are empty because they are fundamentally unarisen and devoid of intrinsic nature or characteristics;
as for unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), such as Buddha-nature and *nirvāṇa*, they are empty because they lack the ten thousand marks.
One should ask, "For what reason is it empty?
and answer, "Because there are no entities.
"No entities" means that emptiness is devoid of entities such as form and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "truly existent," this correctly explains the sūtra’s statement that "it is also not a non-existent characteristic.

When one hears it said that all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are empty, a doubter might think that even unconditioned dharmas such as nirvāṇa and buddha-nature are likewise empty of substance like conditioned phenomena; this is called the "characteristic of non-dharma."

To counteract this misconception, he replied that it "truly exists," clarifying that the essence of Buddha-nature and nirvana is a sublime existence (*sadbhāva*). It is empty because it lacks the ten thousand marks (*lakṣaṇa*); however, one must not hear that all phenomena are empty and conclude that nirvana and Buddha-nature are like conditioned phenomena—empty because they lack substance due to false conceptualization. Therefore, he stated that they truly exist.
Regarding the term "ineffable" (*anabhilāpya*), it correctly explains the "signlessness" (*animitta*) within the sūtra.

Upon hearing that all phenomena are empty, those who harbor doubts might claim that the unconditioned reality of *tathatā* is the same as the emptiness of lack of intrinsic nature found in conditioned phenomena, or even the same as the non-existence of a tortoise's hair or a rabbit's horns; therefore, [the Buddha] replies that it "truly exists."

Having heard that True Suchness (tathatā) truly exists, those who harbor doubts conceive of it as having existence like that of conditioned phenomena—such as form, odor, taste, and touch; yet upon hearing that it is non-existent, they conceive of it as being non-existent like form or a rabbit’s horns.
These two types of conceptualization are termed "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*); because this [teaching] serves as their antidote, it is answered that they are "inexpressible.

This statement that they are "inexpressible" clarifies that the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is both wondrously existent and wondrously non-existent, yet differs from the existence of form and fragrance or the non-existence of intrinsic emptiness according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Because it simultaneously negates the dualistic conceptual attachments to both existence and non-existence, it is said to be inexpressible.
Regarding the phrase "spoken by relying on words," this correctly explains the scriptural statement that "it is also not without characteristics.
Hearing that it cannot be spoken, those who harbor doubts might then claim that *tathatā* (suchness) is categorically ineffable.
If suchness were thus ineffable, how could one generate the bodhicitta based on the scriptural teachings, rely upon the means of expression to practice, and thereby attain the fruit of Buddhahood?
This is called "non-characteristic."

To counteract this misconception, the answer states that it is "spoken based on words. This clarifies that although the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) transcends all verbal characteristics, one cannot realize this principle without relying upon vocal teachings; therefore, it is said to be "spoken based on words."

Regarding the phrase "these four kinds of characteristics of dharmas," this cites the four kinds of characteristics of that which is to be remedied (the *pratipakṣya*), thereby concluding the four kinds of non-existent characteristics of dharmas as the remedies (*pratipakṣa*) within the preceding three lines.
This single verse, moreover, universally enumerates both the remedial factors (*pratipakṣa*) and the factors to be remedied (*vipakṣa*).

Regarding the phrase "What are the four kinds? and so forth: although the fourth line of the preceding verse states that "these characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are of four kinds," their specific names had not yet been mentioned; they are now set forth by listing those four names.

Regarding the question, "What is the meaning of this?", it refers to the four types of names listed as the objects to be remedied in the first three lines of the preceding verse and in the prose commentary; the question asks what the intended meaning is regarding these remedies and their respective objects to be remedied.

"Because the grasper and the graspable ultimately do not exist as entities," this explains the first pair: the characteristic of non-existence (*abhāva-lakṣaṇa*) as the remedy and that which is to be remedied.

"Because those phenomena are empty of self-nature yet truly existent," it is said that they are also not characterized by non-existence; this explains the second pair: the characteristic of non-dharma (*adharma-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of not being non-existent (*na-abhāva-lakṣaṇa*) as the remedy and that which is to be remedied.
Now, regarding the phrase "those dharmas," it refers to those dharmas realized as suchness (*tathatā*).

As for "selflessness and emptiness," this clarifies the essential nature of that dharma of suchness: it is not only empty of a self and of dharmas, but is likewise empty of selflessness and the absence of dharmas.

Regarding the term "truly existent": fearing that some might hear it said that the realized dharma of *tathatā* transcends both existence and non-existence and is termed "selfless emptiness," and consequently conclude that the realized dharma is unilaterally empty and quiescent, it is stated that it is "truly existent" rather than being empty of essence.

Regarding the statement, "That is empty and devoid of substance, and because this cannot be said to be either existent or non-existent, it is called 'signless' (animitta)," this explains the third pair: the sign (nimitta) and the signless (animitta), as the remedial and the object to be remedied.

"From 'relying on words' up to 'relying on the characteristics of words'" explains the fourth pair: that which is neither characterized nor non-characterized, consisting of the remedy and its object to be remedied.

Regarding the phrase "departing from the eight kinds of characteristics by means of the eight kinds of differentiated meanings," this concludes the separate explanation of the two emptinesses—of self and phenomena—and simultaneously presents both the remedies and their objects of treatment to jointly conclude the two emptinesses.

Regarding the statement, "Therefore, it is said that he possesses wisdom": Previously, it was asked what further virtues the third person possesses such that they are able to believe in this sutra. Now, having clarified that this person can understand both the emptiness of the self and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and since the intention has been fully explained according to the sutras and śāstras, the term "wisdom" is brought forward here to collectively conclude his virtue of being able to believe.

As in the sūtra’s passage beginning with “the absence of the mark of phenomena” (*dharma-nimitta*), this separately concludes the fourth [point] regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Regarding the statement, “If one possesses wisdom, that is sufficient,” the objection is raised:
If this third type of person, possessing the understanding of the two kinds of emptiness, is able to manifest faith, then such a person is the most excellent.
If this is so, it would suffice merely to speak of the person possessing wisdom; why is it necessary to further clarify the two types of persons who maintain precepts and cultivate merit?
The answer states: "It is for the purpose of generating the meaning of the distinctions between their actual characteristics."
Now, wishing to explain the reason for the distinctions in the manifestations of the actual characteristics of birth, the Master of Treatises asks: "In what manner are they manifested?
He then answers in verse: "Those people, relying on faith, manifest the actual characteristics through reverence."

The reason for clarifying this single verse once again is that the preceding prose commentary states: "A person of wisdom who has realized the understanding of the two kinds of emptiness is certainly able to believe in this sutra and will not follow other teachings."

If that were so, this third person would be the most excellent; one should only clarify this wise person—why then is it necessary to further speak of the two types of persons who possess the merit of ethical discipline?

Therefore, this verse is established to clarify that faith is manifold and its meaning applies to all three types of persons; it is not limited solely to those possessing wisdom. This is because the former two types of persons—by taking the observance of precepts and the cultivation of merit as causes for their reverent faith—are able to attain the untainted wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness (of self and phenomena) pertaining to the stages beyond the world (*bhūmi*). Consequently, it is necessary to clarify these former two types of persons; one must not explain them as being exclusively those who possess wisdom.
Therefore, the long prose section below states, "It is not only that he speaks of Prajñā.

Regarding the phrase "that person relies on faith," this explains the two types of persons who maintain the precepts and cultivate merit; these are bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi) who have not yet attained direct perception of the present reality. Because they hear the Dharma from the Buddha and produce understanding based on faith, it is said that they "rely on faith."

Regarding the phrase "respect gives rise to the true mark" (*bhakti utpādayati bhūtalakṣaṇam*): this clarifies that these two types of persons respect the Tathāgata and, by heeding the Buddha’s words, are able to believe in this sutra; they take this as the true mark. Therefore, it is brought forth again by referring back to the preceding sutra.
