When those such as the *srotāpanna*, having already attained the realization of non-self, have severed the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*), and have realized the noble fruit—is it still possible for them to form a thought and discriminate, 'I have attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*'?"

Therefore, Subhūti replied, "No. He then explained why he said "no": because, in reality, there is no dharma named *srotāpanna*. This clarifies that at the moment of realizing the fruit, one attains the understanding of non-self; regarding nominally designated sentient beings and the dharmas of the five aggregates, they are all obliterated into a single emptiness without any discrimination, extending even to the six sense objects, which are likewise empty.

Within these internal dharmas of the five aggregates of sentient beings, one does not perceive even a single dharma that is fixed and real enough to be named "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) and so forth; nor does one perceive even a single dharma within the objects of the six sense-fields that is to be grasped. Therefore, one does not form the thought: "I have attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth."

From the passage "from the *srotāpanna* up to not having even a single dharma called an *arhat*," the four fruits are collectively cited to clarify that they cannot be grasped or described, thereby resolving the preceding doubt; the underlying principle may be understood by analogy.
Because he asked whether an Arhat does not entertain the thought "I have attained Arhatship," a doubt arose:
if an Arhat does not give rise to the thought "I have attained the fruit" at the time of realizing the fruit, for what reason does an Arhat still say, "I am an Arhat"?
Therefore, he replied: "World-Honored One!
If an Arhat were to have this thought:
'I have attained Arhatship.'"
This refers to being "attached to self, person," and so forth.

The meaning of the answer clarifies that the previous statement, "I do not harbor the thought that I have attained arhatship," means that at the time of realizing the fruit of arhatship, one has completely severed the four abiding delusions; therefore, one does not harbor the thought, "I am able to attain this fruit."

Because this Arhat has not yet severed the delusion of habitual tendencies and ignorance, he subsequently gives rise to the thought, "I have attained the fruit"; this does not mean that he possesses the four abodes of self-view, such as the view of a self, a person, or a life-soul.

However, according to this sutra, it discusses only the residual habits (*vāsanā*) that an Arhat has not yet eliminated, or it may not discuss what has not been severed by those in the first three fruits.

According to the interpretation of the lower treatise (*śāstra*), it comprehensively distinguishes all three types of persons, clarifying that while the first two have begun to sever the two attachments to self (*ātman*) and permanence (*nitya*), they still possess active afflictions (*kleśa*) because they have not yet severed these two attachments.

As for the latter two individuals, because their attachment to purity has also been eliminated, they lack the afflictions associated with formative activity (*saṃskāra-kleśa*), possessing only the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance.
Regarding the passage, “World-Honored One!

I have attained the foremost [status] regarding the Samādhi of Non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*) and so forth,” the Tathāgata has always taught that evil matters should be revealed and wholesome dharmas should be concealed. Why, then, does Subhūti here say of himself, “The Buddha has declared me to be foremost in the attainment of the Samādhi of Non-contention”?
However, Subhūti, wishing to draw upon what he himself had attained, did not form this thought:
"I have realized the Arhatship of one free from passion through the Samādhi of Non-contention, having accomplished the fourth fruit."
Regarding the meaning of "non-appropriation," there are points of agreement and disagreement.

To clarify, when other Arhats say, "I do not harbor thoughts [of self]," this means they lack the grossness of the four abodes (*catur-vāsa*), yet they may still not have severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the self.
Now, when Subhūti says that one does not form such thoughts, it means that even the habit of "self" is absent; because it has been well-subdued, it is not a case of permanent eradication.
The reason for saying this is to inspire faith in people, showing that Subhūti has truly realized this Dharma.
However, when Subhūti says he does not form such thoughts, it is because he constantly maintains mental vigilance to ensure that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of "self" do not arise.
Furthermore, Subhūti is a Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body appearing as a Śrāvaka; because he is eternally free from habitual tendencies, he does not form the thought, "I have attained Arhatship."

Regarding the statement, "The Buddha declared that I am foremost among those who have attained the samādhi of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*)," the reason this samādhi is named the "samādhi of non-contention" is that Subhūti is able to skillfully guard his mind against the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), such that he himself does not give rise to thoughts of greed, hatred, or delusion toward sentient beings, nor does he incite sentient beings to give rise to thoughts of greed, hatred, or delusion toward him.
Therefore, in the sutra, Subhūti himself says: "If anyone should find fault with me for sitting, I shall remain standing all day without moving from my place.
If anyone should find fault with me for standing, I shall remain seated all day," and so forth.

Therefore, when Subhūti went on his almsround, he would always observe sentient beings with a concentrated mind; if those before him did not give rise to obstacles toward him, he would enter the village, but if they did give rise to obstacles, he would stop and not go for alms.

It is explained that Subhūti, within the four modes of deportment, constantly and skillfully guards himself so that habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) do not arise; because he has attained this samādhi and does not compete with others, and because the portion of his afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) has been exhausted, he is said to have attained the "Samādhi of Non-contention" (*araṇā-samādhi*).
Just as Śāriputra and the other arhats were unable to skillfully restrain their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they competed with external objects.
Because they competed with external objects, they lacked the *araṇā-samādhi* (the concentration of non-contention).
If this is so, someone may raise an objection:
"The Tathāgata has exhausted all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); why then is he still subjected to slander and defamation by Sundarī and others?
Could it be that some habitual tendencies have not yet been exhausted?"
The meaning of the answer is that the Tathāgata is not slandered by others because he possesses habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); rather, there are two reasons for this.
First, because the Tathāgata knows the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings, he permits others to slander him so that, through such defamation, those beings may be delivered.
Second, it is for the purpose of manifesting the Buddha’s merits.
Now, although all five hundred great disciples of the Tathāgata have attained samādhi, they differ in degree and each has received the title of being "foremost" in a particular respect.
For example, Śāriputra attained ten thousand samādhis and was foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyāyana also attained ten thousand samādhis and was foremost in supernormal powers (ṛddhi).

Subhūti attained sixty thousand samādhis and was foremost among the disciples in the samādhi of non-contention (araṇā), which is why the Tathāgata frequently praised his virtues within the great assembly.
Subhūti has already attained sixty thousand samādhis and various other merits; for what reason does he praise only this one?
It is because this samādhi is superior among the merits of the sixty thousand samādhis, and therefore it is praised specifically.
"The World-Honored One has declared that I am an arhat free from desire," and so forth—this praises the foremost practice of emptiness.
From what kind of desire is one freed?
That which takes the five sensory objects as its sphere is called "desire."

This clarifies that "desire" refers to the objective realm itself, rather than the affliction of craving being called desire, for [Subhūti] has long since severed and exhausted such afflictions as craving.

It demonstrates that Subhūti has thoroughly realized the emptiness of the five sensory objects; thus, although he takes these five objects as conditions, these objects of desire cannot obstruct his mind.
It is said that he has "left desire" because he has exhausted the portion of obstacles to this samādhi and has attained a degree of mastery over the samādhis he has realized.

Regarding the statement, "Subhūti truly has nothing to practice," this clarifies that because Subhūti is free from the two obstacles, he does not form the thought of grasping at himself as being foremost in the *araṇā-samādhi*, nor does he think, "I am an Arhat who has left desire"; therefore, it is said that he truly has nothing to practice.

Regarding the phrase, "And he is named Subhūti, the one without contention, who practices the conduct of non-contention," this is a double reference to the two preceding scriptural phrases, "the samādhi of non-contention" and "the arhat free from desire. It clarifies that because Subhūti has no mental conception of himself as being foremost in the samādhi of non-contention or as being an arhat, and because even his residual habit-energies (vāsanā) do not function, he is free from the two kinds of obstacles; thus, both names—“without contention” and “practicing the conduct of non-contention”—are established for him.
What are the two kinds of hindrances? First is the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and second is the hindrance to samādhi.

Because Subhūti has skillfully attained the practice of emptiness, the portion of ignorance that ought to be eliminated is exhausted; the samādhi he has attained through purification is clear and discerning. Regarding what he has not yet attained, he does not claim to know it; regarding what he has already attained, he knows it as it truly is, without error. This ignorance cannot obstruct, constrain, or block his mind; therefore, it is said that he is free from the hindrance to samādhi.
Regarding the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), these refer to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion.

It is understood that Subhūti has attained the realization of selflessness and emptiness; having first exhausted the delusions of attachment to the nature of the four abodes (*catur-vāsabhūmi*), he further skillfully guards his mind so that he himself does not give rise to the habitual tendencies of greed, hatred, or delusion toward sentient beings, and likewise causes sentient beings not to give rise to afflictions such as desire toward his own person.
Because his mind is not obstructed by these two types of delusion—the coarse and the subtle—he is free from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*);

and because he has skillfully subdued habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), he is detached from the obstacle of afflictions, thereby enabling him to discern the minds of others and refrain from contending with external objects.

Because one has thoroughly realized that the preceding objects are empty, one is free from the obstacles to samādhi; since the mind is not obstructed by objects nor does it conflict with them, it is called "non-contention" and the "practice of non-contention."
Other arhats were not yet able to thoroughly realize that the essence of the five sense objects is empty; consequently, there were many errors within the samādhis they attained.
For instance, when Maudgalyāyana predicted that it would rain on a certain day, the heavens did not rain at all.

Because the wisdom of those śrāvakas is shallow and their contemplation of the mind is not penetrating, they are obstructed by external objects; consequently, within the samādhis attained at their respective levels, they lack purity and thus possess the obstacle of samādhi. Furthermore, because they are not skilled in guarding against habitual tendencies (vāsanā), they possess the obstacle of afflictions (kleśa-āvaraṇa).
Because these three stages involve practice that is non-dual and free from contention.

However, for śrāvakas, not only are the samādhis they attain impure, but even if they were to perform supernatural transformations by the hundreds, thousands, or tens of millions, they can only produce one at a time with a single mind, and cannot produce many at once with multiple minds.

However, it is not so for the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva understands that the five sensory objects are illusory and fundamentally empty and quiescent; furthermore, they are able to directly perceive the principle of the equality of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, the myriad objects cannot obstruct their mind, and the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) they attain are sovereign according to their will, pervading the entire Dharma-realm and manifesting diverse activities through manifold minds.
The śrāvakas do not merely act with a single mind or perform a single deed; furthermore, their knowledge is limited and does not reach back into the distant past.
For example, there was once a man who went to the Jetavana Monastery seeking to leave the household life.
At that time, five hundred arhats simultaneously entered meditative absorption to observe this person's faculties and dispositions; having emerged from concentration, they spoke to him, saying:
"You have passed beyond all roots of goodness."
"Even if you were to enter the Path, you would ultimately not realize the fruits; therefore, you may not go forth.
At this, the man’s afflictions arose and he wished to leave; he went to the gate of the vihāra and wept there.
Just then, the Tathāgata arrived from outside; seeing this person, he asked, "For what reason are you weeping?
The man replied to the Buddha:
"I wish to leave the household life, but the bhikṣus will not permit it; therefore, I weep and am about to depart.
The Buddha knew that although this man lacked roots of goodness in his immediate past, he had possessed them in the distant past and now desired to attain the Way.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu. Immediately,
he became an Arhat, fully endowed with robes and bowl.
Although he had attained arhatship, because he had only recently left the household life, he did not yet understand the dignified deportment of a bhikṣu.
The Tathāgata, wishing to cause him to manifest supernormal powers so that his disciples might see them and inquire about them, instructed him, saying:
"Wash your alms bowl, but do not place it on the ground."
Nor did he instruct him to place the bowl upon a bed, on grass, leaves, or similar surfaces.
After the bhikṣu had finished washing it, he placed it in mid-air; by means of his supernormal power, the bowl remained suspended in space and did not fall.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they asked in wonder,
"What bhikṣu is this whose supernatural power is such as this?
The Buddha then replied:
"The layperson who previously sought to leave the household life—the one of whom you all said had no roots of goodness—is this very person.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they felt deep shame and remorse.
Therefore, we know that the samādhis attained by Arhats of the Hīnayāna are not only erroneous; even if they were well-attained, they would still be unable to know distant matters.
The *Śāstra* states:
"As previously explained, from 'the sages' up to 'unspeakable,'" etc.; this cites the scriptural passage from the sixth section where doubts were raised.

"If [the state] of a srotāpanna and so forth is attained, how can it be 'inexpressible'? This raises the four fruits as an objection; the phrasing of the objection is no different from that which arises in the Sūtra.

The passage beginning with "From here on, the scriptural text serves to resolve this doubt" refers to the intent of the preceding scripture in providing an explanation that resolves the doubt, thereby establishing the meaning of the teaching as being beyond grasping.
Does this section of the sutra exhaust its exposition through a single verse?

The first two lines of the verse provide a general explanation of the sutra passage concerning the four fruits of spiritual attainment, while the latter two lines specifically explain the subsequent passage beginning with Subhūti’s unique attainment of the *araṇā-samādhi* (the concentration of non-contention).

Regarding the phrase "neither to be grasped nor to be spoken," it clarifies that when a practitioner realizes the four fruits, because they have abandoned the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and so forth, they do not perceive a single dharma within the five aggregates of sentient beings or among the six sense objects; this is what is termed a "fruit."
Furthermore, there is no mental conception that "I can attain the fruit," and thus it cannot be grasped.

Since there is no fixed dharma that can be realized as the fruit, nor any sign or characteristic of realization that can be described and shown to others, it is said to be ungraspable and indescribable.
Regarding the phrase "For what reason is this so? and below, the second line states: "Because its own fruit is not grasped.

This should also have stated that the four fruits are expressible; however, it is omitted from discussion here for the purpose of establishing the meaning of the aforementioned statement that they are "not to be grasped."
Regarding the phrase "relying on that Subhūti," this is the formal rendering of the name Subhūti.

Regarding the phrase "explaining the departure from the two kinds of obstacles," this clarifies that because Subhūti has attained the *araṇā-samādhi* (the concentration of non-conflict) and practices the emptiness of desirelessness, he is thus free from the two obstacles.
Regarding the section of the treatise beginning with "What is the meaning of this? there are two general intentions:
from the beginning up to "I am able to attain the fruit," it explains two lines of the verse and interprets the scriptural passages concerning the four fruits within the sutra.

"Because the noble ones (ārya) are named by virtue of the unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma), up to being named Arhats"—this explains that those who have realized the four fruits of the path are called "noble" because they have attained the unconditioned dharma.
"From Srotāpanna up to Arhat" clarifies the aforementioned doubt and establishes the teaching that [the fruits] are not to be grasped.

"However, it is not that the Noble Ones do not take up unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) in order to realize their own fruit. This clarifies that although these Noble Ones of the four fruits do not grasp [the fruit] at the moment of realization so as to establish the teaching of "that which cannot be grasped," once they have emerged from realization, they nevertheless refer to themselves as having attained this unconditioned fruit; thus, there is also the sense of a teaching regarding "that which can be grasped."
Regarding the statement, "If a noble one were to give rise to the thought 'I can attain the fruit,' he would then be attached to a self and persons," what is the meaning of this?
It is explained as follows: "This is because there are latent afflictions (*anuśaya-kleśa*), not manifest afflictions (*paryavasthāna-kleśa*)."
"Afflictions that cause [action]" refers to the two afflictions of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).

"Afflictions not manifesting [in this life]" refers to the coarse deluded conduct of those in the latter two fruits who, though lacking the signs of manifestation or non-manifestation, maintain wives for worldly affairs.

Among the four fruits of the path, the first two belong to householders. Although the srotāpanna and sakṛdāgāmin have severed the *naimittika-ātman* (the self characterized by signs), they still possess the *anaimittika-ātman* (the self not characterized by signs).
Because they still maintain wives and engage in worldly affairs, they possess active afflictions (*carita-kleśa*);
furthermore, because they still possess the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance, they also possess latent afflictions (*anuśaya-kleśa*).
In the latter two fruits, there are no manifest signs nor non-manifest signs; because they do not engage in worldly affairs, there are no active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).
However, because there is ignorance and residual habituation (*vāsanā*), there are latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The current statement regarding "the absence of afflictions" specifically explains the *anāgāmin* and the *arhat*; it should also be understood generally to apply to the first two fruits as well, for they possess both latent afflictions (*anuśaya-kleśa*) and active afflictions (*paryavasthāna-kleśa*). However, the author of the treatise prefers brevity and thus addresses only the latter two types of persons.

"Why is this? Because at the time of realization, he is free from the afflictions such as grasping at a self. Why does the Master of the Treatise clarify this point here? He intends to reveal this meaning.
Hypothetical Objection:

If those in the two fruits while remaining householders still possess active afflictions (*kleśa*), why is it said that the *srotāpanna* and other practitioners of the two fruits are called "noble ones" (*ārya*) because they have abandoned grasping at the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth?
Therefore, it asks, "For what reason? The answer is:

"Because at the time of realization, they are free from afflictions such as grasping at a self. This clarifies that when the aforementioned two types of persons realize the fruit, they attain the understanding of non-self; having eliminated delusions characterized by the view of a personal body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the like, they possess no mind that grasps for a fruit, and are thus called "sages" (*ārya*).

As for the existence of active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), they arise even after realization; because one does not manifest the signs of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth, or engages in worldly affairs, there are thus active afflictions.
"Therefore, there is no such thought as 'I can attain the fruit'" concludes the point that when the two types of persons previously mentioned realize the fruits, they do not grasp at them.
Thus, it is said in the Sūtra: "There was a bhikṣu who attained the stage of Srotāpanna and proclaimed:
'The affliction of sensual desire has scorched my mind.'"
He then immediately abandoned the path and returned home to practice worldly dharmas.
From this evidence, it is known that the former two individuals possessed active afflictions (*kleśa*).

The section beginning with "For what reason did Subhūti himself praise his own attainment of the prediction" is the second part; its intent is to explain the latter half of the verse, and since it interprets the scriptural passage concerning the "Samādhi of Non-contention" (*araṇā-samādhi*), it first poses a question.
The Tathāgata has always taught that evil deeds should be exposed and wholesome dharmas should be concealed; why then does Subhūti praise himself within the assembly as having received a prediction?

Therefore, the commentary explains: "by realizing the fruit through his own body. This clarifies that this *araṇā-samādhi* (the samādhi of non-contention) is attained only by Subhūti and not by others, thereby manifesting his own merit.
Regarding the phrase "in order to generate faith in that meaning," this answers the preceding objection.
The intent of the doubt is as follows:
someone might think, "Although the Tathāgata has stated that Subhūti has attained the *araṇā-samādhi* and is an Arhat free from desire, we do not know whether he actually attained it or not."
By what means is it verified that Subhūti has attained this?

Because doubts might arise and lead to a lack of faith, Subhūti, amidst the great assembly, proclaimed: "The World-Honored One has said that I have attained the Samādhi of Non-contention. By dispelling the doubts of the multitude, he caused them to give rise to faith, thereby fulfilling the aforementioned point: "I do not harbor the thought that 'I can attain the fruit.'"
Subhūti does not form such thoughts because he has attained [realization].
Furthermore, another interpretation states: Why does Subhūti manifest his own merit?

Therefore, the answer states, "In order to give rise to faith regarding that meaning," clarifying that Subhūti, by means of the superior Dharma he has attained himself, exhorts the other two vehicles to engender faith.
Regarding the question, "Why is it that only the practice of non-contention (*araṇā*) is mentioned? it asks:
Subhūti has attained sixty thousand samādhis; why is it that only the samādhi of non-contention is praised, while his other virtues are not?
Therefore, the answer is given: "Because there are two meanings.

First, "to clarify the supreme merit": it clarifies that within the teachings for śrāvakas, the *araṇā-samādhi* (meditative concentration of non-contention) is the foremost dharma of supreme merit, which Subhūti alone has attained, while others have not.
Because he attained something superior, he praised it specifically.

Second, "for the sake of generating deep faith": he wished to cause other arhats who have not yet attained this state to develop resolute faith in this samādhi and seek its realization; thus, it is called "deep faith."

Regarding the question, "Why is it said that Subhūti has reached the teaching on the departure from the two kinds of hindrances? this presents a scriptural inquiry which is answered by means of a verse.

The passage from "The two kinds of hindrances... to "...therefore it is said there is nothing practiced" extracts the names of the two hindrances from which Subhūti has departed within the verse, thereby explaining the statement in the sūtra that "in reality, there is nothing practiced."
Regarding the phrase "For this reason, they are called the two kinds of dispute," the following provides a dual explanation for the names of the two disputes and the two non-disputes.
As for the phrase "For this reason," this single clause serves as a general explanation for both terms, "dispute" and "non-dispute."
If one does not properly guard the human mind, it will be obstructed by the objects of the five desires; thus, there are two kinds.
Because these possess the meaning of two types of obstructions and because they conflict with persons and objects, they are designated by the name "two kinds of strife."

Regarding the statement, "Because he is free from those two kinds of obstacles, he is said to have no sphere of activity," this clarifies that Subhūti skillfully guards the minds of others and is not obstructed by the objects of desire; therefore, he is free from the two obstacles.
Because it has the meaning of being free from these two obstacles, it is called the "two kinds of non-contentious practice.
As for the passage, "The Buddha told Subhūti:
'In the past, when the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he received his prediction,'" this is the third section within the seventh chapter on Comparative Measurement.
Why is this so? It is because in the preceding sixth major section, it was clarified that all dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are neither graspable nor expressible; thus, a doubt arises:

how is it that when the Tathāgata was formerly a bodhisattva, he received the prediction from Dīpaṃkara Buddha that he would become a buddha—this would imply that the realized dharma is indeed graspable and expressible?

If that were so, then the realized Dharma would possess names and characteristics that could be grasped and expressed; how then can it be said that the names and characteristics of the realized Dharma cannot be grasped or expressed?
This doubt arises because it is thought that at that time, the Bodhisattva has already attained the prediction of the realization of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
To sever this doubt, it is answered:
when the lamp is lit, the prophecy is conveyed through words; since the wisdom of realization has not yet been attained, those words may be accepted as a teaching.

Furthermore, at the time of subsequent realization, one is severed from names and signs; how then could the Dharma that is difficult to realize be bestowed as a prophecy through speech, such that it could be described as having names and signs that can be grasped?

To sever this doubt, it is clarified whether the Bodhi attained by the Tathāgata in the past under Dīpaṃkara Buddha was [the same as] this, which is the Tathāgata of the *nirmāṇakāya* (Emanation Body).

If one were a *saṃbuddha* (a Buddha by nature), they would not cultivate or realize the fruits [of the path]; for what reason, then, is the prophecy bestowed by Dīpaṃkara Buddha cited as proof that this person is indeed a true Bodhisattva?

However, although the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body) Buddha is not ultimately real, he never says, "I am a manifested transformation. This is because the true reality serves as the basis for the response; speaking from the perspective of the fundamental source, he cites the Bodhisattva of True Practice during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha as his witness.

This clarifies that it is not the case that there are no bodhisattvas; however, because they have not yet attained any realization, it is said that "in reality nothing is attained," thereby establishing the meaning of the aforementioned teaching on "non-apprehensibility.

At that time, the Tathāgata was still an ordinary bodhisattva within the stage of the "nature of the seeds of practice" prior to the bhūmis, and thus did not receive a manifest prediction of enlightenment. There was only speech, and no realized Dharma; therefore, it could be described as "apprehensible," yet nevertheless, it was not that there were no bodhisattvas who possessed actual realization.

However, the opponent bases their question on the fact that [the nature of] the stage prior to realization has not yet been proven; therefore, the answer is given in accordance with the point of the question.

Yet, regarding those who have actually realized the state of a bodhisattva, the subsequent sutra states: "One who penetrates non-self and the dharmas of non-self, and is free from both forms of non-self—this is called a true bodhisattva. This refers to the correct answer.
Regarding this term "Dīpaṃkara," there are generally four types of predictions (vyākaraṇa) bestowed across three periods:
first, within the stage of the lineage of practice;
second, within the stage of the lineage of nature, which is a prediction not yet manifest.
Third is the prediction bestowed face-to-face within the first stage (*bhūmi*);
fourth is the prediction of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) within the Buddha-stage.

As for the present mention of the "prediction by Dīpaṃkara," at that time Śākyamuni was still a bodhisattva of the nature of the stage of practice (*śikṣā-bhāga-jāti*), and had not yet attained the realization of the dharma of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena from the first stage upward.
Now, it is explained that the Tathāgata asked Subhūti:
"Do you think that at that time I had already realized the prediction of non-arising bodhi on the first bhūmi? Subhūti replied:

When the Tathāgata received his words of prophecy from Dīpaṃkara, he had not yet attained the prophecy of the non-arising of the first bhūmi; therefore, it is said that at Dīpaṃkara’s place, there was truly nothing to be obtained.

As stated in the *Bhagavat-sūtra*: "In the past, when I was at the stage of the nature of practice (*śikṣā-gotra*), during the Star宿 Kalpa, I made offerings to seventy billion nayutas of Buddhas. Each Buddha remained in the world for sixty billion nayuta kalpas, yet none of those Buddhas bestowed a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) upon me."
Why is this? Because they have not yet attained the stage of the endurance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Commentary says:

Furthermore, there is doubt; because the Master of the Treatise intends to provide a verse commentary on this third section of the sutra text, he first sets forth the meaning of the fourth doubt within the aforementioned discourse that should not be grasped.

First, regarding the one who raises the doubt: they erroneously cite the "teachings that can be grasped" (upādāya-vyākaraṇa) belonging to past Buddhas to challenge the present teaching, arguing that the dharma realized [by the Buddha] must likewise be a teaching that can be grasped.

To sever this doubt, the Master of the Treatise answers by citing the scriptures; his intention is to clarify that the dharma realized by the Bodhisattva among the teachings of past Buddhas constitutes a "teaching that cannot be grasped" (anupādāya-vyākaraṇa), thereby answering the doubt concerning the existence of "teachings that can be grasped."
Regarding "As stated in the sutra," this is a general citation that concludes the resolution of doubts.

As for the question, "Why is it said thus?"—the doubter cites the Buddha Dīpaṃkara to raise the objection that [enlightenment] is something that can be grasped. In response, one should instead explain the intent that it cannot be grasped; why, then, is it given this incorrect answer, stating that "in reality, there is nothing to be attained in anuttarasamyaksambodhi"?
The single verse, "The Buddha’s words to Dīpaṃkara," explains this section of the sutra.
The term "Buddha" here refers to the present Śākyamuni Buddha.
"Regarding the words of Dīpaṃkara" means that at the time of that Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he received the prediction solely through words.

"Not yet attaining the wisdom of the ultimate reality" clarifies that at the time he was to receive the prediction, he had not yet attained the realization of the wisdom of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā-jñāna) through the patience toward the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Regarding the phrase "by means of this true meaning," there are two aspects:
first, it establishes the statement in the sixth preceding section that [the Dharma] is ungraspable; second, it establishes the preceding point regarding what is not the Dharma.
How is it established that the aforementioned is "inapprehensible and ineffable"?

The previous statement—that the realized Dharma transcends names and characteristics and is therefore inapprehensible and ineffable—was challenged by citing the prediction received from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the past as a counter-argument. The respondent’s intention was to clarify that the original prediction from Dīpaṃkara consisted merely of words; since words are of the nature of sound, they can be apprehended and expressed. However, this does not mean that the realized Dharma itself can be apprehended or expressed. Thus, the point that it is "inapprehensible and ineffable" is established.

Second, if one were to argue that the realized Dharma is likewise nameless and signless, thus incapable of being grasped or explained, this would revert to the second doubt mentioned above—that the verbal teaching is not at all the Dharma. The intent of the response clarifies that although the realized Dharma is beyond words, because it can be realized, it can be explained; by following these explanations, one can again attain realization. Therefore, the verbal teaching is indeed the Dharma, and not something that is not the Dharma.
Therefore, it is said: "By means of this true meaning, that teaching of non-apprehension is established.

Because this verbal prophecy cannot realize the true meaning of realized wisdom (*pratyātmajñāna*), it nevertheless succeeds in establishing that teaching of the non-apprehensibility of realized wisdom.

Second, because the essence of realized wisdom (pratyakṣajñāna) is devoid of names and characteristics, it likewise cannot be grasped; since this explains the meaning of reality, the subsequent line states: "It establishes that non-grasping discourse."
Regarding the prose section beginning with "What is the meaning of this?", the treatise has two intended meanings:
from the beginning up to "because it is taught as being without grasping," the first half-verse and its scriptural commentary are explained; what follows concludes with the second half-verse.

The passage beginning with "Furthermore, if a sage... constitutes the second part of the Master’s introduction, wherein he addresses the doubts of the interlocutor and introduces the Sūtra on the Simile of the Mountain King of the Pure Land.
From "the noble one" to "inexpressible," these are citations from the scripture in the sixth section above.
As for the question, "How do the bodhisattvas take up a pure buddha-field? this doubt specifically gives rise to the subsequent scripture on the pure land.
Regarding the two doubts concerning "How is it that [the Buddha] receives the retribution of bliss? and so forth, they are separately developed in the *Śailendrarāja-sūtra*.
"The Buddha told Subhūti:
'If a bodhisattva should say, "I adorn the buddha-fields"'—this is the fourth scriptural passage within the section on comparative evaluation."
For what reason does it arise?
Because within the sixth section, all [phenomena] are stated to be ungraspable, which gives rise to the fifth doubt.
The aforementioned doubt is as follows:

If the name "unconditioned dharma" is applied to the sages because these dharmas cannot be grasped or described, then are the pure lands—the environments obtained by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) or ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)?
If it pertains to the ultimate truth (paramārtha), it is indeed ungraspable and inexpressible;
if it pertains to conditioned conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), then it is graspable and expressible.
A doubter says:
"If this Pure Land is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), then since the bodhisattvas have already taken up this Pure Land, why do you say it cannot be taken up and is beyond description?"

If the dependent retribution of the Pure Land were conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), then even sages would still undergo conditioned retribution; how then could it be said that sages are named for their unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma, which is "inapprehensible and ineffable"?
This doubt means that one might think the supramundane pure land is identical to a conditioned realm.
Therefore, in the sutra below, the Buddha answers by stating that there are two kinds of pure lands:
the first belongs to those prior to the stages [of the bodhisattva path], characterized by conditioned forms and adorned with the seven treasures, and is subsumed within the three realms.
The second is the stage of the grounds (*bhūmi*), which is the ultimate adornment of the supramundane pure land, not subsumed within the three realms (*tridhātu*).
Since the retributive bodies of sages from the first ground upward manifest in lands beyond the three realms, how can you use a mundane pure land to challenge a supramundane pure land?
This true pure land is not like the worldly pure lands that can be grasped and described.
This directly answers the doubt regarding the "inexpressible" (anupādeya) raised in the sixth section, and it also indirectly answers the doubt in the fifth section.

The phrase "For example, there is a person whose body is like Sumeru, the king of mountains" serves to resolve the doubt raised in the sixth section concerning the impossibility of grasping and explaining [the Dharma].

If it is said that the name of the Unconditioned Dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma) belongs to the Sage, and that this Dharma cannot be grasped or explained, then how can the Retribution Buddha (vipākabuddha) Tathāgata—who has perfected the practices of the ten stages (daśabhūmi), received the office of the Retribution Buddha upon the lotus throne, attained immeasurable merit, and declared of himself, "I am the Dharma King," while further taking up the adornment of a pure land—be so?
If it were so, then the realized Dharma would be something that could be grasped and explained.
If it were something that could be grasped and explained, this Buddha of Retribution would be subsumed under the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If it were subsumed under the conditioned, then it would be impermanent.
If it were impermanent, then the outflows would not be exhausted.
If the outflows are not exhausted, one cannot be called a Buddha.
If it were unconditioned, would it be identical to or different from the Dharma-Buddha?
If they were identical, then since the Dharma-Buddha has no physical form or characteristics, the Retribution-Buddha (Sambhogakāya) should likewise have no physical form or characteristics.
If it were different from the Dharma-body, then this Retribution-Buddha would be produced from a productive cause.
If that which arises were produced by a cause of arising, then it would be that what was originally non-existent now exists, and what already existed returns to non-existence; this is impermanence.
How then can you say that the unconditioned dharmas of the Sage are named as being "ungraspable and inexpressible"?

Furthermore, within the treatise, the statement regarding arising asks, "How is it that other worldly beings again take him to be the body of the Dharma King? This constitutes the seventh doubt arising from the sixth section concerning the teaching on non-apprehensibility.
A doubt may arise:

The Buddhas of the ten directions and others in the world also say that in such-and-such a world, such-and-such a Bodhisattva has fulfilled the practices of the ten stages and received the office of Buddhahood; they also declare that he is a Dharma King.
If the retributive Buddha could be grasped or explained for others, why would it be said that unconditioned dharmas cannot be grasped or explained?

Therefore, the Buddha cites the analogy of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, to answer this doubt, clarifying that the essence of the retributive Buddha is unconditioned and thus cannot be grasped or explained, rather than being conditioned and capable of being grasped or explained.

The reason for this is that through the causes and conditions of the Buddha’s cultivation and severance of delusions, the originally inherent nature manifests its function; this is termed the *Sambhogakāya* (Reward Buddha).

Since there is the *Sambhogakāya* as the primary fruit, there is consequently the sovereign function of the true Pure Land as the supporting reward. Thus, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) rather than conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and because it is not something discrete or fragmented, it is eternal.

The reason it was stated above that the retributive Buddha, the Tathāgata, arises from the cause of birth is because, from the perspective of the functional aspect of retribution, he first comes into being; thus, within this context, he is said to be "born. It does not mean that the essence of the retributive Buddha arises from the cause of birth and is therefore impermanent.
This directly answers the doubt raised in the seventh section and also indirectly answers the doubt in the fifth section; therefore, it is explained next:
"If a bodhisattva says, 'I adorn the Buddha-lands.'"
"That bodhisattva speaks untruth.

This refers to the practice of grasping at signs by bodhisattvas prior to the stages; they take the adornments of conditioned phenomena—various jewels—as their true pure land, while failing to realize that there exists a distinct, supramundane, truly pure land.

They take only what they themselves have attained to be the true Pure Land, asserting it to be identical to the Lotus Treasury World (*Sahālokadhātu*) and the like; since they claim there is no other distinct, truly unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) Pure Land, they are said to speak words that are not true.
The phrase "For what reason? expresses the arising of doubt. The objection is raised as follows:

If the adornment of physical forms were not the true Pure Land, for what reason did the Tathāgata say, "The superior marks and adornments of the Pure Land I have attained are like the palaces of the Lord of Śakra," and "The sentient beings in my Pure Land are free from desire, like Brahmā or the gods"?
Furthermore, for what reason do you teach sentient beings, saying:

"When I cultivated the causes for the Pure Land, I leveled the roads, removed thorns and brambles, and transported soil from high places to low places; by taking these as the causes for the Pure Land, I obtained the retribution of this Pure Land"?
Considering the Tathāgata’s sincere words, this Pure Land appears to possess form and shape.

Since it has such characteristics, it would be subsumed within the three realms and could thus be grasped and described; why then do you say that the Pure Land is not adorned with form and shape and cannot be grasped or described? If it were adorned with form and shape, would your words not be untrue?

Therefore, it asks "Why? For this reason, the Buddha replied, "That which the Tathāgata calls the adornment of Buddha-lands," intending to lead and encourage beginners by using what is near to illustrate what is far; thus he said that the pure land he has attained is like the palaces of the Sovereign Deity (Īśvara) and so forth.

Furthermore, in accordance with worldly conventions, because people of the world regard such physical forms and the splendor of the seven treasures as a "Pure Land," the Buddha speaks of it as a Pure Land following worldly custom; this does not refer to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of a truly real Pure Land. Thus, it is said that the Tathāgata speaks of the adornment of Buddha-lands; yet, this is not to say that there are no worldly, conditioned, and outflowing (*sāsrava*) adornments of form.

Regarding the phrase "then it is not adornment": this refers to what is described as a Pure Land according to conventional truth; it is not the true Pure Land of the supramundane ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), and therefore it is said to be "not."
Regarding the phrase "this is called adorning the Buddha-land," such adornment that is not of form or appearance is precisely the adornment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, it may be said that while the adornment of physical forms is not true adornment, this is what is meant by "non-adornment.

Now, as for these "Pure Lands," they are precisely the lands of ultimate truth and supreme wisdom—the dependent retribution of all Buddhas. This land takes the *dharmatā* of True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its essence; it is the Lotus Treasury World (*padmagarbha-lokadhātu*).
This Pure Land and the True Reward Buddha are identical in essence, yet differ in their function.

This land was established by the Tathāgata through the two kinds of adornment—merit and wisdom—cultivated since his initial aspiration for enlightenment; it is the fruit of supramundane, untainted, and supreme causes.
The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "It transcends all worldly spheres and is produced from supramundane roots of goodness.

It cannot be attained through the tainted causes of grasping at signs prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), for its essence is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and is comprised of the adornment of its formal characteristics.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The pure lands of all Buddhas are not subsumed within the three realms of desire, form, or formlessness.
How can it be said that this true pure land is not subsumed by the three realms?
The commentary states:

Because it does not abide in the earth, it is not subsumed under the desire realm; because it does not abide in space, it is not subsumed under the form realm; because its essence is form, it is not subsumed under the formless realm.
Although it is not subsumed within the three realms, it exists in the same location as them without mutual obstruction.
Even when the three calamities arise and the world is consumed by fire, that Pure Land remains serene and unchanging.

Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "When sentient beings see the kalpa coming to an end and being consumed by a great conflagration, my land remains peaceful and secure, constantly filled with devas and humans."
This is precisely the true, eternal, and pure land; therefore, it is not destroyed by the three calamities.

Furthermore, because the pure lands of all Buddhas are equal, pure, non-dual, and undifferentiated, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "One Buddha-land is all Buddha-lands; all Buddha-lands are one Buddha-land."

Now, in explaining this Pure Land, the statement that "the pure and the impure occupy the same location" differs from the meaning of "a single substance perceived differently" (ekadravya-vicitradarśana) as analyzed since ancient times.

The reason for this is that, fundamentally, the two lands of purity and impurity have no distinct locations; they are not like the lands of Sahā and Sukhāvatī, which are separate and exist as entirely different entities.
If this is so, for what reason are there immeasurable distinctions among realms such as those of stone, sand, copper, iron, the seven treasures, lapis lazuli, and emeralds?

Or why is it that some sentient beings perceive space as earth and earth as space? Such differences all arise because of the defilement or purity of the karma of sentient beings, and the clarity or obscurity of their wisdom; thus, the myriad variations in what they see do not stem from any actual difference in the lands themselves.

It is like the flowing waters of the Ganges, where various hungry ghosts go together to drink; some see flowing fire, some see pus and blood, some see ashes and charcoal, some see it as parched and dry, and some see spirits and deities guarding it so they cannot approach. All of these are due to the causes and conditions of the sentient beings' own karmic offenses; what each perceives of this single river differs, and thus their visions are not the same. It is not that the water is one and the visions are different.
As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, "The views of Śikhin and Śāriputra differ.
This is also similar to the case where "two devas eat together, yet the color of their rice differs. It is the same in this instance as well.

Thus we know that while dwelling in a single land, differences arise according to one's vision; it is not that a single substance is perceived differently by various observers—this principle is as clear as a blazing flame.

Therefore, the passage beginning with "For this reason, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should thus give rise to a pure mind" is the teaching of this sutra exhorting bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds on the method for attaining a truly pure land.

The phrase "for this reason" means that because these practices prior to the stages involve grasping at signs, one only attains a worldly, conditioned adornment of the pure land through formal characteristics; it does not have the meaning of the supramundane, ultimate-adornment pure land.

All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must practice the non-apprehension of signs (*animitta*) from the first bhūmi upward; only then can they attain the supramundane, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), truly pure land. One must not mistake the conditioned lands of worldly forms obtained through a mind that grasps at signs for a true pure land; therefore, it is said that one should give rise to a pure mind in this manner.
"Thus one should give rise to a pure mind" means that one should, as in the fourth section above, maintain a mind that does not grasp at the three things.

"And without abiding anywhere" means not being attached to one's own self, not seeking to dwell [in anything], and not being attached to the various distinctions such as form, nor to the fruits of retribution—the five desires of humans and devas within the triple world.
"Should not dwell on anything" means not being attached to the requital of gratitude.

These three are identical to the first three matters mentioned previously; this clarifies that the ultimate realm (paramārtha-kṣetra) attained by the Tathāgata is perfectly pure, representing the purity within the stages from the first bhūmi upward.
*Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Four;
*Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci at Luoyang during the second year of the Tiānpíng era of the Wèi dynasty.
The phrase, "For example, there is a person whose body is like Sumeru, the king of mountains," cites the metaphor of a vast body;
it illustrates the principle that the *vipākabuddha* (retribution Buddha) is similar to the reflected image of that mountain king.
Furthermore, because this mountain excels all other mountains, it is called a "king.
As for the phrase "there is a person," this refers to the *vipākabuddha* (the Buddha of Retribution) as a person.
It may also be said that "there is a person" refers to an ordinary person of the world.
The "king" is used as a metaphorical illustration to clarify that the human body in this world may be as vast as Mount Sumeru, and the *vipākabuddha* (retribution Buddha) is likewise so.

After the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*) are fulfilled and the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) is attained, the manifestation of the original nature is called the *dharmabuddha* (dharma Buddha). Because his myriad virtues, wisdom, and insight are perfected, he is called the *vipākabuddha*. Among all the sages, he is the sovereign and thus termed the "Great Body. His essence is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and eternally abiding, unlike conditioned bodies; therefore, it is borrowed here as a metaphor.
"Subhūti! What do you think? Is this body great?
This means that after the Tathāgata has finished using the analogy of the king of mountains to explain the greatness of the Buddha-body, he asks Subhūti whether the Buddha-body is indeed great.
Subhūti understood and immediately replied, "It is exceedingly great, World-Honored One!

He spoke thus of its being "exceedingly great" because he clearly recognized that the Buddha’s myriad virtues are perfectly fulfilled; as the King among all Sages, he shares the same majesty as the King of Mountains.

Those who harbor doubts, upon hearing that the Retribution Buddha is named "Great Body Like the King of Mountains," will claim that the Retribution Buddha possesses a conditioned body of form and appearance derived from the King of Mountains; if it is a body of form and appearance, then it must be an impermanent body subject to arising and ceasing.
Because this principle exists, he replies: "The Buddha says that what is not a body is called the Great Body.

The intent of this reply clarifies that the Great Body of the Reward-Buddha (*vipākakāya*) is not like the bodies of conditioned forms found in the world; its essence is serene and tranquil, devoid of the characteristics of the conditioned, outflowing mind, thought, consciousness, and false discrimination.
Because the King of Mountains possesses a resemblance to the Buddha’s portion, it is cited as a metaphor;
yet to speak of its reality, it is categorically and utterly distinct from him, and thus it is said to be "not the body."
Yet, possessing immeasurable merit and wisdom, it is a serene, eternally abiding, most exalted and vast body; this is called the "Great Body" (*mahākāya*).

Furthermore, it may be said that "that body is not a body, and thus it is called the Great Body. This explains that the Great Body of the *vipākabuddha* (retribution Buddha) is a non-body, because it is not a body characterized by the outflows (*āsrava*) of conditioned existence; for this reason, it is called the Great Body.
This reveals the manifest function of the originally existing nature, which is called the *saṃbhoga-buddha*.
Its wondrous marks are serene and profound, and its great function manifests through both existence and non-existence; this is what is termed the true, great body of the *saṃbhoga-buddha*.
"The Commentary states:

'This meaning should be understood as follows. This refers to the meaning of the Reward Buddha (vipāka-buddha) of the Pure Land; it should be understood according to what is taught in the Sūtra regarding the dialogue between the Buddha and Subhūti, though the Master of the Commentary has not yet provided an explanation for this."
Why does it say "should be known"?
This clarifies that Subhūti had doubts in his mind which he had not yet expressed in speech;

thus, the verse replies: "Through the practice of wisdom, one penetrates consciousness-only. This single verse explains [the passage]: "If a Bodhisattva should speak thus: 'I shall adorn the Buddha-lands,' and so forth, until 'he gives rise to such a thought.'"
"Wisdom" refers to true wisdom; the Pure Land takes wisdom as its essence. As for why this Pure Land takes wisdom as its essence:

it clarifies that while the two types of retribution—the primary (the Buddha) and the secondary (the environment)—of the Tathāgata’s fruition share a single *dharmatā* as their essence when discussed in terms of substance, they are distinct as body and land when analyzed in terms of their pervasive function. Thus, although the primary and secondary retributions differ, neither does not take wisdom as its essence.
Regarding "cultivation" (*xi*): subsequent wisdom seeking after prior wisdom is termed cultivation.

Taking the preceding mind as the cause, this cause is able to evoke subsequent understanding; because it evolves with increasing refinement and excellence without being different from its source, it is called the "cause of cultivation. Because it can manifest the true nature without obstruction, it is called "penetration" (*tong*).
"Penetration" (*tong*) means that the eighth consciousness of Buddha-nature has no obstruction; thus it is called penetration. Therefore, the verse says:

"Through the practice of wisdom, one penetrates the nature of consciousness. This refers to the eighth *ālaya*-consciousness; it is only through the pure, untainted, true understanding of the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and the wisdom of the Buddha-fruit that one can penetrate far and see this Pure Land, thereby attaining the functions of this land.
The subsequent line exhorts: "Thus one takes up the Pure Land.
The preceding question asked what the meaning of the Pure Land is;
as explained here, the nature and characteristics of the causal practices for the Pure Land are precisely like this.
To practice in this way and to grasp in this way is neither inverted nor false grasping; therefore, it is said that one grasps the Pure Land in this way.
"Not practicing the primary essence" and "not having form" mean that this true Pure Land does not consist of conditioned forms or characteristics.
Regarding "the primary substance": if this Pure Land were not a conditioned form, would it then be entirely without form, identical to empty space?

Now it is clarified that although this land is not a form characterized by conditioned phenomena, it is not without the form of supramundane unconditioned reality; it is the foremost essence of the Pure Land adorned with ultimate truth.
"Non-adornment" refers to the absence of worldly forms and ornaments mentioned in the preceding phrase;
"adornment" in the subsequent phrase refers to the adornment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This phrase should have been stated as "the adornment that is not an adornment," but because of the constraints of the verse, it is simply called "non-adornment.
The intended meaning is to capture the sense of the Pure Land; the intent is precisely this.
The phrase "What is the meaning of this? asks how the meaning of this single verse explaining the Pure Land is to be understood.

It specifically explains that "the Buddhas have no such thing as adorning a land" and that they do not speak untruths; it interprets the first two lines of the verse and also elucidates the passage from the beginning of the sutra: "If a bodhisattva were to say... [it would be] an untruthful word."
The phrase "the Buddhas have no business of adorning their lands" clarifies that the Tathāgatas possess no worldly forms or characteristics for the purpose of adorning their lands.

The phrase "the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, penetrate the habitual consciousness of true wisdom" clarifies that the adornment of Buddha-lands attained by the Tathāgatas is solely the function of the ultimate truth (paramārtha) adorned by supramundane wisdom.
These two lines precisely set forth the essence of the Pure Land.
As for the phrase "Therefore, that land cannot be grasped," it concludes the preceding section and summarizes the intent of resolving doubts at the beginning of the sutra.
"As for the phrase 'therefore': these pure lands of all Buddhas are not conditioned forms; they are the mark of ultimate truth and true wisdom, and thus cannot be grasped."

How can one harbor doubts, claiming that the Buddha-lands adorned by Bodhisattvas are things that can be grasped or described, and thus should not be designated by means of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas?

As for the passage beginning with "If a person grasps the forms and characteristics of that land," it clarifies that the essence of this Pure Land is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and is therefore not a conditioned form or characteristic.
If one were to grasp this Pure Land as having the same characteristics as conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), that would be an unreal teaching.

Regarding the phrase "as in the sūtra" and so forth, this cites a subsequent sūtra passage to resolve doubts; it serves to establish that those who grasp the characteristics of the conditioned as being the true Pure Land are propounding an unreal teaching, and thus this sūtra is cited here.
Since this sutra clarifies that the adornment of conditioned forms is not the true Pure Land, it follows that what is produced cannot be the true Pure Land.

Regarding the question, "Why is it said thus?"—this is posed as an introductory inquiry before the latter half of the verse explains the preceding sutra passage. The question asks: while this sutra speaks of adorning the Buddha-land, it then says it is "not adorning"; why does it make such seemingly contradictory statements?
He then replied with a verse, saying: "The supreme essence is not form; it is the intention that adorns through non-adornment.
Regarding the phrase "there are two kinds of adornment," this explains the two types of adornment mentioned within the verse.

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, not an adornment," etc.: above, by correlating the sutra with its verses, the enumeration of the two kinds of adornments has been completed; now, they shall be explained in sequence.

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, because it is not an adornment, it reaches the state of being non-adornment," this explains the Buddha’s teaching in the sutra that "adorned buddha-lands are precisely non-adornments. It interprets the line in the verse "neither form nor adornment" as referring to the first of two types of names: "form-characteristics" (*ākāra*).

The phrase "Thus, from the absence of adornment to the accomplishment of adornment" explains the sūtra’s statement, "This is called adornment," and clarifies the meaning of the first type of adornment—the adornment of essence—within the verse; it refers to the "second [type], the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-lakṣaṇa*)" among the two types of adornment.

Regarding the passage, "If a person discriminates regarding the Buddha-land and gives rise to such a mind," the following section intends to explain the sūtra on how one should give rise to a pure mind by not abiding in the three things; thus, it cites the case of those who abide in the three things as being unable to attain the truly pure land.

If there is someone who gives rise to conceptual discrimination, thinking that the Buddha-land is a conditioned form, and practices by dwelling in the grasping of the three things, claiming, "I shall thus acquire a truly pure land," this person is not cultivating the cause for a truly pure land.
To preclude this [misconception], the following correctly sets forth that those who wish to cultivate the causes for a Pure Land should not abide in three things;
this may be understood from the conclusion of the sutra.

Regarding the introductory statement on "receiving the retribution of a Buddha," this is intended to introduce the second verse by means of an explanation based on the *Śailendrarāja-sūtra*. Thus, it restates the two aforementioned doubts and cites a partial similarity between the retribution of a Buddha and a mountain king (*śailarāja*) to provide the context for the following verses.
Regarding the phrase "What is the meaning of this?", it asks: "What is the meaning of the response that addresses the doubt by stating that the Dharma and the simile share only partial similarity?
This is answered in verse with the lines beginning, "Like the king of mountains, there is no grasping," and so forth.
This single verse explains the passage in the sutra, “For example, there is a person who arrives [there], and this is called a ‘great body’,” thereby answering the latter two doubts.
Regarding the phrase “like the king of mountains”: it is like Sumeru, the king of mountains, which is the foremost among the ten mountains and is therefore called a “king.”

Regarding "absence of grasping": because Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) entity, it lacks the intention to grasp itself by saying, "I am the King of Mountains, superior to the other nine mountains. Therefore, it is said that he is like a king who is without grasping.
Regarding the phrase "The experience of retribution is likewise so," this single line corresponds to the analogy of the Mountain King (*śailarāja*).

It should have been stated as "The Buddha who experiences the retribution of bliss is likewise so," but it is abbreviated because the verse is restricted in length. This clarifies that the Buddha who experiences the retribution of bliss attains immeasurable merits such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*); he is sovereign within the Dharma and surpasses all other sages, and is therefore called "King."
Because he lacks a discriminating mind that grasps at signs, he does not even think, "I am the Dharma King"; therefore, it is said that his reception of retribution is likewise so.
Here, the Master of the Treatise raises an objection:
because the Mountain King has no mind, he does not grasp at the thought, "I am the Mountain King."
If the Buddha has a mind that bestows [the result], why does he not take me as his Dharma King?
Therefore, the second half of the verse answers: "Because he is far removed from all outflows (āsrava) and conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma)."

"Far removed from all outflows" clarifies that the two obstacles of the Buddha of Retribution are forever exhausted; it signifies being severed from discrimination and detached from the causes of grasping at signs associated with outflows.

Regarding the phrase "and conditioned phenomena," this clarifies that one is not only free from the cause of grasping at signs, but is also free from the fruit of conditioned phenomena that arise from grasping at signs.

Because the discrimination of grasping at signs has been forever exhausted, one does not grasp at oneself as the Dharma King; this does not mean that one is like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, who does not grasp because it is mindless.

This clarifies that the Buddha of Retribution, because his essence is detached from the causes and effects of conditioned birth-and-death, is not grasped by them; because he is profoundly quiescent and eternally abiding, not subject to the three marks [of arising, abiding, and ceasing], he is called "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta), and is also termed "outflow-free" (anāsrava).

The prose commentary beginning with “What is the meaning of this? and ending with “because it is non-conceptual” concludes the explanation of the similarity between the metaphors of the Mountain King and the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma as presented in the first half-verse.

The section beginning with "As stated in the sutra" introduces a scriptural passage that resolves doubts, thereby establishing the meaning of the non-differentiation between the Retribution Buddha and the Mountain King.
Following this, a question is posed regarding this very sutra, after which each point is explained individually.
Regarding the phrase "Why is it said thus?":
This asks why, within this sutra, the Buddha says, "That which is called 'non-body' is named 'great body,'" making these two statements in such an apparently inconsistent manner.
He then answers with the latter half of the verse: "Because of being far removed from all outflows (*āsrava*) and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).

Regarding the phrase, "That Buddha-body which receives the retribution of bliss is free from all outflows," this text explains the verse to clarify that the *vipākabuddha* (Retribution Buddha) is free from the outflows of the two obstacles; because he lacks a mind of conceptualization that grasps at signs, he does not grasp himself as a Dharma King.

Regarding the phrase "If it is thus, then there is no entity": if the body of the Buddha is thus free from the two obstacles and all outflows (āsrava), then there are no entities characterized by the myriad marks of the conditioned or the false mark of a self.
Therefore, the subsequent phrase states, "Because it is far removed from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*)," which explains the Sūtra’s statement, "The Buddha said it is not a body.

Regarding the phrase, "If it were thus, it would be called a substantial entity": if the essence of the Reward Buddha (*vipākabuddha*) is thus endowed with the two kinds of adornment, there exists the substance of the true self consisting of the myriad virtues of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Furthermore, if one is thus devoid of the false mark of a self, that is the very substance of the true Reward Body; hence the subsequent phrase says, "Because there is only the pure body."
This explains the sūtra’s statement, “This is called the Great Body.

Regarding the phrase, “For this reason, there truly exists the substance of the self”: because it is a non-substantial thing and possesses only the meaning of the pure body, there truly exists the eternally abiding, wondrous body of the *saṃbhoga-buddha*, which is the true self-substance endowed with the eight masteries.
"Abiding without relying on other conditions" clarifies that the essence of the Tathāgata’s true self does not arise from causes and conditions.
"The Buddha said to Subhūti:

'As many as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River'" is the fifth scriptural passage within this section on comparative measurement; it is the second analogy within the comparative measurement of external material giving.

The reason this second analogy is presented is as follows: Although it was previously explained that the merit of receiving and upholding even a single verse of this sutra surpasses the blessings of giving the seven treasures of the trichiliocosm, and this comparison has already been concluded, a further doubt arises:

"Even though the Tathāgata has extensively explained above that the merit of upholding the sutra is greater than the gift of the seven treasures—thereby establishing that the former is 'incalculable'—the meaning of 'many' may still vary.
For instance, something might be called 'much' simply because it exceeds an immeasurable amount, or it might be called 'much' because it is slightly superior within a category of equals."
Is this multitude because it exceeds two or three thousand worlds by a small margin,
or is it because it exceeds immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, being truly inexhaustible?

If a small victory were to outweigh much, then it would merely surpass the merit of giving these seven treasures throughout the three thousandfold world system; such merit would have its limits and boundaries, rather than being an infinite and inexhaustible, profoundly superior blessing.

To eliminate this doubt, the Buddha’s intended meaning in his reply clarifies that the merit of upholding this sutra not only surpasses the merit of giving the seven treasures filling three thousandfold worlds, but even if one were to take the seven treasures filling immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them in charity, it would still not equal the merit of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting a single four-line verse of this sutra; how much less could it compare to the meager merit of giving in the three thousandfold world? Therefore, he employs this analogy of the sands of the Ganges to resolve that doubt.
How are doubts resolved?
When it is said here that [the merit] is "much," this clarifies that it is much because it is immeasurable, not because it is much by virtue of being superior to a small amount.
Furthermore, even if one upholds but a single verse—its wording being difficult to master yet requiring little effort—it serves as a supreme cause for the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood.

Although the giving of the seven treasures and other such gifts involves vast material wealth and great effort, these are karmic acts performed with grasping at signs; they merely induce worldly, conditioned retributions, and thus are inferior [to the aforementioned practice].

However, while those previous instances of giving the seven treasures three thousand times merely mention "holding them to give as alms" without specifying to whom they were given, this present instance of giving the seven treasures as many times as there are sands in the Ganges clarifies that the gift is made to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas;

since the objects are so numerous, the merit obtained is even more excellent, yet it still does not equal the merit of upholding a single verse, let alone the lesser amount of goods involved in giving the seven treasures three thousand times.
Furthermore, since it was not previously distinguished how much merit is obtained through such acquisition, this passage now serves to further clarify the excellence of the comparison.
As for "the sands of the Ganges," they emerge from the Lake of Cool Purity (Anavatapta) and flow into the Eastern Sea; they are eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in length and forty *li* in width.
There are places ten *li* wide, as they pass through the sandy mountains.
There is drifting sand that is white in color, and the water is likewise white, appearing like milk; yet once it flows out of the river, it becomes clear.
This river is extremely deep; elephants, horses, chariots, and all other vehicles that enter it sink completely.

As for the grains of sand within this river, no ordinary person or follower of the Two Vehicles can calculate or know their number; only the Buddhas know them with perfect clarity. Bodhisattvas from the First Ground upward are also able to count and know their exact number. Although Bodhisattvas on the Stage of Nature (gotrabhūmi) cannot count them, because they have not uttered a single falsehood throughout one great asaṃkhyeya kalpa, they do not need to deliberate before speaking.
As for "that": since the sands in this river are already such as described, it is cited as a metaphor.
Furthermore, because the people of India all see this river, many sūtras cite it as a metaphor.

If each grain of sand in this river were itself a river, and one were to fill as many trichiliocosm world-systems as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers with the seven treasures to give as offerings to the Buddhas, it would still not equal the merit of receiving and upholding a single verse.
Regarding the question, "The treatise says:

'Previously, many analogies for great merit were already explained; why are they explained again here? the commentary explains: Previously, it was explained that the comparison of giving away the seven treasures throughout the three thousandfold world system is not equal to upholding even a single four-line verse of this sutra. Why, then, is the analogy of the sands of the Ganges explained again here?
Because there is such a question, the verse replies: "The teaching of the differentiation of many meanings.
Regarding "the teaching of the differentiation of many meanings," the Master of the Treatise composes this verse to resolve the preceding doubt and intends to clarify the various names.

Although it is said that there is a distinction between the finite and the infinite, this analogy is repeated to illustrate how this infinite giving differs from the merit of the three-thousandfold world system; thus, it is said that the meaning of "much" is explained through its various distinctions.

Regarding the phrase "it also establishes a superior comparison": although previously the merit of upholding even a single verse was shown to surpass that of the three thousand metaphors through comparison, the meaning of establishing a superior comparison had not yet been fully demonstrated.

Now, once again, I shall use the analogy of the sands of the Ganges to compare and measure the merit of upholding this sutra. It clarifies that although the merit from giving away immeasurable, Ganges-sand-like quantities of the seven treasures is vast, it is a merit derived from grasping at signs; it yields worldly retributions which must inevitably come to an end.

It is because one realizes that the merit of upholding this sutra results in the inexhaustible reward of the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood that the superiority of the merit of upholding the sutra is revealed; thus, the merit of upholding even a single four-line verse surpasses the merit of the two aforementioned types of giving.
Having heard this, he again gave rise to doubt, saying:

"Since the principles of this sutra are so profound and weighty, I do not yet know whether the merit of merely receiving and upholding a single verse of this sutra surpasses the blessings of the two previous kinds of giving, or if there is something even more excellent."

Regarding the meaning of this comparative evaluation—whether it is sufficient or not—the intent of the response clarifies that one does not merely gain immeasurable merit by upholding this sutra; rather, if there is anyone who can simply honor the place where this sutra is preached and respectfully make offerings to the person who preaches it, they too shall obtain merit that is immeasurable and boundless, surpassing the two kinds of giving from three thousand Ganges-sands of worlds. Therefore, he exhorts [the assembly] to make offerings.

By this teaching, two points are superior: the ability to relinquish wealth and the location where the sutra is preached. Because the place where the sutra is preached is honored by those who uphold it, this location is explained next.
This section of the sutra consists of six parts:
first, honoring the place where the Dharma is taught;
