Second, revering the person who can expound it;
third, inquiring after the name of the sutra and the method for its reception and retention;
fourth, clarifying that all Buddhas of the three periods of time have spoken this sutra together, and that it was not spoken by me, a single Buddha, alone.
Fifth, two analogies regarding atoms and worlds are clarified to resolve doubts concerning the previous analogy of the sands of the Ganges;

sixth, it is clarified that the merit derived from the expedient causes of the thirty-two marks of physical perfection is still not equal to the merit of upholding this sutra, which is its true cause.
First, regarding the emphasis on the place where the Dharma is taught: this extends from “Furthermore, Subhūti... up to ‘it is like a stupa and temple.

As for the phrase “wherever this sutra is preached,” it refers to wherever one may be—whether in a lecture hall, a village, a desolate marsh, or a wilderness—any location where the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is being expounded.

The reason for encouraging humans, devas, and asuras to make offerings at the site where the Dharma is preached is to clarify that the reason humans, devas, and asuras obtain these exceptionally superior rewards of the five sensory pleasures is entirely due to their reliance on the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtras to practice the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, thereby securing these results; thus, they are exhorted to make offerings at the place where the Dharma is taught.

Regarding the phrase "like a stupa of the Buddha," it means one should encourage the thought that a place where this sutra is honored should be regarded as a stupa enshrining the bodily relics of a *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body) Buddha.

One should exhort: "Honor the place where this sutra is preached, just as one honors the sutra itself. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Know that this place is like a vajra; if it is on the earth, then the earth becomes noble."

One should not say that this is "like a Buddha stūpa or temple. To take it as such would be incorrect, for while this sūtra elucidates the Dharmakāya, the śarīra within a stūpa is merely the relic of a Nirmāṇakāya Buddha; therefore, it is not comparable.
Therefore, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the Buddha said to Śakra:

"Suppose there were one portion consisting of śarīra relics filling a trichiliocosm, and another portion consisting of this single case of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* scripture; which of these two would you choose?"
Śakra addressed the Buddha:
“I would rather take this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
It is not that I do not revere the relics of the Tathāgata; it is because of the Prajñā that the relics even exist.”
"Furthermore, because the *śarīra* (relics) are venerated due to the cultivation of *prajñā*,
one should take up the sūtras rather than the *śarīra*.
Since they are not equal [to the Dharma], one should not venerate the place where the sūtra is preached by regarding it as a stūpa or temple."

The compilers of the sutra, noting that worldly people generally hold stūpas, temples, śarīras, and images in high esteem, encouraged them to regard the empty space where the Dharma is preached as being like a stūpa or temple when making offerings.
2. Regarding "honoring those who can preach," this refers to the passage from "How much more so for anyone... up to "...respecting them as if they were the Buddha.

As for the phrase "How much more so for anyone who is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra in its entirety," it means that whether one is an ordinary person or a sage, if they are able to receive, uphold, and expound this sutra—or even provide offerings to such a person—one should know that this individual has accomplished the most supreme, foremost, and rare merit.

Previously, when explaining the passage concerning the recitation of even a four-line verse, I already encouraged making offerings to obtain great merit; how much more so for a person who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra—if such a person also raises offerings, you should know that the merit they obtain will be even greater and immeasurable.

Regarding the phrase "the most supreme and rare merit," this clarifies that those who make offerings to and uphold the person of this sutra will certainly attain the rewards of the first bhūmi and above in the near term, and ultimately attain the most supreme, rare, and foremost merit of the fruit of Buddhahood.
This most supreme and foremost rarity is of two kinds:
first, explaining the name based on worldly conventions, where the latter explains the former;
and another interpretation:
"Supreme" means there is nothing that can surpass it;
"exalted" means there is nothing beyond it;
"foremost" means it is not shared with the lower stages.
"Rare" means that which does not exist in the world.
Because the Sūtra states that one who clearly and completely receives and upholds [this teaching] attains this most supreme merit, it exhorts one to make offerings to those who uphold the Sūtra.
The phrase "wherever this sutra may be located" clarifies that the person who upholds the sutra is itself the locus where the sutra dwells.

The phrase "therein is a Buddha present" clarifies the exhortation to make offerings to those who uphold the sutra; regardless of whether they are ordinary persons or sages, one should regard anyone capable of receiving and upholding this sutra as being like a Buddha, and should thus encourage them to receive offerings.

The reason for this is that while the Tathāgata was in the world, he personally preached this sutra to transform and awaken sentient beings; therefore, in the final age, anyone who follows the Buddha’s intent and upholds this sutra is no different from the Buddha himself.

Although this person is still an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) and is not called a Buddha, they circulate the Mahāyāna, preach the Dharma to transform others, engender understanding, sever delusions, and realize the fruits of sainthood; because they share these qualities with a Buddha, it is therefore urged that one should make offerings to them as if to a Buddha.
Therefore, the Sūtra states: "The people therein are also people of the place of Vajra-vidyā," meaning they are honored among men.
Furthermore, because what this Sūtra symbolizes is the ultimate Dharmakāya, it is also said that there is a Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "if one honors those who resemble the Buddha," this refers to Bodhisattvas. It clarifies that when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain wisdom to eliminate delusions, and engage in the practice of teaching the Dharma to transform sentient beings for the benefit of both self and others, they possess a portion of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) and a partial awakening identical to that of a Buddha; therefore, they are said to "resemble the Buddha."

Because it clarifies that the merit of one who upholds this sutra in transforming sentient beings is equal to that of a bodhisattva, it exhorts one to make offerings to such a person as one would to a bodhisattva; thus, it says they should be honored "as if they were the Buddha."
Third, regarding the inquiry into the title of the sutra: it extends from "At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha" up to "it is not the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The reason for inquiring into the title of the sutra here is that Subhūti thought to himself:

although the Tathāgata has above praised the profound and deep nature of the sutra's principles, and exhorted [the assembly] to receive, uphold, make offerings to, and preach this teaching, as well as to honor those who maintain the sutra; [he has yet to state its specific name].

However, I now say that if one wishes to receive, uphold, and circulate [this teaching] in the final age to benefit all sentient beings, yet does not know the name of the sutra or the method for its upholding, there will be no means by which one can preach it to benefit all sentient beings.
Therefore, he asked for the name of the sutra.
"The Buddha told Subhūti:
'This Dharma-door is named the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā.'"
"By this name you should uphold it" is the answer to the question regarding the title of the sutra.
"Vajra" means firm and solid. "Prajñā" refers to the wisdom at the pinnacle of the Tathāgata’s fruition that illuminates the characteristics of all phenomena.
"Pāramitā" means "reaching the other shore.
This refers to the merit of the Tathāgata’s wisdom on the other shore; because its essence is as solid and firm as a vajra, it is called the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.

Regarding the phrase "You should uphold it by this name": because the sutra is named according to its principle, it is also called the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. Therefore, he instructs Subhūti that one should receive, uphold, and circulate it among sentient beings during the final age by means of this name.
Regarding the phrase "For what reason," why is this taken up and brought forward?
Having just heard the name of the sutra from Subhūti, he ought to have asked the World-Honored One:
"Why is this sutra named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*?"
However, because he merely had this thought but did not pose a question, [the Buddha] spoke directly, asking, "For what reason?

The answer states: "The Buddha speaks of the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet it is not the *prajñāpāramitā*," and so forth. This is the Tathāgata’s worldly analytical explanation of the sutra’s title; it clarifies that this sutra expounds the unconditioned *dharmakāya* (Dharma-body) and the wisdom of the *pāramitā* (perfection) of the Tathāgata. Since it is solely the merit of the firm wisdom of the *pāramitā* attained by the Tathāgata at the stage of fruition, it is called "the Buddha speaks of the *prajñāpāramitā*."
However, this wisdom of the other shore is the realm of the Buddhas alone, not something known by those of the two vehicles or ordinary beings; therefore, it is said that "it is not Prajñāpāramitā."
Because this is the realm of the Tathāgata and cannot be attained by others, it is called the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Fourth, regarding why the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time all preach this sutra: [From] "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
There is no dharma taught by the Tathāgata. This is the second instance within this sutra of the teaching that there is no dharma taught.

In the sixth section above, it was stated that "there is no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can teach"; this clarifies that because the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body Buddha) does not speak based on the realization of ultimate reality, it is said that he does not teach the Dharma.
Now, when Subhūti says, "World-Honored One!
There is no dharma taught by the Tathāgata," these two passages from the sūtra share the same intended meaning and yield a great fruit.
The preceding sutra states: "For what reason?

The Buddha says that the pāramitās are not actually pāramitās. The commentary explains: "This Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā is exclusively the domain of the Tathāgata; it is not something that can be attained by others."
Based on this, a doubt arose: Is it that only Śākyamuni Tathāgata alone has attained and alone taught this, while other Buddhas have neither attained nor taught it?
Or is it that the Buddhas of the ten directions have all equally attained and equally taught it?
Since the speech of others is ambiguous, it is necessary to investigate and distinguish [the meaning].
Herein there should be questions and answers, yet no questions and answers are provided; instead, [the Buddha] asks directly: "Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
Has the Tathāgata preached any dharma?
Subhūti, understanding the Tathāgata’s intention, replied, "World-Honored One!"

"The Tathāgata has not preached any dharma" clarifies that this [teaching] serves as the supreme cause for the present fruit of the dharma-realization of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; thus, the Buddhas of the three periods of time collectively declare: "I have all attained the arousal of the bodhicitta because of upholding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*."
"Relying on this sutra, one cultivates the practices of the ten stages and achieves *sambodhi*.

It is thus equally attained and equally taught—neither more nor less, neither increasing nor decreasing. Since it is not I, Śākyamuni alone, who has attained and taught it, it is said that 'there is no dharma taught.'"

Therefore, in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, the Buddha himself said: "From the night I attained the Way until the night of my parinirvāṇa, there is not a single word that I have not spoken during that interval."
However, although the Tathāgata has preached immeasurable sūtras throughout his entire life, why do you say that he did not speak a single word?
This clarifies that the twelve divisions of the teachings I have now spoken are identical to those spoken by the Buddhas of the three periods of time and are no different from them;
as for what the Buddhas of the ten directions have spoken, I have not spoken a single word separately from them.

Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows: when it is said that from the night the Tathāgata attained the Way until his parinirvāṇa, he did not speak a single word, this clearly demonstrates that dharmas are without name or characteristic (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*). Because they transcend the path of speech and the sphere of mental activity, they cannot be explained by means of names or characteristics; therefore, it is said that he did not speak a single word.
“Subhūti! What do you think?

Are all the motes of dust existing within a trichiliocosm many? This is the third analogy within the section on comparative measurement; it explains the preceding second analogy of the *gaṅgā* sands, and thereby comprehensively explains the preceding first analogy of the trichiliocosm.
A doubt arises:
Since the first two metaphors involve giving away vast amounts, why does the resulting merit become so small that it does not equal the merit of upholding even a single verse?
Holding and reciting a single verse involves very little effort; why, then, does one obtain blessings far exceeding those of giving, immeasurable and boundless?
Having this doubt, he cites this analogy to explain how holding [the Dharma] yields great merit.

Therefore, it is intended to clarify that although the merit of giving may be vast, because its cause is tainted by outflows and afflictions, its fruit is a state bound within the three realms and incapable of liberation; thus, it is not as excellent [as the other].

It is clear that although the upholding of a single verse is small in scale, it can lead to transcendence from the three realms and distantly summon the fruit of Buddhahood. Because this cause is untainted and free from the defilement of afflictions, its fruit is not one of bondage; therefore, it surpasses the merit of giving.
Therefore, the analogy of a minute particle is raised to resolve this doubt. One might ask:
"In wishing to compare the two kinds of merit—upholding the sutra and practicing giving—which is superior and which inferior, why is an external, indeterminate particle cited as an analogy?"
According to worldly discourse, the name "atom" (*paramāṇu*) is explained as being both determinate and indeterminate.

To speak directly of the atom: it may be called affliction (*kleśa*), or defilement (*saṃkleśa*), or bondage (*bandhana*), or realm (*dhātu*), or nature (*prakṛti*), or impurity (*mala*), or dust (*rajas*), or stain (*upakleśa*); thus, it has various names.

Generally speaking, when one speaks of "dust particles" (*rajas*), this refers both to the dust particles of afflictions (*kleśa-rajas*) and to the dust particles of the earth; for these two names are similar.
Furthermore, as their meaning and referent are identical, the dust particles of the earth are cited as a metaphor.

This clarifies that although the merit obtained from giving the two aforementioned types of seven treasures is great, because the mind gives while grasping at signs and is thus conjoined with afflictions such as greed, it is a defiled dust of affliction.
Because its essence is not liberation, it is inferior;
whereas the merit of upholding even a single verse of this sutra has non-apprehension of signs as its cause and liberation as its fruit, and is therefore superior.
Regarding the phrase "Would this be much?", this is the Tathāgata asking Subhūti whether all the atoms contained within the three thousandfold world system would be many.
Subhūti said, “Those atoms are exceedingly many,
World-Honored One. This is Subhūti’s respectful response to the Tathāgata, clarifying that the atoms are indeed very numerous.
Regarding the statement, "These atoms are said by the Tathāgata not to be atoms," this clarifies that the indeterminate atoms of the earth are not the atoms of defiled afflictions.

They are called "not" because they are not [the same as] the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), yet they are not entirely non-existent; rather, they are called "not" because they are not the atoms of defiled afflictions.

Regarding the phrase "this is called a minute particle," it refers to the indeterminate minute particles of the earth within the trichiliocosm; it may also be described as a minute particle that is neither afflicted by nor stained with the defilements of affliction (*kleśa*).

The reason for again citing the analogy of the world in the fourth [section] is that while the preceding discussion was made from the perspective of the subtle, this one is stated according to the coarse.

Although the coarse and the subtle differ, their names and meanings are identical; they likewise encompass both the determinate (*vyākṛta*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and thus do not differ from the analogy of the sense objects. Furthermore, it is because the names used to distinguish them in the world are different.
"Subhūti! What do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? Why does this question arise?

The preceding section clarified that the merit derived from the two kinds of giving performed with grasping at signs merely results in the conditioned retributions of gods and humans within the triple world; therefore, it does not equal the merit of upholding this sutra.

However, it is not yet known what the causal merit of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man bestowed by the Buddha is; these myriad practices of the ten stages are likewise supramundane, untainted merit—how do they compare to the merit of upholding this sutra?

The reason for this is that in the sūtras, the Tathāgata himself declared: "In the past, because I prostrated with my head in reverence to my parents, teachers, and elders, I have now attained the mark of the invisible crown of the head."
Because he rejoiced in and assisted others in performing meritorious deeds, he obtained the mark of webbed fingers and toes on his hands.

Because for three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas he never spoke falsely, he obtained the mark of a broad and long tongue. However, since these marks are likewise all summoned by supreme causes that are free from outflows (*anāsrava*), are these causes the same as the merit of upholding this sutra, or are they different?
Because of this doubt, the Buddha asked Subhūti, "Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man?

The intent of his reply clarifies that not only do meritorious acts such as giving the seven treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—performed with attachment to signs—not equal the merit of upholding even a single verse of this sutra; even the merit resulting from the favorable causes and skillful means for the reward of the Buddha’s thirty-two marks of a great man does not equal the merit of receiving and upholding a single verse of this sutra.
Furthermore, an objection is raised:
"In that case, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man are a revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*), and the upholding of this sutra is also a revealing cause.
Since both are revealing causes, why is the merit of upholding the sutra superior to the blessings of the marks of a Great Man?"

Therefore, the reason for answering as such is to clarify that this sutra comes from within the Dharma-body; because it is a part thereof, it in turn elucidates the Dharma-body, and by investigating these expressive words, one realizes the Dharma-body.

Although it is said that one receives and upholds the scriptural teachings, the intent lies in the principles expressed therein which are to be realized. Therefore, one who receives and upholds this sutra receives the Dharma-body; thus, it surpasses the merit of the marks of a Great Man. This does not mean that the meaning of the "revealing cause" (liao-yin) regarding the merit of the upheld scripture is being discarded.
"What do you think?

Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man? This is the Buddha questioning Subhūti: "According to what you understand within your own mind, can the Tathāgata—the eternally constant Dharma-body of space throughout past and present—be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man?"
Therefore, it is said: "Can one see the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man?

Subhūti replied, "No. This indicates that the meanings of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) are distinct; since there is a difference between what is attained through cultivation and what is attained without cultivation, one cannot perceive the Tathāgata of the Dharma-body by means of the marks and signs of the Reward-Buddha.
This explanation is given because the name of this Tathāgata is identical [to that of the Reward Buddha].
As for the phrase "For what reason," some may harbor doubts, thinking:

"If the Dharma-body Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man as a Reward Buddha, why did the Tathāgata himself say: 'After I had completed my practice over three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas and attained the vajra-mind, I manifested the originally existing Dharma-body as the Reward Buddha'?"

"At that time, the Dharma-body Buddha and the Reward-body Buddha are essentially one and without distinction; for what reason, then, do you say that 'the Reward-body Buddha with the marks of a Great Man cannot be seen by means of the Dharma-body Buddha'?"
Therefore, it is asked: "For what reason?

Subhūti replies, "The Tathāgata speaks of the thirty-two marks of a great man as 'the thirty-two marks of a great man,'" because these are the marks attained through the retribution of the Buddha-Tathāgata’s cultivation; thus, the Tathāgata speaks of them as the thirty-two marks of a great man of retribution.

The phrase "it is precisely the absence of marks" clarifies that the thirty-two marks of a great man obtained by this Reward Buddha are not the marks of the Dharmakāya, which are fixed as either ancient or modern.

Why is this? Because the two Buddhas—the Dharma-body and the Reward-body—are one in essence without distinction. Yet, the Reward-body cannot be perceived through its physical marks. This is because the Dharma-body, which is the eternal and unchanging void, cannot be seen through physical characteristics whether one practices the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) or does not practice them. Since these thirty-two marks of a Great Man are not the marks of the Dharma-body, it is said that they are "non-marks."
Because of this distinction between their respective characteristics, one cannot perceive the unconditioned Dharma-body Buddha through the marks of the Reward-Buddha attained through cultivation.
Thus far, the comparison has shown how the merit of upholding this sutra is superior and distinct from others.

However, since the essence of the two Buddhas—the Dharma-body and the Reward-body—is not distinct and there is no differentiation of superiority or inferiority between them, the statement that "one cannot perceive the Dharma-body Tathāgata through the marks of a Great Man belonging to the Reward-body" is made to clarify that the cause possesses a degree of excellence different from the fruit; it does not mean that while the essence of the two Buddhas, Dharma and Reward, is one, they differ in quality such that the Buddha of the Reward-body with his masculine marks cannot be seen as the Buddha of the Dharma-body.
Someone may raise a doubt based on literal attachment:

"If these thirty-two marks of a great man do not constitute the Dharma-body Buddha, then these thirty-two marks of a great man would be entirely non-marks. To this, the answer is given: they are called the thirty-two marks of a great man; that is to say, they are called the marks of the thirty-two marks of a great man belonging to the *saṃbhoga*-body Buddha (*vipāka-buddha*), and they are also termed non-marks of the Dharma-body.

This is discussed from the perspective of the distinct characteristics of the Dharma-body and Reward-body Buddhas, rather than from the perspective of their non-dual unity; thus, it is called the "male form of the Reward-body Buddha.
The *Treatise* says:

"How is that supreme merit accomplished? Here, the Master of the Treatise, intending to provide a verse commentary on this section of the sūtra, first raises a question to provoke inquiry: he asks how the merit of upholding this section of the sūtra, as described in this passage, surpasses the merit of giving the gift of the seven treasures mentioned above.
He then replied with a verse.
This section of the sutra, however, is explained by means of a single verse alone.
Regarding the phrase "honoring two places," this single line explains the two sūtras concerning persons:
First, the World-Honored One’s reverence for the place where the Dharma is taught;
second, his reverence for the person who can teach it.
This should be stated as "reverence for two places," because through practice one realizes the Great Essence (mahātattva).
One should also say that there is a lack of respect in two respects, due to the habituation of afflictions:
first, a lack of respect for the object given; second, a lack of reverence for the person who gives.
However, because the verses are concise, this is omitted from discussion.
Regarding the phrase "through practice one realizes the Great Essence," this explains the reason for honoring the two locations mentioned above.

Specifically, it is said that one honors the person who preaches the Dharma rather than the person who gives away material goods; this is because by receiving, upholding, and practicing even a single four-line verse of this sutra, one is able to realize the Great Essence of the Dharmakāya. Therefore, it is stated that one honors the place where the Dharma is preached, but not the place where wealth is relinquished.

Furthermore, regarding the second line of this verse, one should explain it in detail according to the sequence of the subsequent prose commentary, which addresses two sections of the sutra: the title of the sutra and the passage stating that "the Tathāgata has not preached any dharma."

Regarding the phrase "he practices afflictions because of them": this clarifies that although the giving of the seven treasures may be extensive, the merit derived from grasping at signs is a cause for rebirth as a human or deva; it is a dharma of defiled bondage. Therefore, it is said that "he practices afflictions because of them," rather than saying he values the person to whom the objects are given.
Regarding the phrase "this subdues the merit of defilement," it clarifies that the cause for the thirty-two marks is superior to the merit of giving with the intention of seeking marks.

Although the merit of the thirty-two marks is indeed superior to the merit of the aforementioned giving, it still does not equal the merit of upholding even a single verse of this sutra. This clarifies that the merit of upholding this sutra not only surpasses the causes for fulfilling [the physical form], but also surpasses the expedient causes for the marks of a Great Man; therefore, it is said that "this subdues the merit of defilement."
Regarding the phrase "What is the meaning of this? and so forth, from here below the author explains this single verse, interpreting the sūtra in successive order.
The phrase "Venerating in two places" quotes the first line of the verse, explaining the first and second *yuga* (couplets) of the sūtra.

"The first is the place where it was taught, and the second is the person who taught it," and so forth; this refers back to what was previously called "the place of respect," which is now enumerated here.
Because the sūtras and śāstras are to be respected, these persons and places are cited to exhort [the audience] to offer worship.

Regarding the phrase "not with the seven treasures and so forth," because the merit of giving the seven treasures is a cause for affliction, one does not encourage others to make offerings; this refers to the person who relinquishes material wealth.

Regarding the phrase, "Because this dharma-gate serves as the supreme cause for all realized dharmas," this explains the second line of the verse and clarifies the third and fourth lines of the sutra text. It demonstrates that the Buddhas of the ten directions declare, "I have all attained realization of the unconditioned Dharma-body and realized Great Bodhi precisely because I upheld this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*"; therefore, they speak in unison.
From "As stated in the Sūtra" up to "the Tathāgata has no dharma to teach," the author cites the Sūtra to provide a conclusion, and then offers further explanation.

Regarding the question "What is the meaning of this?", since this Sūtra states that "the Tathāgata has no dharma to teach," the Master of the Treatise explains it as the sense that the Buddhas of the ten directions take the realization of the Dharma as their supreme cause and preach it in common.
What is the conclusion of this?

It is explained as follows: "Because there is not a single dharma that is spoken by the Tathāgata alone and not spoken by other Buddhas. This explains that the Tathāgata has no dharma he does not teach; it establishes the meaning that the Sūtra is taught equally by the Victorious Ones (Jinas) of the ten directions as its superior cause.
The passage beginning with “those precious jewels” explains the third line of the verse by identifying the causes for the defilement of afflictions; it interprets the fifth sub-phrase of the sutra.

The statement, “the merit of giving those precious jewels is a cause for defiled afflictions,” clarifies the meaning that the merit from giving the seven treasures acts as a cause for outflowing (*sāsrava*) existence.

Regarding the phrase "because it can accomplish the affairs of afflictions," this clarifies that the fruit obtained from the preceding causes consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of humans and devas within the three realms.
Regarding the phrase "Because this cause is far removed from the causes of affliction," it clarifies that the merit of upholding the sutra is not a cause of affliction.

As for the term "therefore": since the merit of giving the seven treasures is a cause of affliction, whereas the merit of upholding the sutra is not a cause of affliction, the analogy of the dust motes of this earth is taught. This clarifies that while the dust of this earth consists of minute particles, it is not a cause of defilement; thus, it is proven that the merit of giving the seven treasures—though also termed "minute particles"—is nonetheless a cause of defilement and cannot compare to the merit of upholding the sutra.
The phrase "As stated in the sutra" and so forth serves as a conclusion by citing such scriptures as those concerning the world-systems of atoms.
Regarding the question, "Why is it said thus?":
this asks why the preceding sutra first speaks of these atoms and then says that the Tathāgata has taught them to be non-atoms; why are they spoken of in such a contradictory manner?

This means that those atoms are not the substance of afflictions such as greed; it clarifies that the atoms of the earth within the trichiliocosm are not the defiled atoms of afflictions such as greed and hatred, and is therefore said to be "not atoms."

Regarding the statement, "For this reason, it is called 'earth-microdust' (*pṛthivī-rajas*)," because this earth consists of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) microdust and does not possess the sense of being a "dust" such as greed (*rāga*), it can only be described as "earth-microdust. The meaning of the world (*loka*) is likewise the same as that of microdust.
"What does this clarify? refers to the previous statement that the atoms of the earth are not defiled by afflictions; for what purpose was this explained? It is clarified as follows:

those merits are the cause of defilement by afflictions. This precisely sets forth the matter illustrated by the metaphor, in order to clarify that the merit from giving the seven treasures is a particle of defilement by afflictions; thus, these two metaphors of the atom-world are presented.

Regarding the statement, "Therefore, with respect to external indeterminate objects, those roots of merit consisting of blessings are proximate": the merit from the gift of the seven treasures is a cause for the defilement of afflictions; because it can induce the retributive fruits of humans and devas within the three realms, it is considered proximate.
External indeterminate objects are not the cause of afflictive defilement and cannot induce karmic results; therefore, they are not called "proximate.

As for the phrase, "How much more so this merit can bring about the Bodhi of a Buddha," the merit from the aforementioned gift of the seven treasures has the sense of being a cause only for worldly retributive fruits; compared to external objects, it is still considered proximate. How much more so is the merit of upholding this sutra, which can manifest the Dharma-body and the Bodhi of a Buddha—this is the most proximate among all that is proximate, as it is superior even among the merits that accomplish the marks of a Great Man.

This clarifies that the merit of upholding this sutra possesses the significance of being a superior cause for the Bodhi of the Dharmakāya; it not only surpasses the seven treasures as a cause for the merit of humans and devas, but also excels the causes for the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa) of the Reward Buddha (vipākaphala-buddha).
This merit of upholding the sutra is the cause for the marks of a superior man, for it is untainted (anāsrava) merit.
How much more so, then, does it surpass the tainted merit of giving the seven treasures?
Therefore, it is said that it excels that merit.
Regarding the phrase "For what reason": it may well be that the merit of upholding this sutra surpasses the tainted merit of giving the seven treasures;
however, since these marks of a Great Man arise from untainted merit, for what reason is it further said that they do not equal the merit of upholding the sutra?
The commentary immediately explains: "Because those marks are not marks with respect to the Buddha’s bodhi.

As for why the causes of the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) do not equal the merit of upholding this sutra, it clarifies that the marks of a Great Man are exclusively the marks of the *vipākabuddha* (retribution Buddha) and not the marks of the *dharmakāyabuddha* (dharma-body Buddha). Since these untainted merits can only serve as causes for the marks of a Great Man of the *vipākabuddha*, they cannot serve as causes for the bodhi of the *dharmabuddha*. Therefore, one who receives and upholds the sutra is receiving and upholding the bodhi of the *dharmabuddha*; thus, the merit of upholding the sutra surpasses the causes of the marks of a Great Man. This is concluded by stating: "Because they are not those marks of the *dharmakāya*."
At this point, a follower of the Vehicle raises a doubt and objection:

"If these marks of a Great Man are not the marks of the Dharma-Buddha or the Bodhi-Buddha, for what reason does the Tathāgata teach that the manifestation of the originally existing nature constitutes the Reward-Buddha (Sambhogakāya)?"

If manifesting the nature that has existed from the beginning were to constitute the Reward Buddha (vipākabuddha), then the two Buddhas would be one and the same body; why, then, do you say that the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa) are not the marks of the Dharma Buddha?

The commentary immediately explains: "Therefore, it is said that these are the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). This clarifies that although the Dharma-body and Reward-body Buddhas are identical in essence, they also possess the sense of having distinct characteristics. Therefore, I say that the marks obtained through the cultivation of a Great Man are exclusively the marks belonging to the Reward-body Buddha and not the marks of the Dharma-body. This is concluded by stating, "Because of those marks," which clarifies that because those marks of a Great Man are precisely the marks of the Reward-body Buddha.

The preceding statement, "Regarding the Buddha’s bodhi, it is not a mark," does not mean that the *saṃbhoga*-buddha’s bodhi is also not a mark; rather, it is this very upholding and explaining [of the teaching] that can bring about the attainment of the Buddha’s bodhi.

Regarding the phrase "Therefore, because that is not supreme," this concludes the description of the marks of a superior person (*puruṣa*) whose merit from upholding the sutra is untainted (*anāsrava*).

Furthermore, the statement "Moreover, that merit reaches the most immediate and supreme" explains the meaning of the fourth line of the verse concerning "subjugation. It clarifies that because it is an untainted merit, it is able to subjugate; even the merit from giving the seven treasures is not equal to the merit of upholding the sutra, let alone the tainted merit of giving inferior jewels.
This single phrase concludes both types of superior merit.

"In this way, that generosity reaches its ultimate excellence" universally concludes the establishment of the two types of analogies for the relinquishing of external wealth, as well as the establishment of the ultimate meaning regarding the merit of the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
"The Buddha said:

'Subhūti! If a son or daughter of good family were to give away their lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in alms,'" refers to the seventh section of the text within this chapter on comparative measurement (*tulanā*).

The reason for this coming is that the preceding section clarified two kinds of giving—each as numerous as the sands of three thousand Ganges Rivers—which spoke only of relinquishing external wealth; yet, by comparison, these were not equal to the great merit of upholding this sutra. Thus, it was not yet sufficient to manifest that the merit of upholding this sutra is the most supreme among the supreme.
However, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, there are two kinds of relinquishment:
first, internal relinquishment, which refers to body and life;
second, external relinquishment, which refers to wealth, treasures, and so forth.

Now it is clarified that not only does the gift of external wealth fall short of the merit of upholding this sutra, but even the renunciation of one's own life and body—which is the most difficult form of giving—does not suffice; for even if one were to renounce as many lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, enduring physical and mental suffering thereby, it would still not equal the merit of upholding a single verse of this sutra. Therefore, this is explained next.
Although it is said that the merit of sacrificing one's body does not equal the merit of upholding this sutra, it was not yet known which of these two is superior;
therefore, this is elucidated based on this very sutra.
Now, this section of the sutra contains eight distinct clarifications of its meaning:

first, it clarifies that if a good son or a good daughter were to give up as many lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in practicing *dāna*, it would not equal the merit of one who receives, maintains, and recites even a four-line verse from within this sutra for the sake of others.

The commentary states: "Austere physical practice surpasses that. This clarifies that even if a bodhisattva prior to the stages, while still within a mind that grasps at signs, were to sacrifice their own body and life for the sake of enlightenment—though this may surpass the renunciation of external wealth—it would still not equal the merit of upholding this sutra.
What is meant by the "mind that grasps at signs"?
There are generally two meanings.

Since immeasurable eons past, sentient beings have reckoned a self within their own bodies and been greedily attached to it, seeking only the superior fruits of humans and devas within the triple world. They do not know that Bodhi is wondrously transcendent of worldly phenomena; though they hear of the supreme excellence of Bodhi, they still claim it is identical to the retributive fruits of worldly humans and devas—substantial, conditioned, and inevitably subject to arising and ceasing.
If one gives up the body for the sake of this bodhi, yet still invites the conditioned retribution of that realm, it is therefore a grasping at signs.
Because it is a grasping at signs, it is not as good [as the other].
Furthermore, even if those from the first bhūmi upward were to sacrifice their bodies without grasping at signs, their merit would not equal that of upholding a single verse.
This clarifies that one who receives and upholds this sutra, though said to uphold a single verse of the scripture, intends by it to uphold the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) which is its ultimate meaning.

Although verbal teachings consist of names and signs (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), that which they express pertains to the dimension of the unconditioned *dharmakāya*; because it is signless (*animitta*), it is not the grasping of signs.

Since one practices in reliance upon the sūtras and knows that the *dharmakāya* is not identical to the three realms, it surpasses the merit associated with the physical forms of bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Second, regarding the passage: "At that time, Subhūti, having heard this sutra being preached, had never before heard such a Dharma-gate.
This commentary explains it as "rare" (āścarya).

Regarding the statement, “When Subhūti heard this sutra being preached, he deeply understood its meaning and purport,” this clarifies that it was precisely because Subhūti heard the Tathāgata preach this sutra that he was able to understand the unconditioned Dharma-body; this is what is meant by “deeply understanding its meaning and purport.”
However, Subhūti, if this bodhisattva is one who has expediently assumed the guise of a śrāvaka, he manifests through skillful means that he has a profound understanding;
if, on the other hand, he were a true śrāvaka, he would have truly neither heard nor understood it until now, and it is only today that he hears and understands its profound meaning.
Regarding the phrase "weeping with tears," Subhūti’s weeping has two meanings:
first, Subhūti weeps because he contemplates how profound and weighty this teaching is, something he has never heard before;
second, he weeps out of grief that his own realization of the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle prevented him from attaining this Dharma-gate of the Great Vehicle.
"If he were merely acting as a śrāvaka out of expedient means, he ought to shed tears.

Regarding the phrase "he wiped away his tears and addressed the Buddha, saying 'Rare indeed!'"—this section is titled "The Rare" because these two characters, "rare" (希有), are specifically extracted to serve as the title for the second section.
There are two kinds of rarity:

first, it clarifies that this resultant, unconditioned *dharmakāya* of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, the profound *dharmadhātu*, is obtained solely by the Tathāgata and does not exist on lower stages; therefore, it is called rare.

2. Second, it clarifies that Subhūti himself declared: "Although I have attained the fruit of arhatship, possessing the ten knowledges, the three samādhis, and the eight liberations, I have never before heard this most profound dharma-gate."
Because those who possess faith are difficult to find, it is said to be "rare.

Since the Tathāgata attained the Way five years ago, he has constantly preached the Prajñāpāramitā without interruption; furthermore, as stated above, the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time also constantly preach this Dharma. For what reason, then, does Subhūti say that he has never heard it before and that it is rare?

Although the Tathāgata has constantly preached this sutra, which is the Dharma-wheel of the Mahāyāna, Subhūti is a person of the Hīnayāna who has never before heard it; even if he were to hear it, he would not understand it. Therefore, in the case of Subhūti, this is called something rare.

Regarding the statement, "The eye of wisdom that I have attained since ancient times has never before heard such a Dharma-gate," this clarifies that Subhūti himself says: although he previously attained the eye of wisdom of the emptiness of intrinsic nature and non-self, he had never before heard this profound Dharma-gate of the unconditioned Dharmakāya.

Why is it that he speaks only of "the eye of wisdom attained by me" and does not mention attaining the "dharma-eye"? This clarifies that although followers of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) contemplate both the outflowing (sāsrava) and non-outflowing (anāsrava), they understand the emptiness of persons (pudgala-nairātmya) through the teachings; however, because they have not yet attained the essence of the dharma of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) nor the emptiness of dharmas (dharma-śūnyatā) which is True Suchness (tathatā), he speaks only of the eye of wisdom attained and does not discuss the attainment of the dharma-eye.
"Why is this? Subhūti!
That which the Buddha calls the *prajñāpāramitā* is precisely not [the *prajñāpāramitā*]"—this is the third chapter-gate.
The commentary states: "That shore of wisdom is difficult to measure.
Regarding the phrase "For what reason," the objection is raised:
Since Subhūti has already attained the eye of wisdom, for what reason does he not hear such a Dharma-gate?
Therefore, it is asked: "For what reason?

The answer is intended to show that this Dharma—the supreme, ultimate meaning of the merit of the Tathāgata’s fruition at the further shore—is not something that can be fathomed by those of the Two Vehicles; for this reason, they do not hear it.
This single point constitutes the supreme rarity.

Regarding the phrase "The Buddha speaks the Prajñāpāramitā," this is an explanation of the name according to worldly convention; it clarifies that what is realized by this dharma-gate is exclusively the realm of the wisdom of the ultimate fruit of all Buddhas, which is the "other shore" (pāramitā), and thus it is called the "speaking of pāramitā."

The phrase "it is not a pāramitā" clarifies that this wisdom of the other shore is the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata, and is not the sphere of knowledge accessible to the two vehicles; therefore, it is said to be "not a pāramitā."
Furthermore, this second intention [is explained] by the passage beginning with "This itself is not the Prajñāpāramitā" up until the third section, "That shore of wisdom is difficult to measure.
[The text continues: "O Bhagavān!"
"If there are further people who hear this sutra and their faith becomes pure, they immediately give rise to the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), and it is even designated as the 'true mark'.
This is the fourth section.
The Commentary explains: "It is also not the same as other dharmas."
"Furthermore, if there be a person" refers to a Bodhisattva of the stage of faith (śraddhā-bhūmi) prior to the first bhūmi.

"Upon hearing this sutra, their mind of faith becomes pure, and thus the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) arises" means that having heard this sutra, they are able to decisively believe in the unconditioned Dharma-body (asaṃskṛta-dharmakāya) and give rise to the understanding of the true mark; because they are free from the turbidity of doubt, it is called "pure."

Regarding the statement, "One should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme and foremost rare merit": if a bodhisattva believes in the unconditioned *dharmakāya* signified by this sutra and gives rise to faith as its true nature (*lakṣaṇa*), they are then able to practice according to the sutra and realize the rare merit of the resultant unconditioned *dharmakāya*; therefore, it is said that they "accomplish" it.
It clarifies that this unconditioned Dharma-body is attained only after three great *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas; as it surpasses the Lesser Vehicle, it is called "foremost.
Since it has not been attained by anything prior to the stage of the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), it is said to be "rare."
“World-Honored One!
‘This true mark’ refers to the fact that within this very sūtra, it is clarified that the Tathāgata has attained the true mark of the dharma-body of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
‘It is then a non-mark’ clarifies that the true mark attained by this Tathāgata is not the true mark attained within the teachings of the Two Vehicles.”
Regarding the statement, “Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of the ‘true mark, the true mark’,” there are two ways of understanding this.
To clarify that the principle of the true mark of this unconditioned *dharmakāya* is exclusively the true mark attained by the Tathāgata alone, he repeats the term “true mark, true mark.”
Furthermore, regarding the second interpretation of this intent, some may have a doubt:

"If the Mahāyāna teachings of the Buddha contain the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) while the teachings of the Two Vehicles do not, for what reason do the teachings of the Two Vehicles also themselves claim that there is a true mark?"

Therefore, the response is as follows: When it is said that the Tathāgata possesses the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) while others do not, this refers to the principle of the unconditioned *dharmakāya* true mark, which has been constant throughout past and present; thus, it is said that they lack the true mark. This does not mean that the true mark of the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) elucidated in the teachings of the Two Vehicles is also non-existent.

Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of the "true mark" (bhūtalakṣaṇa). As for this "true mark," there is first the true mark of the unconditioned Dharma-body attained by the Tathāgata; second, the true mark of the emptiness of nature (prakṛti-śūnyatā) attained by the followers of the Two Vehicles. Hence, it is called the "true mark, the true mark."
“World-Honored One!
That I have now been able to hear such a Dharma-gate is not to be considered difficult,” this is the fifth chapter-gate.
The commentary explains it as: “Firmly grasping the profound meaning.”
Regarding the statement, "It is not difficult for one to hear this Dharma-gate and believe and understand it," there are four intended meanings:
First, Subhūti speaks for himself, saying that he has now been born in the age of a Buddha and is furthermore a renunciant; being one who possesses faith, he has attained the path of an Arhat;
having heard the Buddha’s teaching, how could he possibly fail to believe?
Second, although Subhūti is a follower of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), because he has already generated the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta), he is able to believe upon hearing this.
Third, Subhūti is actually a Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body manifesting as a Śrāvaka; how could he possibly fail to believe when hearing this Dharma-gate?
Fourth, because Subhūti has obtained the power of the Tathāgata’s secret empowerment, he is certain to understand whatever is taught.
Since these four reasons exist, it is said that this is not difficult.

Regarding the statement, "If in a future age there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma and, having heard it, believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, such persons shall be the most rare and extraordinary," Subhūti speaks for himself: "I encountered the Buddha while he was still present in the world and possessed the aforementioned four conditions; therefore, I gave rise to faith and understanding without finding it difficult.

However, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, when one no longer encounters the era of a Buddha, if one can still give rise to faith in this sutra, such a person is one who has attained the first stage (bhūmi) or above—the most rare and extraordinary of beings."
Because the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) surpasses the two vehicles and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) prior to the stages, it is called "the first.
Regarding "rare" (*āścarya*): since it is only attained at the completion of one great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* of practice, whereas those prior to the stages have not yet reached it, it is called "rare."

"Why is this? Because this person lacks the mark of self (ātman) up to [the mark of sentient beings]; one should know that such a person is truly rare. This further clarifies that those who will give rise to faith during the final age will be rare.

However, within this fifth section, there are three instances of "For what reason," the first clarifying the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the latter clarifying the emptiness of the self (*ātma-śūnyatā*), and the third resolving doubts.
For what reason are the first three [cases] explained together as being the foremost rarity?
And for what reason are these two [the last two cases] explained separately? If they were both explained as the foremost rarity based on the same cause, what would be the difference between them?
Regarding the question "Why is this so at the outset?"—it asks why those who clearly understand, believe, and uphold this sutra are considered the most rare and marvelous.
The answer is:

because such persons do not manifest the mark of a self (*ātman*), it is clear that they have attained the realization of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*); therefore, they are able to believe in this sutra.
Ordinary beings prior to the stages and those of the two vehicles have not yet understood the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā), and therefore they cannot believe it.
Thus, one should know that those who are able to believe through realization are the most rare and extraordinary.
Regarding the second "for what reason," the question asks:
Is it solely because one has attained the realization of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) that one is able to believe in this sutra,
or is there something further attained by which one is able to believe it?
He immediately replied:
"The marks I have shown are themselves non-marks.

The intent of this reply clarifies that one is not only able to believe and understand this sutra by attaining the realization of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā), but must also attain the realization of the emptiness of the self (pudgala-śūnyatā) before one can truly believe it; thus, he further explains the second "Why is this so? (tat kasya hetoḥ).

Regarding the third "for what reason": having heard previously that the characteristics of non-self clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and further hearing that the characteristics of "mine" are precisely non-characteristics clarifies the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*), it is explained that both the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*) are empty.
Thereupon, a doubt arises:
"Now we clearly perceive that the six internal bases (ādhyātmika-ṣaḍāyatana) are the grasper and the six external objects (bāhya-ṣaḍviṣaya) are the grasped; how can it be said that these are empty?
If all were empty, there should be neither grasper nor grasped; therefore, [the text] asks: 'For what reason?'"
Therefore, the answer is:
because one is free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), one is called a Buddha; thus, one knows emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

This clarifies that the Buddhas perceive this grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*), as well as the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*), to be deceptive and unreal, for they are all empty; it is for this reason that they are detached from them.
This clarification regarding the emptiness of dharmas refers only to the emptiness of dharmas as dependent origination; it does not clarify the emptiness of the dharma of Buddha-nature.
Regarding the passage, "The Buddha told Subhūti:

'So it is, so it is,' and so forth," although Subhūti has previously stated that those people in future ages who are able to give rise to faith belong to the first stage (*bhūmi*) and above—the foremost rarity—there may be those who doubt whether these words can truly be trusted. Therefore, the Buddha confirms them by saying "so it is," meaning that it is just as Subhūti has said; do not harbor doubts. For this reason, he repeats "so it is, so it is."

"If there be anyone who hears this sutra and is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear it, you should know that such a person is most rare"—this further completes the preceding fifth section, clarifying why Subhūti’s words are not in vain and are trustworthy, being exactly as he has said.

It clarifies that this person has already attained the realization of non-self on the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), is free from the five fears, and is devoid of the turbidity of doubt; therefore, upon hearing the sutra, they are not startled, terrified, or afraid.
If one explains the meaning according to worldly conventions, the latter is used to interpret the former.
Why is there no alarm?
Because there is no fear.
Why is there no fear? Because one does not fear.
Such is the sequence.

Furthermore, "not being startled" means that within the marks of the body, one attains the realization of non-self at the first stage (*bhūmi*) and becomes free from the five fears; upon hearing that all phenomena are without self, the body exhibits no sign of dread, and is therefore said to be "not startled."
"Without fear" means that when dwelling within the mind, upon hearing that all dharmas are without self, the inner mind is resolute and free from doubt; therefore, it is called "without fear.
"Without dread" means that, in body and mind, one ultimately does not engage in slander.
Another interpretation is as follows:

because this person has attained the understanding derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), when they first hear the Mahāyāna teaching on selflessness, their mind remains settled in the principle; therefore, it is said that they are not startled.
Because one attains the understanding of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), profound faith arises and doubt ceases; therefore, it is called "fearlessness.
Once faith has arisen and one attains the understanding of wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), one practices without disparagement; therefore, it is called "dare not fear."

Regarding the statement, “One should know that such a person is most rare,” the Tathāgata reiterates this to confirm the preceding passage; it does not differ from the previous explanation. Why is this?
"The Tathāgata says that the foremost pāramitā is not the foremost pāramitā" clarifies the sixth section.
The commentary explains the name as "surpassing other sūtras."
Now, this phrase "For what reason" serves as a general explanation, through the sixth, seventh, and eighth sections below, of the meanings established in the preceding five topical headings.
How is this explained? The preceding explanation states:

Why is it that giving up body and life as numerous as the sands of the Ganges for the sake of practicing giving does not equal the merit of receiving and upholding even a single four-line verse of this sutra?
Furthermore, Subhūti, having already attained the eye of wisdom, for what reason has he never before heard this sutra? Why is it called "rare"?
Moreover, for what reason is the scope of this sutra beyond the measurement of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles?
Furthermore, for what reason can upholding this sutra give rise to the understanding of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which does not exist within the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas?

Moreover, for what reason must those who attain the understanding of the emptiness of both self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*) be able to believe in, uphold, and practice this sutra, thereby becoming the most rare and extraordinary?

Regarding the meaning of the five preceding chapters, why is it that they are as they are? Therefore, the answer is given with the words, “The Tathāgata speaks of the foremost pāramitā,” and so forth. This is because this sutra is the foremost merit of the ultimate fruition (phala-koṭi) of the Tathāgata, surpassing all other sūtras;
furthermore, because this sutra can serve as the great cause for attaining the fruit of Buddhahood;

and moreover, because it does not merely serve as the superior cause for the manifest fruit of a Buddha, but serves as the superior cause for all Buddhas of the ten directions—thus its explanation is established.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation:
the sixth chapter-gate directly explains the preceding five chapter-gates.
When the Tathāgata speaks of the "first pāramitā," he clarifies the supreme merits prior to the fruition of Buddhahood on the other shore; therefore, it is called the "first pāramitā."
Generally speaking, there are three stages to the *pāramitās*:
first, the semblance *pāramitās* prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*);
second, the true *pāramitās* from the attainment of the stages upward. Both of these constitute practices within the causal state.
What is now called the "first *pāramitā*" refers to the merit of the eternally abiding *dharmakāya* at the pinnacle of fruition on the other shore; therefore, it is termed "first.
Regarding the commentary’s explanation that its name is superior to other *sūtras*, this clarifies that the fundamental principle is superior to the fundamental teaching.
The verbal teaching is not the unconditioned *dharmakāya*; therefore, it is said that it is not the foremost *pāramitā*.
Furthermore, the term "not" also excludes the preceding two *pāramitās*.
Furthermore, "not" means it is not the realm of the two vehicles; it is also termed "not.
Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgata speaks of the foremost pāramitā," this seventh section is titled in the treatise "The Great Cause."
The "Great Cause" refers to the True Cause.
The True Cause is precisely the vast principle of the Pure Dharmakāya.

It is clearly stated that Śākyamuni Tathāgata himself said, "Because I have upheld this sutra, I have understood the unconditioned Dharmakāya and realized the merit of the Buddha-fruit on the other shore"; therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata speaks of the foremost pāramitā.
Regarding the phrase, "Those immeasurable Buddhas also taught the pāramitās," this is the eighth [chapter], titled "Purification" (*viśuddhi*) in the treatise.

Previously, it was stated that the first pāramitā serves as the great cause for the manifest fruit of a Tathāgata; however, is it only the Tathāgata Śākyamuni who, by upholding this sūtra, alone realizes and alone teaches it as the great cause?
The Buddhas of the ten directions all declare that they attained the fruit of Buddhahood because they upheld this sutra; they take its practice and its teaching as their great cause.

Therefore, the answer states: "Those immeasurable Buddhas also speak of the *pāramitās*. This clarifies that those Buddhas of the ten directions all say that they attained the fruit of Buddhahood by upholding this sutra and realizing the unconditioned *dharmakāya*; it is not that I alone practiced or taught it that makes it the great cause.
The phrase "this is called the foremost *pāramitā*" serves as a general conclusion for the preceding three phrases, identifying them as the supreme fruit—the merit of the foremost shore (*pāra*).
Because this sutra contains these eight kinds of superior merits, it surpasses the merit of sacrificing one's own body.
The Commentary states:

"From here on, the sutra text further clarifies that among those merits, this merit is even more superior. This means that as the Master of the Treatise intends to provide a verse explanation for this section of the sutra, he does not offer a brief summary of the meaning of the merit of upholding the sutra—which was already clarified within the sutra itself—as being even more superior.

The preceding section, which compared the merit of giving away immeasurable treasures as numerous as the sands of three thousand Ganges Rivers unfavorably to the merit of upholding this sutra, was intended to clarify that relinquishing external wealth is relatively easy; it was not yet a demonstration of the highest excellence among superior merits.

Now it is clarified that while it is difficult to renounce internal wealth by giving away one's own body and life, even if one can renounce such things despite their difficulty, this still does not equal the merit of upholding this sutra; is this not a manifestation of the principle of progressive superiority?
In this section, eight topical headings are established by means of two verses to explain this passage of the sutra.

Regarding the phrase "To suffer for the sake of the body is superior to that," this explains the portion of the sutra from "The Buddha said to Subhūti" down to "shedding tears and weeping with grief. It clarifies that while it is easy to renounce external wealth, it is difficult to renounce internal wealth; for sentient beings harbor deep and heavy attachments to their own bodies, and if they were to renounce them, they would experience great suffering.
Because it is for the sake of the Dharma, one is able to relinquish even suffering; therefore, the relinquishing of the body is superior to the relinquishing of external wealth.
Yet, although this relinquishing is superior to the relinquishing of external wealth, it is still not equal to the merit of upholding a single verse; thus, it is said to be superior to that.

Regarding the term "rare" (*āścarya*): it explains the passage in the sūtra from "wiping away his tears and addressing the Buddha" up to "having been able to hear such a Dharma-gate. This clarifies that this extremely profound realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*) at the pinnacle of the fruit of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* is attained only by the Tathāgata. Although Subhūti has attained the state of an Arhat and possesses merits such as the ten knowledges (*daśa-jñāna*), he had never before heard this extremely profound Dharma-gate; therefore, it is said to be rare.

Regarding "and the superior meaning": because that wisdom is immeasurable and explains a single sūtra in the same manner, it links like a chain to the third section and further constitutes the second rare wonder.
Although it was stated above that Subhūti had never heard this before, it is not yet known for what reason he did not hear it.
It is because this Dharma is the ultimate fruit of the Tathāgata and the supreme meaning of his meritorious virtues; as it is not within the realm of the two vehicles, he did not hear it.
Because it is not heard [by others], it is called "rare"; thus, it is said to accord with the meaning of the preceding section.

Regarding the phrase "that wisdom-vessel is immeasurable," this correctly explains the third part of the sutra: "The Buddha’s teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* is itself not *prajñāpāramitā*. Since this shares the same phrasing as the preceding meaning but differs in its intent, it is treated separately as the third section.
"His wisdom-sea" (彼智𭎋) is, in the Hu language, *prajñāpāramitā*, and in the Han language, "wisdom and the other shore.

"Difficult to measure" means that this shore of wisdom is the ultimate fruition (*phala*) of the Tathāgata; it transcends the realms of calculation and estimation belonging to the lower stages of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Therefore, it is said that "his wisdom-sea is difficult to measure."

The phrase "nor is it the same as other dharmas" explains the sūtra passage beginning with, "If there is another person whose mind of faith is pure, reaching the true mark, the true mark," and so forth.
This sūtra clarifies the principle that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is eternally abiding in the true mark—a reality not elucidated within the teachings of the two vehicles or non-Buddhists.
Since these matters are neither clarified nor given credence within the teachings of the Hīnayāna or non-Buddhist paths, it is said that they are "also not the same as other dharmas.

Regarding the phrase "firmly grasping the profound meaning," this explains the passage in the Sūtra from "World-Honored One, I have now heard... up to "...is most rare. It clarifies why the scriptural text is called "firm and solid": because when this Bodhisattva ascends to the first stage (bhūmi), he attains a true understanding of the principle of the two emptinesses (the emptiness of self and the emptiness of phenomena) before his very eyes; as this understanding cannot be obstructed or destroyed, it is called "firm and solid."
The reason this understanding cannot be obstructed or destroyed is that it penetrates the profound meaning of the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
Regarding the phrase "surpassing other sūtras," this explains the passage in the sūtra beginning with, "For what reason did the Tathāgata say that the foremost pāramitā... and so forth.
"Sūtra" is a term from the Western Regions; in the Han language, it is translated as "root" (mūla).

This indicates that because the principles realized and elucidated by this scripture are supreme, the teaching that expresses them is likewise supreme. Since it surpasses the principles and teachings of the Two Vehicles, it is said to be superior to other sūtras.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation:
to explain the fundamental meaning in its broadest sense, both principle (*li*) and teaching (*jiao*) are present.
This is because the *dharmakāya*, which is the reality devoid of names and marks (*nāmanimitta*), serves as the basis for the verbal teachings of the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
It is also said that because it can give rise to wholesome states of existence, it is called the "root.

The *sūtra*, as the verbal teaching that expresses the Dharma, likewise serves as the root for that which is expressed; because it expresses the Dharmakāya and can give rise to the myriad virtues, it is called the "root."
Because the fundamental principle (li) is superior to the fundamental teaching (jiao), it is said to surpass other sūtras.
Regarding the phrase "Great Cause and Purity," this single sentence provides a general explanation for the preceding seventh and eighth sections of the sūtra.

Regarding the term "Great Cause" (*mahāhetu*): it correctly explains the phrase "the Tathāgata speaks of the foremost *pāramitā*. This clarifies that the principle of the Buddha-nature, which is the unconditioned *dharmakāya* expounded by this sutra, can serve as the direct cause (*samyag-hetu*) for the wondrous fruit of all Buddhas; because it excels the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*), it is called the "Great Cause."

The phrase "and purification" explains the sūtra’s statement, “Those immeasurable Buddhas also speak of the pāramitās,” clarifying that all Buddhas equally teach the names, phrases, and meanings of this Dharma, neither adding to nor subtracting from them.
Because it is spoken in common with others, what is spoken must necessarily accord with principle.
Since there is no commonality that deviates from principle, it is called "pure.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation:

All those immeasurable Buddhas have taught that I realize the fruit of Buddhahood through this principle of the equality of buddha-nature and the intrinsic purity of self-nature; therefore, it is called "pure."

Regarding the phrase "the most excellent merit among merits": because this sutra elucidates such virtues as those mentioned above, the merit of upholding even a single verse surpasses the merit of sacrificing one's body and so forth.

"What is the meaning expressed by these two verses? To demonstrate this, a passage of prose is presented; after each chapter heading within the verses has been explained in sequence, the sutra is then cited to conclude the point, as should be understood.
Among these, if there are points in the text that are obscure, they are explained by skipping ahead.
As for the phrase "For what reason," it introduces a doubt or objection, saying:
"If one who gives up as many lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River gains such immense merit, why does this not equal the merit of upholding even a single verse of this sutra?"

The commentary explains: "Because they abandon the suffering of body and mind when giving up their lives. This clarifies that at the time such a person abandons the body, there is still a mind that grasps at signs; therefore, body and mind suffer affliction, and even the fruit attained later will be suffering.
Because both cause and effect are impure, it is not as good.
To clarify the merit of upholding this sutra: since the cause does not grasp at signs, the resulting fruit is pure; therefore, it surpasses the sacrifice of one's body.

Regarding the phrase "how much more so for the sake of the Dharma," this clarifies that even the renunciation of body and life for the sake of worldly rewards is not comparable to even a small portion of the merit of upholding this sutra; how much less so, then, is the renunciation performed with a mind that grasps at signs for the sake of the Dharma of unsurpassed bodhi, which likewise does not equal the merit of upholding this sutra.

Furthermore, even if those from the first bhūmi upward were to sacrifice their bodies for the sake of the Dharma of bodhi, though they do not grasp at signs, they would still not equal this; hence it is said, "how much more so for sacrificing for the sake of the Dharma."

In the sutra, it is merely stated that the merit of sacrificing one's body does not equal the merit of upholding even a single verse of this sutra; it does not say that the former is inferior because it is performed while grasping at signs (*nimitta*).

Since this meaning is obscure and difficult to understand, the Master of the Treatise explains: "If that sacrifice of the body involves affliction of body and mind, it is because one is grasping at signs. Thus, although one may sacrifice many bodies and lives, it is not equal to upholding the sutra, which is characterized by non-grasping at signs.

Therefore, because he abandons the suffering of body and mind, he mounts upon and emerges from the profound doubts within the sutra; he initiates the application of the Dharma that gives rise to doubt regarding the lower *kṣānti-pāramitā* (perfection of patience), just as it arises [in the subsequent] sections of the sutra without difference.

Regarding the phrase "for this reason" in the fourth chapter, it means that because there is no reality other than the Buddha-dharma, one has never before developed the conviction that [the Buddha-dharma] is unprecedented and has never arisen.

Only within the Mahāyāna teachings of the Buddha is this principle of the true mark of the unconditioned Dharmakāya elucidated; since the teachings of the Hīnayāna do not discern the existence of this principle of the true mark, it is said that this is not the same as other dharmas.
"The Tathāgata spoke this meaning for Subhūti" refers to the Tathāgata’s confirmation of the scriptural passage.
This section of the sutra has not yet been explained from the point where it says, "The Buddha told Subhūti: 'So it is, so it is.'"

From the passage beginning with "Those precious treasures and sandalwood," etc., it generally concludes that the aforementioned comparison of the relinquishing of internal and external wealth is inferior to the merit of upholding this sutra.

The phrase "those precious treasures and sandalwood, etc., do not possess such merit" clarifies that within the two types of giving—internal and external—previously mentioned, there is no merit equal to the eight kinds of merit explained above in the sutra.

Regarding the statement, "Therefore, among those merits, this merit is superior," it is because these eight kinds of qualities do not exist within the internal and external forms of relinquishment (*tyāga*), whereas they are present based on this sūtra.
Therefore, the merit of upholding this sutra surpasses the merit of previously sacrificing one's body, wealth, and so forth.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra*, "From here below, the text of the sutra further serves to eliminate doubts," etc., this indicates that the Master of the Treatise anticipates the thoughts of those who harbor doubts and thereby introduces the subsequent portion of the sutra.
However, as for the application of the teachings that give rise to doubt, they do not differ from those in the sutras;
therefore, they are not explained in detail. *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Five; *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Six.

The passage "Subhūti! As the Tathāgata has spoken of the perfection of patience," translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci in Luoyang during the second year of the Tiān píng era of the Wèi dynasty, is the eighth sūtra within this section on comparative evaluation.

The reason for this [coming] is that the preceding section of the sutra clarifies that giving away as many bodies and lives as there are sands in the Ganges does not equal receiving, upholding, and expounding for others even a single four-line verse of this sutra; its merit is beyond calculation. It should be said that because that person’s initial resolve to give away body and life constitutes a cause of outflow (*sāsrava*), it cannot compare to the merit of upholding the sutra.

The Master of the Treatise should explain it in this way; however, the reason he says, "Because they abandon the suffering of body and life, as well as that of mind," is that he speaks thus in order to give rise to this sūtra, thereby setting forth the intention of the doubter.
What is meant by "one who doubts"?
Such a person relinquishes bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; yet because this is done with a mind that grasps at signs, the cause is impure.
Consequently, the retribution obtained does not transcend the triple world, and for that reason, it is also impure.
Those who obtain little merit—such as the bodhisattvas who, relying on this sutra, practice by relinquishing their bodies and lives—their causes must likewise be impure.
If the cause is impure, the resulting retribution will also be impure, being identical to a fruit of suffering.
It is like the case of the Rishi Kṣāntivādin, who had his body cut to pieces by King Kali; at that time, his body and mind were afflicted with suffering.

Taking this as an objection, the Sūtra replies to clarify that those who previously gave up bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were still ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) prior to the stages of the Path of Preparation (*prayogamārga*).
